## 1 QHSE

Schlumberger QHSE information is accessible via the Schlumberger QHSE Policy and Standards and OFS QHSE Standards Reference Page, InTouchSupport.com content ID 3312250.

This section is a collection of all QHSE Danger, Warning, and Caution notes found throughout this manual. The user must read and understand this entire section before installing or servicing any Artificial Lift equipment. Failure to read and follow QHSE directives is non-compliant with Schlumberger QHSE policy and consequences may include sanctions up to and including termination.

## 1.2.1 Transformer QHSE

The following precautions must be followed. Failure to do so can result in death, serious injury or property damage.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Catastrophic

Potential Loss:

Personnel

Hazard Category:

Electrical

Only trained and qualified personnel should service transformers. Dangerous voltages, pressures and other hazards are present that can result in death or serious injury.

Improperly performed work can result in catastrophic failure or explosion of the transformer.

All sources of power to the transformer must be disconnected.

All sources of power must be locked out and disconnected.

1. Before installing a transformer, be sure the transformer kVA, voltage, winding configuration and other characteristics are suitable for the application. This information is listed on the transformer nameplate.
2. Always lift the transformer by all four tank lifting lugs. Ensure the weight of the transformer does not exceed the capacity of the equipment used to lift it.
3. Do not lay a transformer on its side. Doing so will cause air to be trapped in the windings resulting in the failure of the transformer.
4. Solidly ground the transformer tank before it is energized.
5. Never operate a tap switch or a delta-wye switch while the transformer is energized. The transformer can violently fail.
6. Before connecting any equipment to the secondary of the transformer, measure the secondary voltage to ensure that it is suitable for the equipment to be connected. Since deadly voltages will be present, use suitable measuring equipment, hot gloves and observe all safety practices.
7. When a transformer will be serviced, all sources of power must be disconnected and locked out. The HV (high-voltage) and LV (low-voltage) terminals should be grounded when you are positive there is no voltage

## Private

- present at these terminals. The HV and LV leads should then be disconnected from the transformer bushings. Remove the grounds placed on the terminals prior to reapplying power.
8. The transformer tank cover or inspection access cover must not be removed when conditions exist that may allow moisture, dirt, foreign objects or other contamination to enter the transformer tank. You should remove loose items from your pockets prior to opening the cover. The entry of these materials in the transformer tank may result in the premature failure of the transformer.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Major

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Electrical

Danger

All pressure must be relieved from the transformer tank prior to removing the cover. This can be accomplished by pulling the ring on the pressure relief valve.

The transformer must be resealed so that it is pressure tight. The transformer should be pressure tested to 7 lbf/in 2 (48.3 kPa) with dry nitrogen after it is resealed. Thoroughly inspect the transformer for leaks.

9. If the level of the insulating liquid must be lowered to perform service, under no circumstances should the level of oil be any lower than 3 in (7.6 cm) above the top of the transformer coils. This helps prevent the coils from being exposed to air or moisture.

The liquid removed from the transformer must be stored in clean, tightly sealed barrels. The hoses and pump used to transfer oil must be clean. If there is a doubt, obtain enough extra insulating fluid of the same type as in the transformer to thoroughly flush the hoses and pump. Do not reuse this fluid.

When the transformer is refilled, take care to ensure that air is not forced into the windings of the transformer. Air that enters the coils will cause the transformer to fail.

After the transformer is refilled, wait at least three hours before energizing the transformer. This allows time for air in the insulating fluid to dissipate. Prior to energizing the transformer, all switches should be operated to dislodge any trapped air.

A transformer with a winding voltage that exceeds 5,000 V should be vacuum filled. Contact the transformer manufacture for specific instructions.

## Private

## 1.2.2 QHSE for Extended Runlife Protector

This section reviews the manufacturing and field handling procedures and the potential hazards shop and field service personnel may experience while assembling, testing, installing, pulling and dismantling an Extended Runlife Protector.

## 1.2.2.1 HSE summary

The Extended Runlife Protector has undergone independent HSE reviews by SRC and BPC engineering, manufacturing and QHSE personnel. The findings of the review are

- No hazardous materials such as radioactive or explosive materials are used in any of the Extended Runlife Protectors.
- No electrical components are used in any of the Extended Runlife Protectors.
- No high-pressure components are used in any of the Extended Runlife Protectors.
- Only normal wellbore temperatures are experienced in the Extended Runlife Protectors.
- All of the Extended Runlife Protectors contain hydraulic oil and require normal hygiene precautions.
- The Extended Runlife Protectors can be heavy. Manual lifting is not recommended. Standard lifting methods are provided in the Wellsite Procedures .

## 1.2.2.3 Assembly

## Quality

All material handling shall be performed in accordance with QAD 3054. General assembly shall follow QAI and TI 3019 Assembly Quality Plans.

- Oil All current motor fluid used in protectors is considered nonhazardous.
- Thread lube Current lubrication used on housings and head, base and body threads is food grade and is considered nonhazardous.
- Loctite® Thread locking chemicals are considered nonhazardous.
- Teflon® tape Nonhazardous.
- Bellows The bellows are constructed of Inconel® 625. This material is already common within the system and not considered hazardous.

## Safety

- Handling and lifting During the course of assembly, several awkward and/or heavy components will require lifting. The most notable of these is the housing and the assembled unit. In each case, lifting should be done with a lifting sling and a hoist in accordance with MPI 57101.

## Private

Other heavy items such as the head, base and shaft should be lifted and transported using proper stepping, handling and lifting procedures.

When possible all shop transport of long heavy objects should be done using a housing dolly.

- Making up joints Protector joints are routinely tightened to only 200 ft-lbf. Appropriate documentation and tooling is available and in place.

## 1.2.2.4 Final test

## Quality

Standard protector test parameters and procedures will apply except for the following:

- Valve pressure setting An increase from 10 psi to 20 psi requires a change in the testing procedure for both the individual valve and the top-level assembly after the valve is installed. (See QAI 2013.)
- Metal bellows A pressure and vacuum test needs to be performed on the bellows.

## Safety

- Lifting for test Lifting should be done with a lifting sling and a hoist in accordance with MPI 57101.
- Pinch points When making flange to flange connections, keep fingers clear while mating the units.

## 1.2.2.5 Shipping

## Quality

All material handling should be performed in accordance with QAD 3054. Boxing and/or loading of equipment should be done in accordance with MAT-B019.

## Safety

The protector should not be lifted by hand. Lifting of the unit either for loading in a shipping box or loading onto a truck shall be done with a hoist and sling in accordance with MPI 57101 or with a forklift in accordance with QAD 3054.

## Private

## 1.2.2.6 Equipment installation

## Quality

The unit installation and wellsite procedures will be in accordance with current practices. Unit flange bolts will be tightened in accordance with the torque requirements in ED-119.

## Safety

- Lifting This unit should not be lifted by hand. All lifting clamps shall be used in accordance with FSB 119/rd and lifting should be performed in accordance with procedures.

- Pinch points When making flange-to-flange connections, keep fingers clear while lowering unit.

## 1.2.2.7 Equipment pull

## Quality

Equipment pulls should be performed in accordance with procedures provided in the Wellsite Procedures .

The Extended Runlife Protector shall be dismantled per appropriate manufacturing process instruction (MPI).

## 2.15 Hercules HSM Wellheads

The HSM design permits positioning the cable and pack-off assembly prior to being lowered through the BOP into the body of the tubing head. The pack-off is affected by tightening the six bolts of the assembly around a high strength alloy steel mandrel nipple. Pack-off procedures are provided in the cables section.

## 2.16 Hercules HHS Wellheads

A Hercules HHS wellhead is used when a bolted packing gland is preferred. The packing gland is split to facilitate installation after the tubing and cable have been run. All bodies are full opening, with heat-treated hinged slips for ease of installation and positive alignment.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Hercules HHS wellhead pack-off procedures are provided in the Cable section.

Figure 2-2: Hercules HHS Wellhead Drawing

<!-- image -->

## 3.1 Motor Resistance Tables and Winding Codes

The following tables show motor winding phase-to-phase resistance values at 68 degF (20 degC) and winding codes for various motors. Winding codes are not available for all listed motors. In some cases, different motors will have the same winding code indicating the stator winding as being the same, however, the motor's insulation system, bearings and mechanical configuration are different.

## 3.3 Motor and Cable Resistance Calculation

Motor and cable resistance tables and the temperature multiplier factors for increasing temperatures are used to determine if the phase-to-phase resistance measurements of the downhole system are reasonable. The resistance measurement can also be useful for isolating the location of a fault.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Resistance values for the motor and cable are provided in the Motor Resistance Tables and Winding Codes and Cable Resistance sections. Temperature multiplier values are provided in the Cable Resistance section.

<!-- image -->

## Note

For calculation purposes, the cable length doubles. The resistance value is the resistance down the cable, through the motor and back up the cable to the meter.

This is the calculated resistance. In practical application, measuring instruments are not capable of measurements to this accuracy, and splices may contribute to additional resistance. These calculations are used as a guideline. A resistance measurement considerably higher or lower than the calculated resistance indicates a potential problem. Resistance measurement interpretation is a function of experience and should be recorded for each installation.

Unbalanced phase-to-phase measurements indicate a problem and in the majority of cases are indicative of a motor problem.

One of the most important uses of the motor resistance tables is to ensure that the motor voltage listed on the motor nameplate is correct. Never assume the nameplate data is correct. Measure the motor phase-to-phase resistance and compare the measurement to data provided in the Motor Resistance Tables and Winding Codes section before installation of a unit.

Equation 3-1 is used to calculate the total phase-to-phase resistance.

## Equation 3-1:

total phase-to-phase resistance = motor resistance + (cable resistance × [cable length × 2] × temperature multiplier)

<!-- image -->

## Example

| Example Data   | Example Data                          |
|----------------|---------------------------------------|
| motor          | 456 series, 60 HP, 970 V, 39 A        |
| cable          | #4 copper conductor, 6000 ft (1829 m) |
| temperature    | 160 degF (70 degC)                    |

Using Equation 3-1 -

total phase-to-phase resistance = 0.83 + (0.258 ohms x 12 x 1.21) = 4.576 ohms

MLE temperature rating: An MLE includes the flat cable length and the pothead that fits into the motor head. Typically the flat cable has a higher temperature rating than the pothead connection itself.

The attached spreadsheet (under InTouch Content ID 3016052) calculates the conductor temperature of the most common REDA cables, based on cable type, current, and downhole temperature. Note that for MLE's included in the spreadsheet, the calculation result DOES NOT include the pothead limitation. Be aware that this can be misleading.

The MLE temperature rating of the combined flat cable and pothead is based on the weaker component (usually pothead) and is found under the attributes in OneCAT details.

The use of the attached spreadsheet (under InTouch Content ID 3016052) is straight forward when checking power cable operating temperature under certain well conditions against published cable temperature rating. The rating is built into the spreadsheet.

However, to check the temperature limit of an MLE (combined flat cable and pothead) using the attached spreadsheet, make sure you do the following:

## Private

1. Find the temperature rating of the MLE through OneCAT or GeMS.
2. Use the attached spreadsheet (InTouch Content ID 3016052) to calculate operating temperature (after entering your application data)
3. Compare the calculated operating temperature of selected cable to MLE rating determined in step -1- above. Calculated operating temperature must be below the MLE temperature rating for acceptable application.

DesignPro, in its current version (Jan 08) does not check selected MLE's against temperature rating. MLE rating check has to be done by the AE separately using the described procedure, above.

Future versions of DesignPro will include MLE rating calculation and comparison. This will be announced separately at the time of new version release.

## 3.4.1 Voltage Drop Calculation

Voltage drop is sometimes calculated using a temperature multiplier. This is not the best method because the voltage loss in the cable is not in phase with the voltage drop in the motor, but rather the current. To get the true voltage drop in the cable requires a power factor calculation that shows the voltage drop to be less than what would be predicted by making a resistance calculation. Ignoring the temperature multiplier results in a lower voltage drop calculation based on resistance only so this tends to offset the effect. Using a temperature multiplier and not accounting for power factor will result in an over-prediction of voltage loss and may provide more voltage at the motor than expected.

Cable voltage drop should be calculated using Equation 3-3 and Figure 3-1.

## Equation 3-3:

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

<!-- image -->

Figure 3-1: Cable voltage drop

<!-- image -->

## Note

A horizontal line at 30 V/1000 ft is shown on Figure 3-1. Typically, voltage drops in excess of this amount will not be economical due to the loss in efficiency.

<!-- image -->

## Example

Calculate the cable voltage drop with a motor rated a 1130 V and 20 A with 7200 ft of #4 AWG copper cable in a well at 185 degF (85 degC).

Find the motor nameplate amperage on the X axis in the Figure 3-1. Move vertically to the diagonal cable size line. Move horizontally to the left to find the voltage drop per 1000 feet on the Y axis.

Using Equation 3-3, the cable voltage drop = (7200 + 100) (9)/1000 = 66 V.

## 3.6 Voltage/Current Relationship of Motors

When designing or troubleshooting installations, it is useful to understand the voltage/current relationship of motors. This is especially true for deep wells. The voltage drop on initial startup should not be so great as to prevent the unit from starting. It is possible for a unit to start initially with no problems, then at a later time to encounter startup problems due to deposition buildup or wear in the unit.

The minimum voltage required to start a unit can vary due to different operating conditions. Schlumberger submersible motors require 2.5 to 3 times nameplate current or 50 to 55% of nameplate voltage at the terminals to start.

## 3.6.1 Voltage/Current Relationship

The following assumptions can be used to associate nameplate voltage to nameplate current.

- 100% nameplate volts gives 5 times nameplate current
- 80% nameplate volts gives 4 times nameplate current
- 60% nameplate volts gives 3 times nameplate current
- 40% nameplate volts gives 2 times nameplate current

## 3.6.2 Voltage Comparison Calculation

The following example is provided as a troubleshooting aid for analyzing applications. When sizing units for deep applications, the starting voltage percentage of the selected motor should be considered.

The calculations involved are based on assumptions and the assumptions are acceptable for practical use. The calculations are not intended to be mathematically exact, but an approximation that can be used.

The calculations and method are shown for the selection of the proper voltage motor for an application. This comparison of two motors of the same horsepower but different voltages illustrates how the available starting voltage at each motor can vary.

## Private

| Example Example Data   | Example Example Data    |
|------------------------|-------------------------|
| depth                  | 8,000 ft of 4 AWG cable |
| size of motor required | 70 HP                   |
| casing size            | 5.5 in, 17 lbm/ft       |

## 3.6.2.1 Trial and Error Calculation Method

We find there are two motors available in the 456-series 70 HP size (980 V, 45 A and 1170 V, 38 A).

For our example determine the estimated starting voltage that will be present at the motor for the 980 V, 45 A motor.

1. The 4 AWG cable has 25 V/1000 ft of cable voltage loss (Figure 3-1) or a total of 200 V drop in the cable at motor nameplate amps. The required surface voltage would be 980 + 200 = 1180 V.
2. Determine the percentage of full-load voltage that this motor will start at. This is done by using a 'rule of thumb' and by trial and error. The percentage can be arrived at quickly with experience.
- a. Assume 80% voltage; the current is 4 times nameplate. The cable voltage drop is 4 x 200 V or 800 V. 1180 V - 800 V = 380 V. This is not 80%.
- b. Assume 60% voltage; the current is 3 times 200 V or 600 V. 1180 V 600 V = 580 V. This is not 60%. 580 V divided by 980 V is 49%; this is near percentage.
- c. Assume 50% voltage; the current is 2.5 times 200 V or 500 V. 1180 V 500 V = 680 V. 680 V ÷ 980 V = 58%. (Note: The percentage is between 50% and 60%)
- d. Assume 55% voltage; the current is 2.75 times 200 V or 550 V. 1180 V - 550 V = 630 V. 630 V ÷ 980 V = 54%. The proper percentage that agrees with the current on start-up is 54%. This motor is marginal for this application.

Determine the estimated starting voltage that will be present at the motor for the 1170 V, 38 A unit.

## Private

1. The 4 AWG cable has a voltage drop of 20 V/1000 ft (Figure 3-1) or 160 V drop in the cable at motor nameplate amps.
2. The required surface voltage is 1170 V + 160 V = 1330 V.
- a. Assume 80% voltage or 4 times nameplate current. The cable voltage drop is 4 x 160 V or 640 V. 1330 V - 640 V = 690 V. This is not 80%.
- b. Assume 65% voltage or 3.25 times nameplate current. The cable voltage drop is 3.25 x 160 V or 520 V. 1330 V - 520 V = 810 V. 810 V ÷ 1330 V equals 61%, not 65%. The voltage percentage is approximately 63%. The 63% is much better (than the 980 V, 45 A motor) and this motor should have no start-up problems during its operation.

## 3.7 60 Hz Versus 50 Hz Operation

A Schlumberger submersible motor rotates at a nominal speed of 3500 rpm at 60 Hz. The motor rotates at 2915 rpm at 50 Hz. For each individual pump series, the diameter of the stages cannot be changed so the only variables available to modify performance within a series are the different types of stages, the number of stages and the speed they rotate. The rotational speed can only be changed by varying the frequency. When this speed change occurs, it changes the pump operation according to mathematical relationships known as affinity laws.

## Affinity laws for a speed change

<!-- image -->

## Note

These affinity laws apply only to pump behavior, not to well or system performance.

50 Hz capacity flow = 50÷60 x 60 Hz flow = 0.833 x 60 Hz flow

50 Hz head = (50÷60) 2 x 60 Hz head = 0.694 x 60 Hz head

50 Hz hp pump load = (50÷60) 3 x 60 Hz hp load = 0.579 x 60 Hz hp pump load

50 Hz motor hp load = 50÷60 x 60 Hz hp rating = 0.833 x 60 Hz hp rating

50 Hz motor voltage = 50÷60 x 60 Hz motor volts = 0.833 x 60 Hz motor volts

50 Hz motor amps = same as 60 Hz motor amps

50 Hz pump efficiency = same as 60 Hz pump efficiency

## 3.11 Total Dynamic Head

One stage in a pump will move fluid a certain distance at a given flow rate. Numerous stages are required to pump fluid longer distances or at higher pressures. This total distance is expressed in head feet and is called total dynamic head (TDH). The TDH consists of three components

- vertical lift
- friction loss
- tubing discharge pressure.

## 3.11.1 Vertical Lift

Vertical lift is the distance from the producing fluid level to the surface. The fluid level above the pump can be obtained by either a 'fluid shot' or, if a downhole monitoring instrument is installed, the static bottomhole pressure can be converted to head feet using Equation 3-5.

| sg     | fluid specific gravity               |

## 3.11.2 Friction Loss

Additional pressure is required from the pump to overcome the friction losses caused by the fluid flowing inside the tubing. Figure 3-5 shows the friction loss (water) due to flow in various pipe diameters.

## 3.11.4 Total Dynamic Head Calculation

The TDH at a specific flow rate must be calculated to determine the number of stages required in a pump. The TDH can be calculated using Equation 3-7.

## Equation 3-7:

TDH = vertical lift + fricti on loss + tubing discharge head

vertical lift = pump setting depth - fluid level above the pump

2. Calculate friction loss.

friction loss = friction loss per 1000 ft x tubing length

friction loss =(36/1000) x 4800 ft = 173 ft

3. Calculate tubing discharge head.

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

tubing discharge head =(200 x 2.31) ÷ 0.93 = 497 ft

4. Calculate total dynamic head.

Using the equation for calculating total dynamic head, TDH = 4200 ft + 173 ft + 497 ft = 4870 ft

The total dynamic head in this example is 4870 ft.

Add the total head loss required for the pump to overcome to the calculated total dynamic head and calculate the new number of stages and motor horsepower required. If the new pump requires a higher horsepower and longer motor, the procedure for calculating head loss across the motor should be repeated.

## 3.11.6 Fluid Time-To-Surface after Startup

The following procedure can be used to estimate the time required for fluid to reach the surface after startup. Two examples are provided. Both examples assume the pump is operating at B.E.P. (in the middle of the performance curve).

- In Example 1, the fluid level is unknown so the tubing length is used as a worst-case scenario.
- In Example 2, the static bottomhole pressure ( p ws ) is known so the fluid level can be calculated. This will give a more accurate estimation of fluid time-to-surface.

tubing fill = bbl/1000 ft x tubing length/1000

pump flow rate (bbl/min) = pump flow rate (bbl/d) ÷ 1440

pump flow rate (bbl/min) = 1750 ÷ 1440 = 1.215 bbl/min

3. Calculate the time to pump the fluid to the surface.

fluid time to surface = tubing fill (bbl) ÷ pump flow rate (bbl/min)

## 3.12 Calculation of Protector Thrust Loads

The following example shows how to determine the thrust load transferred to the protector thrust bearing when floater constructed pumps are used.

| protector                       | 540-series LSL                  |
| BHST                            | 200 degF                        |
| fluid sg                        | 0.95                            |

## 1. Calculate the total shutoff head.

total shutoff head = shutoff head per stage x number of stages

total shutoff head = 63.5 ft x 154

total shutoff head = 9779 ft

<!-- image -->

## Note

Shutoff head per stage data is provided in the Pump Stage Information section.

## 2. Calculate the shutoff pressure.

shutoff pressure = (total shutoff head x fluid specific gravity) ÷ 2.31

shutoff pressure = (9779 ft x 0.95) ÷ 2.31

shutoff pressure = 4022 lbf/in 2

<!-- image -->

## Note

On all applications where the clearance is very close, a full gauge tool (slightly larger than equipment OD) should be run prior to the installation of equipment. This is to ensure that there are no burrs or tight spots in the wellbore. This operation will prevent many expensive mistakes when installing a submergible system in tight or heavy-wall casing.

## Drift Diameter

The drift diameter is the minimum ID that the supplier (mill) must provide for API standard casing, drill pipe and tubing. The pipe ID should never be less than drift diameter if there is no casing damage and in many cases will be larger than drift. This is why it is important to run a gauge before installing equipment. Drift diameter standards (API) for casing are shown in Table 3-29.

Table 3-29: Drift Diameter Standards for Casing

| Casing Size                                | Drift Diameter                    |
|--------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| up to 8-5/8 in OD inclusive                | 1/8 in smaller than tabulated ID  |
| over 8-5/8 in OD to 13-3/8 in OD inclusive | 5/32 in smaller than tabulated ID |
| over 13-3/8 in OD                          | 3/16 in smaller than tabulated ID |

The thickness of flat cable can vary from a maximum to a minimum due to manufacturing tolerances. The maximum thickness for 6 AWG 3kV high-temperature flat cable is 0.55 in. The maximum thickness value should be used when calculating the maximum dimension of equipment. Cable dimensions and tolerances are provided in the Cable Specifications section in the Cables chapter.

Using the Equation 3-9 -

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

pump clearance on flat cable side = 2.506 - 2 - 0.55 - 0.030 + 0.226

This maximum dimension (clearance) takes into consideration the entire unit with the centerline dimensions of both pump and motor. This indicates the unit will go into the wellbore.

The actual clearance at the pump and protector is (5.012-in pipe ID) - (4.00-in pump OD + 0.55-in flat cable + .030-in band) = 0.432 in.

If flat guards are used, the OD is increased by approximately 0.16 in.

The OD at flanges and the motor head is reduced by passing flat through a slot cut out in equipment.

## 3.14.1 Ordering

Because the selected oil is application dependant, the type of oil must be specified when placing an order. If the type of oil is not specified when the order is placed, motors and protectors will be shipped with the oil shown in Table 3-31.

Table 3-31: Standard Oil Types

| Motors                 | Protectors            | Oil Type   |
|------------------------|-----------------------|------------|
| 562-series and Hotline | 540-series and larger | Reda No. 5 |
| all others             | all others            | Reda No. 2 |

## 3.14.2 Oil Compatibility

All Schlumberger motor or protector oils are compatible and may be mixed without chemical degradation. The resultant viscosity will be approximately equal to the proportional volume mix. Oils obtained from other sources (not Schlumberger approved) may not be compatible with the internal components of submergible equipment.

It is permissible to drain and refill motors, protectors and any oil-filled motor accessories with a different Schlumberger oil. Standard factory filling instructions and field service procedures apply.

For cold climate installations, the oil and/or the equipment may require heating to facilitate servicing.

## 3.14.3 Other considerations

Numerous commercial issues (for example, customer requirements for specific oils) may influence the selection of motor or protector oils. Contact InTouchSupport.com to confirm that a specific oil is appropriate for use in Schlumberger motors, protectors and any oil-filled motor accessories.

## 3.15 Dielectric Strength Test for Oil

The following procedure can be used to test the dielectric strength of motor oil and transformer oil. The applicable document is ASTM D877.

## 3.15.1 Required Equipment

Equipment required to perform a dielectric test is

- Appropriate personal protective equipment.
- 1000 ml (1 qt) clean, dry containers
- Biddle/Foster Model OTS 60 auto, (p/n 99955-7) tester. The Biddle/Foster Model OTS 60 is the preferred equipment. If unavailable, a Hipotronics Model CC 60A, (p/n 56411-2) may be used. (A timer must be used with the Hipotronics tester.)
- Reda No. 2 oil

<!-- image -->

All testing equipment must be kept clean and dry at all times.

## 3.15.2 Equipment Preparation

1. Check the test cup to ensure the gap setting between the electrodes is correct. A 0.100 in (+0.0005 in) gauge is supplied with the equipment.
2. Rinse the test cup with SC 140 solvent (p/n 73540-7) to remove any particulates.
3. Discard the solvent in the cup. Refill the cup with clean Reda No. 2 oil. Check the dielectric strength of the oil. A minimum dielectric strength of 25 kV must be achieved before the cup is ready for use. This may require that the cup be rinsed and filled several times with Reda No. 2 oil.

4.

<!-- image -->

This procedure prepares the Biddle tester.

- a. Open the test chamber cover by turning the interlock knob ¼ turn counterclockwise.
- b. Place the test cup in the chamber so that the ends of the electrode supports rest on the cradle terminals at the top of the support horn.
- c. Close the chamber door and turn the interlock knob clockwise.
- d. Turn the power supply on and set the selector switch to Manual .

## Private

5.

- e. Press the Start Test button.
- f. Press and hold the Raise button until either the sample breaks down or the display shows 60 kV.
- g. Upon test completion, press the Trip button to reset the tester.

<!-- image -->

## Note

This procedure prepares the Hipotronics tester.

- a. Place the test cup in the holder.
- b. Close the door and turn the power switch on.
- c. Set the rate of rise to 3000 V/sec.
- d. Press the Start button.
- e. Upon test completion, press the Reset button.

## 3.15.3 Testing the Oil Sample

1. Carefully fill a 1000 ml (or 1 qt) container with the oil to be tested. If testing motor oil, sample the oil from the bottom of the motor.
2. Fill the clean test cup approximately one-third full with sample oil.
3. Gently swirl the cup so that the electrodes and surface area of the cup are well coated with oil. Discard the oil and refill the cup with sample oil. The sample of oil is now ready for testing.

4.

<!-- image -->

## Note

This procedure uses the Biddle tester.

- a. Open the test chamber cover by turning the interlock knob ¼ turn counterclockwise.
- b. Place the test cup in the chamber so that the ends of the electrode supports rest on the cradle terminals at the top of the support horn.
- c. Close the chamber door and turn the interlock knob clockwise.
- d. Turn on the power.
- e. Set the selector switch to the ASTM D 877 test method.

## Private

5.

- f. Press the Start Test button.
- g. The Biddle tester will automatically finish the test procedure. After a two-minute and 20-second initial delay, the sample will be tested five times with one minute intervals between tests. After the tests are complete, the average of the five breakdown voltages will be displayed. Record this average value. Press the Recall button and record the five individual test values.

<!-- image -->

## Note

This procedure uses the Hipotronics tester.

- a. Set the rate of rise to 3000 V/sec.
- b. Place the test cup in the holder.
- c. Close the door and turn the power switch on.
- d. Using a timer, begin an initial time delay of 2 to 3 minutes.
- e. Press the Start button and record the dielectric strength.
- f. Press the Reset button and wait one minute before retesting the sample.
- g. A total of five tests values, at one-minute intervals, should be performed. Record the value from each test.

## 3.15.4 Interpretation of Results

ASTM D 877 requires that the five values be evaluated statistically in the following manner.

(high value - low value) multiplied by 3 = x

If x is lower than the second lowest value, then the average of the five values is statistically acceptable. The average of the values will be recorded as the final test result.

<!-- image -->

## Example

The five recorded values are 32, 30, 28, 34 and 31.

(34 - 28) multiplied by 3 = 18

Since 18 is less than the second lowest value (30), these five results are statistically acceptable. The average breakdown strength of 31 kV is the final test result.

If x is greater than the second lowest value, the five values are not statistically acceptable. For example, the five recorded values are 14, 25, 26, 27 and 27. (27 - 14) multiplied by 3 = 39

Since 39 is greater than the second lowest value (25), the five values are not statistically acceptable. At this point the oil in the test cup would be discarded. The cup would then be refilled with sample oil, and tested using the procedure appropriate to the tester. Assume the second test generated the following values; 27, 33, 35, 25 and 27. The average of the ten values (26.6 kV) would be recorded as the final test result.

## 3.15.5 Acceptance/Rejection Criteria for Motors

- The average dielectric strength of the oil must be greater than or equal to 15 kV.
- The visual appearance of the oil is indicative of the cleanliness, or quality workmanship, of the finished motor. The presence of metal particles and excessive discoloration and clarity of the oil will be considered as cause for rejection.
- The oil sample must pass both the dielectric strength test and visual appearance for the motor to be acceptable.

## 3.18 Stator Codes

On the motor housing there is a field code number stenciled on the stator that provides specific information regarding the internal construction of the stator. This reference information is intended for use by field service and production personnel to verify the stator construction and winding type.

<!-- image -->

## Example

An example stenciled code is shown in Figure 3-7

Figure 3-7: Example stenciled field code on a stator

<!-- image -->

- The first position (alpha) indicates the housing type. The possible types are
- C - carbon steel
- F - ferric steel
- The second position (alpha or numeric) indicates the stator type as indicated by the part number description. Examples are 62 type, 87 type, 90 type, 91 type, 92 type and 93 type. This can also be two letters such as HX, PX, SX, MX.
- The third position (numeric) indicates the number of rotor positions inside the stator.
- The fourth position (numeric) indicates the voltage the part number specifies for the stator (three digits). Examples: 1350 V = 135, 900 V = 90.
- The fifth position (numeric) indicates the lamination type. The standard closed slot lamination is a 4.

## 4 Wellsite Procedures

## 4.1 Transport and Handling

<!-- image -->

## Note

Always ship SPS equipment with the correct shipping caps in place, do not ship pieces of equipment bolted together.

## 4.1.1 Equipment Handling

Equipment transport and handling are important factors that influence the success of submergible operations. The nature of artificial lift equipment requires special handling procedures; procedures not normally used when handling and transporting many other types of pumping systems. The physical length of downhole components relative to their diameters can be large, especially for motors and pumps. For example, a 30-ft motor, 5.5 inches in diameter will deflect considerably if not transported and lifted properly. During the manufacturing process, there is considerable effort made to ensure that the stator is straight to within +/-0.002 in/ft. Allowing the motor to deflect excessively can result in catastrophic failure. For this reason, all downhole components should be transported in steel shipping boxes.

There are three areas of consideration; transportation, handling and placement. Although placement may not seem important, it has surprising influence on the entire process. Proper placement the first time eliminates the need for additional handling and reduces the risk of equipment damage.

## 4.1.2 Use of Steel Shipping Boxes

Handling Steel Shipping Boxes

## Private

Steel shipping boxes should be used to transport motors, protectors, pumps, intakes, gas separators and pressure sensing instruments. These boxes are available in various lengths from 5.5 ft to 36.5 ft and various diameters from 6 to 12 inches (nominal diameter of component being shipped). One end of each box is colored to identify the head end of the equipment; the end that points towards the wellhead. Although metal shipping boxes provide some protection during handling and transport, they do not eliminate the need for special care and attention for downhole equipment.

Before equipment leaves the manufacturing facility, it is packed in the metal shipping box with rubber inserts to help absorb vibration and shock. At no time should the boxes be dragged, dropped or bounced to facilitate movement. In general, all equipment, (either in or out of shipping boxes) must be handled using a spreader bar or a lifting clamp. Never use a single winch line attached to the center of a component to lift it. Component damage, and serious personal injury can occur. Always use a spreader bar with chains or slings attached ¼ of the distance from each end. The sole use of a chain bridle or sling is not recommended.

A fork lift can be used but only when properly distributed support can be given to the box. For long boxes, the use of a fork lift may not be possible. In cases where a crane is being used, ensure that the box is supported securely in at least two places, approximately ¼ of the distance from each end.

Never use the shipping box handles for support. Handles are only designed to open, close and secure the box. They are not designed to support the weight of the box and the equipment inside. The use of a crane with a spreader bar and secured slings threaded through the handles and underneath the box is allowed only if the positions of the handles correspond with the ¼ length requirement. By threading through the handles and underneath the box, the handles are not supporting the weight of the box and the equipment inside it.

Shipping box lifting equipment and dimensions are shown in Figure 4-1.

Figure 4-1: Lifting shipping boxes

<!-- image -->

## Opening and Closing Steel Shipping Boxes

Steel shipping boxes should be opened and closed with a special tool. The tool has been developed to aid field service personnel in opening and closing the cover of a steel shipping box where mechanized lifting equipment is unavailable. The tool is suitable for all boxes including the H box design. When opening or closing a long and heavy box, two field service personnel located at both ends of the box should open and close the box using a coordinated sequence of movement.

The tool consists of two parts; the head (p/n 2010739) and extension bar (p/n 2010915).

Warning

If a substitute extension bar is used, the front-end diameter must not be greater than 0.75 in. The extension bar and opener head must maintain a loose engagement to avoid personal injury during use.

## Steel Shipping Box Opening Procedure

1. Engage the opener head on the shipping box handle.

2. Insert the extension bar into the opener head.
3. Swing the shipping box cover open. As the shipping box cover is swinging open, the extension bar will disengage from the opener head. Do not to drop the extension bar.

2. Insert the extension bar into the opener head.
3. As the shipping box cover is swinging over its center of gravity, the cover will close and disengage the opener head that will then drop off of the extension bar. Do not to drop the extension bar.

## Placing Equipment in Steel Shipping Boxes

Equipment should be placed in a steel shipping box with the top of equipment at the painted end of the box. Ensure shipping caps are installed before the equipment is placed in the box.

When loading equipment into a shipping box, be sure to use the correct two-piece rubber shipping blocks. Two blocks are used per box. Position the bottom half of each block at a distance equal to ¼ the component length from each end of the box.

<!-- image -->

## Example

If a component is 28 ft long, the blocks would be placed 7 ft from the ends of each unit, leaving 14 ft of the component unsupported in the center. Do not use an additional block to support the middle of the unit.

Place the unit inside the box on the shipping blocks using an overhead hoist and a spreader bar. Center the unit as it is being lowered, leaving equal gap distances at each end between the unit and the shipping box. Use two, cut-to-length wooden blocks to fill these gaps between the unit and the shipping box at each end. Leave 0.125-inch clearance for expansion. Place the top half of the shipping blocks in the box directly above the bottom half. Carefully secure the box.

## Shipping Box Transport

Shipping boxes should be placed on 4-inch by 4-inch wooden planks, 3 feet from each end and in the middle when being placed on a truck or on the ground. If the boxes will be stacked, planks should be placed between each layer. No more than one box should be hoisted in a single lift. When placed on a truck,

## Private

no part of the box should extend beyond the end of the truck. Shipping boxes should be securely strapped to the deck of the truck at the location of the planks; shipping boxes should never move while being transported.

## 4.1.3 Cable

## Handling

Power cable is typically shipped on large reels. The purpose of the reel is to allow easy cable feed into and out of the well and to protect the cable during transport and handling.

## Transport

Cable should always be transported on cable reels. In the event that a power cable on a reel is being transported with the spliced flat cable extension on it, independently secure the extension and the power cable. A crane and spreader bar are recommended to lift cable reels. A forklift may be used. If a forklift is used, lift the reel through the spokes from the side, never against the cable. Reels should be secured to the truck when transported. Never allow the reel of cable to roll against objects that might crush or damage the cable or reel.

## Placement

A section of heavy-walled pipe should be inserted through the reel to serve as an axle. Lift with a spreader bar attached to the axle. A short spacer should be placed between the reel and the stand on each side. (A thread protector, collar, Vic clamp or hammer union wing are some examples.) The cable must feed off to the wellhead from the top of the reel. Never handle a reel of cable by making a sling of wire line or chains that touch the cable. Protect the cable from being smashed or cut. The cable reel should be placed 75 to 100 feet from the wellhead and in the rig operator's direct line of sight.

<!-- image -->

## Note

In an offshore environment this may not be feasible, however the spool should be placed as far back as possible.

On semi-submergible platforms or other floating rigs, two wheel and fork assemblies are used. This configuration is used to prevent the cable from being stretched and damaged when the rig compensators are in operation.

Cable reel lifting equipment is shown in Figure 4-2.

## Private

Figure 4-2: Cable reel lifting

<!-- image -->

A clear path should be provided for the cable to prevent it from being hooked or damaged during installation. Wooden planks should be used to keep the cable off the ground, preventing it from picking up any debris which may contaminate the well.

## Cable Sheave Assembly

The cable sheave should be hung in the derrick, inline between the cable reel and wellhead and aligned with the wellhead to avoid any rubbing against tubing support.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Serious

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Machinery equipment hand tools

Warning

Ensure the cable sheave is attached securely with a chain and has a cable or chain safety backup.

The sheave should be no more than 30 feet above the ground in order to permit flexibility and avoid shock against the cable during running and pulling operations. During installation, the sheave should be supported approximately 10 feet above the ground to feed the flat cable extension (FCE) and splice

## Private

through. After the FCE splice has been supported by cable bands, the sheave can be raised to the operational height of 30 feet. This procedure reduces stress on the pothead connection and FCE splice.

Cable running equipment and dimensions are shown in Figure 4-3. The cable must be supported at point B during installation and pulling operations. The cable weight of distance A to B should not exceed 150 lbm.

The switchboard should be located approximately 50 to 100 feet from the well and close to the transformer bank or generator.

## 4.1.5 Transformer or Generator

Transformers are provided with lifting hooks for loading, unloading and handling. A spreader bar and cables should be used to maintain the transformer in a vertical position to avoid damage. Always ensure the transformer cover is bolted in place before moving the transformer.

The transformer should be located approximately 50 to 100 feet from the well and close to the switchboard. The location of power lines, the access road and working clearance around the well should be considered when locating the surface electrical equipment.

## 4.1.6 Junction Box

The junction box is used for connecting the power cable and venting gas (in case gas has migrated up the power cable) between the well and switchboard. It should be in line with the switchboard if possible, and at a distance of approximately 25 feet (minimum 15 feet) from the well to permit a working area for the service rig. ## 4.1.7 Damaged Equipment

If a unit is suspected of being damaged or mistreated while being handled or transported, notify the responsible field service representative. The equipment will be inspected and repaired if necessary before it is placed in service. Pulling operations are time consuming, expensive and can be avoided.

## 4.2 Job Preparation

Prior to a new installation, check the condition of the casing. Run a gauge tool slightly larger than the OD of the equipment to ensure adequate clearance. If there was difficulty in pulling the pump from an existing well, investigate and determine the cause prior to running a new unit. Cable damage, missing bands, or tight spots may warrant the use of a scraper to clean the wellbore and eliminate potential running problems.

## 4.2.1 Checking Equipment

Check all materials and equipment to determine if everything necessary for installation is on location. This should be done immediately upon arrival at the wellsite. Check against the shipping order, quote and workover schedule in the following sequence.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Refer to InTouch content ID 5029387 for ESP Equipment Check lists

1. Remove box covers and record all information directly from nameplates on motors, pumps, gas separator, protector, flat cable extension, well cable, and switchboard.
2. Ensure that all other completion accessories are available at the wellsite and are functional.

## Private

3. Ensure that backup equipment (when required) is at the wellsite and is functional.
4. Ensure that all installation consumables are available at the wellsite and are serviceable.
5. Ensure that all installation tooling is available at the wellsite and is functional.
6. Note the type of tubing support and confirm the proper size of casing, tubing, and cable pack-off.
7. Check the switchboard for proper fuses, potential transformer setup and CT ratio.
8. Ensure each coupling to verify that it is the correct size.
9. In the case of tandem pumps, determine which pump needs to be picked up and installed first.

<!-- image -->

## Note

When installing tandem pumps ensure that the pump with a high-strength shaft (designated HSS on the nameplate) is installed closest to the motor.

10. Ensure the flat cable is the proper length and series for the motor.
11. Check the design of pump (head) against setting depth, rate, etc.
12. Check the power bank transformers for correct primary and secondary voltage ratings and kVA rating.

## 4.2.2 Preventing Galling of Flange Bolts

Installing Monel bolts in carbon steel heads can result in galling of the bolt and flange bolt hole threads. This can cause the bolt to bind in the bolt hole. The different hardnesses of the dissimilar materials are the root cause of this type of incident. If this happens, it may not be possible to back the bolt out to chase the threads with a thread tap. Often, the bolt breaks off in the flange. Application of an anti-seize compound (p/n 0849737) to Monel bolts will greatly reduce the incidence of galling and bolt breakage when bolts are threaded into carbon steel heads. Anti-seize compound should also be applied to carbon steel or Monel bolts being threaded into Redalloy heads.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Some submersible pump components such as VGSA gas separators and ARS/DRS/GRS gas separators include Redalloy heads in the standard product. The Redalloy material may not be noted on the nameplate.

## Private

The use of an air-operated tool to run bolts into dissimilar head material will greatly increase the likelihood of galling, even if an anti-seize compound is used.

If a bolt coated with anti-seize compound begins to bind while being threaded into the bolt hole, stop threading the bolt. Binding can occur with even miniscule debris in the bolt hole. Failure to stop threading the bolt into the bolt hole and continuing to force the bolt into the bolt hole will almost certainly result in bolt breakage and lost rig time. Slowly remove the bolt from the bolt hole and carefully chase the flange bolt hole threads with a thread tap. Clean any debris from the threads of the bolt. Reapply the anti-seize compound and carefully try again.

## 4.2.3 Motor Testing

## Phase-To-Phase Measurements

The integrity of the motor's insulation should be tested prior to installation. Phase-to-phase measurements can be taken most accurately using a digital multimeter. Record the measurements and compare them to the data shown in the motor resistance tables in the Technical and Engineering Information chapter. Measurements must be balanced within 2% and the value cannot be less or more than 10% of the published value. Percentage unbalance can be calculated using Equation 4-1.

## Equation 4-1:

% Unbalance = Maximum Deviation from Average Resistance X 100 Average Resistance

If the motor is an upper tandem or center tandem, a wye or star connection is required to take the measurements. Remove the lower shipping cap and interconnect all three male terminals using three jumper wires. The phase-to-phase measurements can now be taken from the top of the motor

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Major

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Electrical

Danger

Always perform a final visual inspection of the motor terminals for proper spacing in the slot and check for phase resistance after assembling the UMB. Refer to Figure 4-6. For further details refer to InTouch Content ID 3769116.

## Private

Figure 4-6: Base Terminals

<!-- image -->

## Phase-To-Ground Measurements

The megger is used to check the motor insulation resistance to ground. The meter test lead marked earth is clipped onto a bolt head where a good ground can be established. The other probe lead is connected to each phase individually. Each phase on a new motor must measure a minimum of 1500 megohms to ground.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Major

Potential Loss:

Personnel

Hazard Category:

Fire flammable

Never use a megger on the rig floor. A spark generated by a megger can ignite gasses emitted from the wellhead. Complete this test while the motor is in the shipping box. Additional megger tests can be completed safely at the cable reel once the cable is connected to the motor.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Major

Potential Loss:

Personnel

Hazard Category:

Electrical

Always discharge each winding after the megger test. The residual high-voltage charge can shock personnel and/or damage other meters.

## Private

Upper tandem motors require removal of the pothole cover. Each lead to ground is megged individually prior to being picked up.

Center tandem motors should be checked prior to being picked up. Each lead must be checked unless the center tandem motor has a universal base installed. If a center tandem motor has a U base or a PSI monitoring tool installed, megging a single lead is megging all three coils since the Y connection is closed.

Lower tandem motors are megger tested in the same manner as single-section motors and center tandem motors with the Y closed.

## 4.2.4 Cable Testing

Schlumberger cable is thoroughly tested before shipping. Ensure that no damage has occurred during transit.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Light

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Electrical

Caution

Any cable damage should be located and repaired prior to installation. Never take a chance that unrepaired damage will have no effect.

Cable testing can be performed using the following procedure.

1. Remove the shipping cap on the flat cable extension. Conductors at opposite ends must be clean, dry and clear of the cable reel and each other.
2. Using and ohmeter, connect the ground lead to the cable armor and the probe to each individual lead. Record the measurements.
3. Using the ground lead and the probe lead, check phase A-B, B-C and A-C. Record the measurements. New cable should read near infinity both phase-to-ground and phase-to-phase. Depending on weather and humidity, measurements of only 1500 megohms are obtainable and considered normal.
4. Discharge each of the legs to ground after testing. A long piece of cable can hold a very high charge that can take over a minute to discharge.

## 4.2.5 Pothead Testing

The pothead should be pressure tested. Table 4-1 shows part numbers for various pothead testing equipment.

|----------------|---------------------|---------|------------|

Attach the pressure gauge and hand-operated air pump to the test cap. Submerge the pothead in water and apply pressure by operating the air pump. Test pressures and times are shown in Table 4-2. If the pothead leaks, remove the test cap and discard the O-ring. Use a new O-ring and test again. If it continues to leak, reject the flat cable extension.

| Time   | Pressure   | Cable              |
|--------|------------|--------------------|
| 5 min  | 0 psi 1    | used cable only    |
| 5 min  | 5 psi      | new and used cable |
| 5 min  | 40 psi     | new and used cable |

## 4.2.6 PSI Testing

Pressure Sensing Instrument (PSI) units should be tested prior to installation. Using a 1000 V megger, check the resistance of the unit to ground. If the unit is delatched, the measurement should be infinity. If the unit is latched (using a Triplett meter on the x1000 scale), the measurement should be between 35,000 ohms and 65,000 ohms depending on the ambient temperature. Cycling through the latch/delatch procedure and recording pressure and temperature measurements will ensure the integrity of the downhole unit.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Light

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Electrical

Caution

Do not use test equipment with output voltages greater than 1500 volts DC to test PSI units. This can damage the unit.

## 4.2.8 Installation of Downhole Monitoring Equipment (DME)

1. Before removing the shipping cap and gasket ensure the unit is in a clean area.

Hazard Category:

Caution

Be careful do not to pull the three-phase terminal ring. Connected is a signal wire leading down to the instrument. Pulling the terminal ring may result in damage to the wire.

Caution

Use extreme caution when installing or removing adapters from the instrument. Pull the adapter straight away from its mating piece (along the tool longitudinal axis) if the adapter moves sideways and impacts a connector, it could damage the connector or wire.

2. The DME and the motor adapter can be connected to the motor and filled with oil from the sensor's base drain and fill valve. Once the motor cable is connected, the complete system (cable, motor, and DME) may be Megger tested from the free cable end.
3. Install a lifting clamp and lower the DME into the well until the clamp is about 18-in. from the top of the worktable.

## Private

<!-- image -->

## Note

Dedicated DME lifting clamps are not available. Also, there are no alignment pins, so possible damage may occur if tandem motor jacks are not used. Until DME lifting clamps are available, any lifting clamp with a smaller ID then the OD of the DME adapter will work (i.e., 400 series pump clamp or 375 series motor clamp). See Figure 4-7.

Figure 4-7: Tandem Motor (lower end). This photo shows the damage that can occur when tandem motor jacks are not used. If this equipment is damaged due to misalignment, failure of the DME will result due to well fluid entry.

<!-- image -->

4. Tandem Motor jack assembly (P/N 100541677, 375/456/540/562 series motors or 44842, 738 series motors) is now slid into position on the worktable. Ensure that both hydraulic jacks are in their retracted position. Lower the DME down until the clamp rests in the cradle on top of the jacks.
5. Remove the shipping cap and slowly pump oil down the center of tool until full and all air is expelled.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Use extreme caution to ensure no moisture or debris enters this area.

## Private

6. Pick up the motor using procedure in section 4.5: Motor Installation of this manual and remove the lower shipping cap.
7. Select the correct O-ring(s) to be used from ALFORM-D Connection Table. Remove the old O-ring. Lubricate the new O-ring with Dow Corning 111 (p/n 100386898) and carefully install to its correct position.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Do not use metal tool when removing the O-ring from the flange groove. This can be the reason of equipment short runlife due to damage on the sealing surfaces.

A second backup O-ring is NOT required above the groove O-ring on 540 series and 562 series protector bases, between tandem motors and on PSI units.

8. Inspect the terminal pins and insulators to ensure they are not bent or broken. Have the rig operator lower the motor until it is approximately 4 - 6 inches above the DME. Then adjust both jacks simultaneously to slowly raise the DME and engage terminal pins into their respective motor terminals properly.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Use caution not to damage the terminal insulators or O-rings.

9. Install the bolts and lock washers and torque to the required specifications listed in the connection table.
10. Lower the motor(s) and DME into the well. Loosen the top shipping cap and place a lock washer between the cap and the motor head flange to provide a vent.
11. Pull the motor(s) and DME all the way out of the well and fill the DME and motor using filling procedures in section 4.5.2: Motor Oiling Procedure (Single-Section) of this manual, pump oil through both DME and motor(s).
12. Phase-to-phase resistance checks should be made after each connection, keeping in mind the resistances are additive and should always be balanced.
13. In the event that all motors cannot be pulled from the well because of limited (derrick) crown room, fill from the motor head of the lowest possible motor.
14. Repeat the procedure in section 4.5.3: Tandem Motor Connection for each CT motor that is added.

## 4.2.9 Cold Weather Installations

Cold weather is defined as ambient temperatures less than 20 degF (-7 degC). Special procedures must be applied in cold-weather installations to prevent operating failures.

## 4.2.9.1 Equipment

Equipment considerations, best practices and the use of external heat are discussed in the following sections.

## Equipment Considerations

- Ambient temperatures less than -45 degF (-43 degC) are considered too cold to properly assemble and install ESP equipment.
- Material selection should be based on bottomhole operating temperatures rather than surface temperatures. Lubricating oils and elastomers should be selected to ensure that optimum performance and run life is achieved for given well conditions. The installation procedures should ensure the selected equipment is installed and serviced properly.
- When installing equipment in cold temperatures (20 degF [-7 degC] or less), the equipment should be warmed before assembly to maximize run life. Oil in the motor and protector can become so viscous in very cold temperatures it cannot be pumped.
- When equipment is assembled, it must be serviced with oil before lowering into a well filled with kill fluids to warm it. The equipment will become contaminated with well fluids if not properly serviced.
- Working with O-rings in cold temperatures can be difficult. Problems have been observed with Aflas O-rings hanging up between flanges when assembling units in cold temperatures. Certain materials in O-rings become so rigid they can easily be pinched during assembly or break as they are installed. Minimum working temperatures for O-rings are shown in Table 4-3.

Table 4-3: O-ring Minimum Working Temperatures

| O-Ring Material   | Minimum Working Temperature   |
|-------------------|-------------------------------|
| Aflas             | 15 degF (-9 degC)             |
| HSN               | HSN -55 degF (-48 degC)       |

## Private

## Best Practices

Warming the equipment, oil and O-rings before assembly is strongly recommended. Transporting the equipment to the wellsite in a warm condition is recommended. (Overnight storage in a heated building will sufficiently warm the equipment.)

If the equipment temperature is less than 20 degF (-7 degC) and the equipment is submerged in well fluid, O-rings and mechanical seals can leak, contaminating the motor and protector with well fluids. If the equipment is placed in a well (full of fluid) to warm the equipment before the protector is completely serviced, the equipment will be contaminated. Temperature limitations for protector elastomers are shown in Table 4-4.

Table 4-4: Protector Elastomer Minimum Working Temperatures

| Protector Elastomer Material   | Minimum Working Temperature   |
|--------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Aflas                          | 15 degF (-9 degC)             |
| HSN                            | HSN -55 degF (-48 degC)       |

## Using External Heat

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Major

Potential Loss:

Personnel

Hazard Category:

Temperature

Always use caution when handling heated equipment.

The workover rig steam boiler (if available) or a portable steamer or warm-air blower should be used to provide heat. The steam or heat lines should be run to the equipment shipping boxes a minimum of 45 minutes prior to installation. Depending on the ambient temperature, heat source and heat capacity, longer times may be necessary. The warm air or steam line nozzle should be inserted into or connected to the shipping box container leaving container lids closed until the equipment is removed for installation. Enough heat should be applied to the requipment to ensure it stays warm while being serviced and installed. The object is to thoroughly heat the equipment so when the oil is applied during the top-off procedure, it will not be affected by the cold temperatures.

## Private

<!-- image -->

## Tip

The recommended warming temperature should range from 60 degF to 150 degF (16 degC to 66 degC). The best working temperature is 90 degF (32 degC).

Another warming method is to enclose the rig floor with a wind-proof material, usually canvas with a metal frame support. Warm air can be routed into the enclosure from the rig steam boiler or other source during the installation process to keep the equipment warm. This not only keeps the equipment warm, but also shields the equipment from undesirable elements (for example, blowing snow) during critical phases of the installation process.

Oil should be kept as warm as possible. Keep the oilcan in a warm environment. The oilcan should not be removed until it is time to service the equipment. Return the oilcan to the warm environment to maintain the oil temperature.

O-rings can be warmed by putting them inside coverall pockets for an extended time (warming with body heat). An alternative is to keep them inside a warm vehicle until they are ready to be used. This practice should be implemented unless the materials in the O-rings can withstand cold temperatures at the surface as well as downhole temperatures, or until a better heating method is found. The ideal temperature should range from 60 degF to 150 degF (16 degC to 66 degC). Minimum working temperatures for O-rings are shown in Table 4-3.

## External Heating Sources Not Available

The use of external heating sources to warm downhole equipment is recommended, especially when performance-based contracts or alliances where runlife is part of the risk and reward criteria are involved. When ambient temperatures are less than the minimum requirements for fill oils and cable elastomers, alternate elastomer materials and blended oils have been substituted to permit servicing in cold temperatures. All efforts should be made to warm the equipment; material substitutions should be made only as a last resort.

<!-- image -->

## Note

The following sections provide guidelines to heat the equipment by lowering the equipment into the well. Note that some form of equipment warm-up is still discussed, but the limitations are noted and those limitations should not be exceeded at any time.

## Private

Shortcuts and the use of improper methods at time of installation can cause premature equipment failure. Sufficiently warming the equipment before installation is still important. Failure to do so can significantly reduce run life.

## Guidelines for ESP installations when no external heating sources are available

- The fill oil should be warmed before the topping-off procedure is started. Oil temperature limitations are shown in Table 4-5.
- O-rings should be warmed by putting them inside coverall pockets for an extended time (warming with body heat) or by keeping them inside a warm environment until they are ready to be used.
- Some cables will require a warm-up procedure. Table 4-6 shows temperature limits for cable materials.
- Ensure the motor has a metal pothead cap and new O-ring before lowering into the well. Keep the motor in the well for a minimum of four hours to allow the equipment to warm.

Table 4-5: Oil Temperature Limitations

| Oil Type   | Specific Gravity   | Pour Point (Maximum)   | Pour Point (Maximum)   | Fill Temperature Without Heat 1   | Fill Temperature Without Heat 1   |

- If the well is full of kill fluid or is expected to flow while the equipment is being warmed, the protector must be completely serviced before lowering it into the well.
- If the motor has been placed in the well to warm, always check the protector for contamination by well fluids. Tie in the flat cable extension using a vertical tie-in; this puts less stress on the flat cable extension. Re-service the protector with warm oil.
- There have been problems resulting from assembling equipment, not servicing it with oil and lowering it into a well filled with kill fluid. The equipment always fills with well fluid in these circumstances.

## Blended Oils

When the well BHT is greater than 175 degF (79 degC), the use of dual-base bushings in motors is required because a 50/50 blend of No. 3 and No. 5 oil at a concentration greater than 20% in No. 6 oil is too thin for the standard single-base bushing normally used in motors.

## 4.2.9.2 Cables

Cable considerations and best practices are discussed in the following sections.

## Cable Considerations

Cable material selection should be based on bottomhole operating temperatures rather than surface temperatures. Elastomers should be selected to ensure optimum performance and run life for the well conditions. The installation procedures should ensure the selected cable equipment is handled and installed properly.

When installing cable strings and their various component parts in cold temperatures, the cable elastomer material must be heated to maximize run life.

Cable elastomers can become so rigid in cold temperatures that the cables can be pinched during assembly or break as they move over the cable wheel. There is no alternative but to heat the cable string before assembly and during installation when ambient temperatures are below the material useful temperature range. The cable should be transported to the wellsite in a warm condition if possible. Ideally, the cable should be stored overnight in a heated environment prior to running in the well.

Temperature limitations for cable materials are shown in Table 4-6.

## Private

## Best Practices

- A heated cable spooling shack should be used for cabling operations when cold temperatures are expected.
- A workover rig steam boiler (if available) or a large-capacity portable steamer or warm-air blower should be used to provide heat. Another method is to enclose the cable spooler with wind-proof material (usually a canvas or tarp with a metal frame support). A warm-air vent from the rig steam boiler or warm-air unit is attached to the enclosure. This will keep the cable warm during the installation process. The steam line or heat line should be routed to the cable spooler reel as soon as it arrives on location. The cable should be minimally exposed to cold temperatures during installation on the surface. Temperature limitations for cable materials are shown in Table 4-6.
- Never allow the cable to hang suspended overnight between the wellhead and the spooler in cold temperatures.
- Do not assemble the flat cable extension to the motor until the equipment is ready to run.
- For information on suspending the EPS Equipment in the well please see section 4.11.1: Suspending ESP String.

To choose the proper lifting clamps for your installation, please see section 2.4: Mechanical Lifting Equipment.

Measure and record makeup length of pump/protector/motors.

A crane with a spreader bar and slings is used to lift equipment out of the shipping box and place equipment on wooden planks spaced evenly throughout the equipment length.

4.3.2

When equipment is stabilized on the wooden planks and it is safe, install the lifting clamps complete with chains as per the approved procedure.

Clamps must be clean and free from foreign material and visually inspect before each lift.

## Note

Clamp bolts should be tightened according to Table 2-4: Lifting Clamps in section 2.4: Mechanical Lifting Equipment. Use torque wrench p/n 2003754 and sockets p/n 101168703 or p/n 101168675 depending on installation clamp bolt.

## 4.3.1 Motor Clamp Installation

Choose the proper motor lifting clamp and install it so the shoulder of the clamp rests against the lip of the motor head to prevent the clamp from slipping. The cable slot in the clamp should be aligned with the pothole of the motor. This provides the maximum holding strength of the clamp. Tighten the bolts evenly to ensure equal spacing between the clamp faces.

If several tandem motors are being installed, place the clamp on the lower tandem motor first. On lower tandem and center tandem motors, it is important to align the cable slot on the motor clamp with the drain and fill valve to prevent it from being damaged.

Protector Clamp Installation

The protector clamp is installed on the housing just below the top lock plate or lock weld in the case of a modular protector. Ensure the bolts are evenly tightened to ensure equal spacing between the clamp faces.

## 4.3.3 Pump Clamp Installation

Pump clamps can be installed on the bottom two sections of the pump that will be picked up. If the pump clamp is a friction type, it is installed just under the top lock plate. If a shoulder type is used, slide the shoulder of the clamp into the groove located in the pump head.

A clamp is not normally used on the uppermost section of pump. The best method for picking up this section of pump is with a handling pup joint.

## Private

The pup joint should be installed on the upper end of the pump and rig elevators used to pick up the pump if additional handling is necessary. This practice is best described in Figure 4-8.

## 4.4 ESP Gauges

## 4.4.1 Product Description

## 4.4.1.1 Overview

The Phoenix systems are installed on downhole ESP (electric submersible pump) pumping equipment and use the ESP power cable for communication and power. The downhole sensors measure pump and reservoir parameters to give the operator information to better optimize the ESP system.

The Phoenix Select Lite, Standard, and Advanced systems consist of up to three components: Base Unit and either 0, 1, or 2 Remote Sensors. The Phoenix Select Base Unit is installed on the base of the ESP motor and measures intake pressure, intake temperature, tri-axial vibration, motor winding temperature, and current leakage of the ESP electrical system. The Phoenix Select Remote Sensors can be installed at the pump intake and pump discharge. The remote sensors measure intake or discharge pressure, intake or discharge temperature, and tri-axial vibration. The Phoenix Select Remote Sensors communicate to the Phoenix Select Base Unit over a single electrical conductor inside a 1/4-in diameter armored line. Communication to surface is achieved through a connection to the neutral point of the lower ESP motor by the Phoenix Select Base Unit, and consequently, the ESP cable. The Phoenix Select Base Units retransmit the remote sensor information to the surface as required. The Phoenix Select gauge operates at higher temperatures than the previous XT offering, 150 degC (302 degF) vs 125 degC (257 degF).

The Phoenix XT has been the standard ESP gauge in the market for many years. The XT is fully qualified for 125 degC and uses Analog Telemetry to transmit information to the surface panel. It is compatible with all UniConn/PIC equipment as well as with legacy panels like ISP and ISU.

The Phoenix xt150 is based on proven MultiSensor and Phoenix XT monitoring technology for downhole ESP equipment. Improved with microelectronic components, and digital telemetry to ensure that the most reliable, faster and accurate information is provided to analyze artificial lift performance. The Phoenix xt150 operates at 150 degC (302 degF). Phoenix XT and xt150 are offered as a single pressure Type 0 gauge and a dual pressure Type 1 gauge. It measures intake pressure, discharge pressure (Type1 only), intake temperature, motor winding or motor oil temperature, single axis vibration and current leakage

## Private

of the ESP electrical system. The Phoenix xt150 is only compatible with the UniConn and PICv2 surface acquisition system. The Phoenix xt150 offers the following improvements compared to the analogue version (Phoenix XT):

- Higher temperature rating, 150 degC (302 degF) versus 125 degC (257 degF)
- Higher pressure accuracy, 0.1% full scale versus 0.2% full scale
- Digital telemetry that eliminates analogue data uncertainties

The Phoenix UltraLite system is a base unit only. The UltraLite gauge uses plastic surface mount components to reduce cost, but limits the operating temperature to 100 degC (212 degF) maximum. The UltraLite supports a single pressure transducer that measures the motor oil pressure and temperature, which is assumed equal to annulus pressure and temperature, respectively. Unlike the xt150 and Select systems, there is no external thermocouple to measure motor winding temperature. The UltraLite also measures single axis vibration and current leakage.

The Phoenix UltraLite, xt150, and Select systems transmit the acquired measurements over the ESP power cable using digital telemetry. This digital telemetry offers several advantages over the analog telemetry used in the older MultiSensor and XT gauges:

- The data is digitized downhole so that the transmitter and receiver accuracy and performance have no bearing on the accuracy of the measurement. Noise and interference in the communication system cannot cause data to become inaccurate.
- The telemetry protocol uses error checking on the data received at the surface to ensure that the data interpreted by the surface equipment is the same as the data measured downhole.

## 4.4.1.2 Surface Acquisition System Compatibility

The Phoenix XT, Select Lite, Select Standard and Select Advanced systems are supported by the UniConn/Phoenix Interface Card (PIC) and legacy ISP/ISU surface acquisition systems. However, the Phoenix UltraLite and the Phoenix xt150 systems are only supported by the UniConn/PIC (version 2). An earlier version of the Phoenix UltraLite system developed under rapid response uses an obsolete telemetry system and is supported by both the UniConn/PIC and legacy ISP/ISU surface acquisition systems.
