## 4.4.3 Wellsite Procedures

This section covers the wellsite installation procedures for base unit gauge configurations (Ultralite, XT Type 0, xt150 Type 0 and Select Lite). Refer to the appropriate operation manual for more advanced gauge configurations (XT Type 1, xt150 Type 1, Select Standard, Select Advanced, etc.) installation procedures.

## 4.4.3.1 Confirm Firmware Version

The Phoenix Select Lite, Standard and Advanced systems are supported by the UniConn/Phoenix Interface Card (PIC) and legacy ISP/ISU surface acquisition systems.

The XT gauge is compatible with PICv1 (firmware ver. 2.1 or later) and PICv2 (firmware ver. 1.15 or later). The XT gauge is supported by the UniConn/Phoenix Interface Card (PIC) and legacy ISP/ISU surface acquisition systems.

The xt150 gauge is only compatible with surface equipment (UniConn) equipped with a PICv2. The firmware version of the PICv2 must be 1.20 or newer and the UniConn firmware needs to be version 1.404r1 or newer for the tool to work properly.

The UltraLite gauge is only compatible with surface equipment (UniConn) equipped with a PICv2. The firmware version of the PICv2 must be 1.15 or newer and the UniConn firmware needs to be version 1.404r1 or newer for the tool to work properly.

<!-- image -->

## Note

The UniConn/PICv2 (with latest firmware) is recommended for all Phoenix gauge applications.

It is always a good idea to check with InTouch for the latest firmware releases and alerts. See InTouch content 4456403 for the PICv2 and InTouch content 3985891 for the UniConn. Refer to the UniConn manual to see how to install the PICv2, configure, and check the firmware versions.

## 4.4.3.2 Pre-Installation Checks

Before running the gauge into the well, several checks should be made to determine that it is functioning properly. Perform the following checks before running the downhole tool into the well:

## Private

1. Inspect the housing for physical damage or imperfections.
2. If the top connection of the downhole tool is protected with a shipping/handling cap secured by six bolts to the lower flange. Remove the handling cap and ensure that the two O-rings are new. If they are not, replace them with new O-rings before connecting to the ESP motor.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Serious

Potential Loss:

Personnel

Hazard Category:

Electrical

Warning

Caution should be used when using a megommeter. All safety guidelines as outlined in the operation manual for the meter, and Schlumberger polices must be followed.

3. Inspect the pin to make sure it is not bent or damaged. Test the electrical integrity of the feedthru with a megohmmeter (Megger). The gauge should be tested up to 2.5 kV. (see Megger procedure or the Gauge User Manual in InTouch)
4. Before connecting the gauge to an ESP motor, it should be first connected to the surface equipment to verify that the gauge is functioning properly. Power up the Surface equipment and ensure that the readings are being displayed. If errors are reported refer to the Troubleshooting section in the UniConn manual. Be sure to resolve all faults before proceeding with installation of the gauge in the well.
5. Values displayed should represent ambient conditions. Depending on accuracy of each tool, those values could be different. Refer to the User Manual Specifications section for nominal values (pressure, temperature and vibration) and the Functional Test section for the testing procedure.

<!-- image -->

## Note

It is optional (but strongly recommended) to apply pressure and verify proper function of discharge port (XT and xt150 only). Check value read at surface panel is ±10 psi of applied pressure.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Vibration refresh period for digital gauges could be 30 seconds or more. The first vibration measurement is acquired within the first few seconds of applying power to the gauge, after which no measurement is taken until the next sample has been transmitted to the surface gear. There is also an averaging setting on UniConn and the time needed to display a change in Vibration could be even higher.

Also note if the temperature at the wellhead is significantly below operating temperature of the tool (&lt; 0 degC) the tool should be warmed up or the readings could be out of specification.

6. Disconnect the gauge from the surface equipment.

## 4.4.3.3 Connecting the Downhole Gauge

The gauge must be connected to the ESP system. Connection can be done either with an I-wire or if necessary, without an I-wire through the use of an adapter. Refer to Figure 4-16 for an example of an I-wire type connection.

Figure 4-16: I-wire Connection

<!-- image -->

Refer to Figure 4-17 for ESP application without neutral point or I-wire for an example of an ESP system that does not have an electrical neutral point or I-wire available. An adapter is available for applications such as this.

Figure 4-17: ESP application without neutral point or I-wire

<!-- image -->

## I-wire Connection

Perform the following steps when installing a gauge on the lower end of an ESP assembly.

1. Remove the lower handling cap from the ESP motor.
2. Locate the I-wire.

<!-- image -->

## Note

If the motor has three-phase pin connectors, the motor base adapter should be bolted to the ESP motor base. Locate the I-wire in the motor base adapter

3. A boot connector and splice kit is supplied with every gauge assembly. The boot connector is composed of three parts; a crimp connector, a Teflon sleeve and a boot. Refer to Figure 4-18 for how the boot connector and splice kit are designed to go together.
4. Slip the boot and the Teflon sleeve over the I-wire and far enough down the wire to be out of the way for now.

Figure 4-18: Crimping and splicing connector, sleeve, and boot

<!-- image -->

## Private

<!-- image -->

## Note

A splice kit is supplied, in case the I-wire is not long enough to install the boot connector and plug onto the feedthru. Install the splice kit if necessary.

5. Strip approximately 6 mm (~1/4 in) of insulation from the end of the I-wire.
6. Set the DMC crimping tool for #12 AWG. Crimp the crimp connector onto the wire.
7. Slip the Teflon sleeve over the crimp connector and the boot over the Teflon sleeve.

## Connecting Gauge to ESP Motor

The gauge can be connected to the motor in the horizontal position before picking the motor up in the rig or with the ESP string hanging vertical in the rig. Both options are described in the following sections.

## Horizontal Gauge Installation (Before Lifting)

The gauge can be connected to the motor in the horizontal position before picking the motor up (vertical) in the rig. To connect the gauge to the ESP string, perform the following steps:

<!-- image -->

## Note

Remove any gaskets remaining on the motor from the shipping cap. New O-rings should be installed on the gauge flange.

1. The gauge should be appropriately oriented (rotated about the tool axis).
2. Align the gauge with the ESP string and move it within a couple of inches from the bottom of the motor. Remove the dummy boot from the feedthrough.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Care should be taken not to damage the feedthrough.

3. Plug the previously installed boot connector on the I-wire firmly onto the feedthrough on the bottom face of the ESP motor.
4. When the boot connector is securely fastened to the feedthrough, the gauge should be pushed home into the motor flange. Be very careful not to snag the I-wire.

## Private

5. Install and tighten all flange bolts to 30 ft.lbf. The recommended the torque wrench setting is 26 ft.lbf, as per ED-119.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Major

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Machinery equipment hand tools

Do not allow the lower end of the gauge to drag the ground, the V-door, or along the rig floor when hoisting the ESP string up into the derrick or mast. Dragging the tool can cause damage to the joint and damage the internal parts of the tool.

## Vertical Gauge Installation (After Lifting)

The gauge may be connected to the lower end of the ESP motor with the ESP string hanging vertical in the rig. To attach the gauge to the motor while vertical, perform the following steps:

<!-- image -->

## Note

Remove any gaskets remaining on the motor from the shipping cap. New O-rings should be installed on the gauge flange.

1. Lift the gauge onto the rig floor with the transit cap in place, ensuring that the cavity in the upper head is covered to prevent fluid and loose matter from falling into the cavity.
2. Orient the gauge.
3. Pick up (with derrick hoist) the ESP string so that the motor is far enough above the gauge to remove the boot protector cap from the feedthrough.
4. Plug the boot connector (already installed on the I-wire) directly onto the feedthrough.
5. When the boot connector is securely pushed onto the feedthrough and lift the gauge to the ESP motor to fully engage the upper flange of the gauge .
6. Lower the ESP and gauge to a solid work surface so that the bolts can be safely installed.
7. Install and tighten all flange bolts to 30 ft.lbf. The recommended the torque wrench setting is 26 ft.lbf, as per ED-119.

## 4.4.3.4 Functional Testing

Before running into the well, the gauge should be checked to make sure nothing was damaged or disturbed while connecting the gauge to the ESP string. To check this; perform the following:

1. Connect the surface equipment to the pothead of the motor. Connect the positive (+ or LINE) lead to a motor phase. If this is not permitted, then connect it to the cable once connected. The Negative (or CHASIS) lead should be connected to ESP housing or ESP cable armor.
2. Power up the surface equipment. All diagnostic and parameter readings should be recorded. If errors are reported refer to the Troubleshooting section in the UniConn manual (InTouch ID 3953183). Be sure to resolve all faults before proceeding with installation of the gauge in the well.
3. Verify all readings are within specifications. Refer to the User Manual Specifications section for nominal values (pressure, temperature and vibration).

The following nominal values are shown as an example:

Pressure - 15 psi ±10 psi

Temperature within 3.6 degF (2 degC) of surface temperature

Vibration &lt; 0.5 g when not moving and responding to movement

4. Perform megohmmeter (megger) test on both the ESP motor and the gauge to a value of 2.5 kV.

<!-- image -->

## Note

The positive (+) lead of the Megger should always be connected to ground (earth) when attached to a Phoenix Select. Never spark (arc) discharge voltage to ground. Always discharge voltage through the Megger.

Refer to the Megger Test Procedure in the specific gauge operations manual for details about checking insulation resistance.

## Installation Procedures

## Verify Port Depth

When using Reda discharge pressure sub, the port depth must be verified prior to the jam nut installation and cutting the discharge line. The port depth for should be between 2.3-in and 2.4-in.

<!-- image -->

## Note

If the port depth is between 1.0-in to 1.4-in, the control line must be cut close to the MIN line on discharge pressure sub. Do not exceed the measured port length.

1. Verify the depth of the port on the discharge pressure sub.
- a. Insert a short piece of control line in the port.
- b. Mark the control line at the discharge pressure sub.
- c. Remove the control line and measure the distance from the inserted end to the mark.
2. Hold the discharge line against the discharge pressure sub and mark the cable.
- If the port depth is 2.3-in to 2.4-in, mark the control line below MAX line and above MIN line on discharge pressure sub.

<!-- image -->

Figure 4-25: Measure Port Depth

<!-- image -->

Figure 4-26: Standard Port Depth Between 2.3-in and 2.4-in

<!-- image -->

- If the port depth is 1.0-in to 1.4-in, mark the control line at or close to MIN line on discharge pressure sub.
3. Cut the control line at the mark.

Figure 4-27: Port Depth Between 1.0-in and 1.4-in

<!-- image -->

## Jam Nut Installation with New Discharge Line

<!-- image -->

## Note

The discharge line has been filled with fluid of a known density so that error correction for the length of the line can be made when the data is being analyzed. It is important to minimize the loss of hydraulic fluid during this process.

1. Refer to Figure 4-24: New Gauge Discharge Pressure Line. Remove the blanking cap (1) from one end of the line and replace with the Discharge Line Adaptor. Attach the other end of the Adaptor to a hand pump and close the bleed valve on the pump.
2. Remove the blanking cap on the other end of the line and make up to the gauge discharge port. Tighten the connection to 15 ft-lbf (equivalent to 1-1/4 turns).

<!-- image -->

## Note

Before installing the discharge line inspect the ferrules on the end of tubing. If they are damaged or scratched cut off the end of the tubing and replace them with new parts.

3. With the hand pump, apply pressure (3,000 psi) to the hydraulic oil. Hold pressure at 3,000 psi for 10 min. Watch the fitting and tubing for pressure drop-off to ensure no leaks are present.
4. Once the tubing and Swagelok fitting pass the hydrostatic pressure test, position the 1/4-in discharge line so that it can be banded to the ESP string or is contained in the ESP neck clamps.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Position the 1/4-in discharge line as close as possible along the OD of the gauge and the ESP string to avoid snagging when the string is run into the well.

5. The discharge line will be terminated at the discharge pressure sub.
- a. Cut the discharge line to length. Refer to 4.4.3.5 Verify Port Depth for details.
- b. De-burr the discharge line edges.
- c. Insert the precut discharge line into the discharge port.

## Private

Figure 4-28: Install Discharge Line

<!-- image -->

- d. Screw the Swagelok fitting into the discharge pressure sub port.
- e. Tighten the jam nut connection to 15 ft-lbf (equivalent to 1-1/4 turns). Refer to Figure 4-24: New Gauge Discharge Pressure Line for details of the jam nut and ferrules.

Figure 4-29: Tighten Connection

<!-- image -->

## 4.5 Motor Installation

<!-- image -->

Note: Maximus information

For Maximus, refer to Appendix C: Maximus.

Before picking up the first section of the motor into a vertical position, a tail clamp should be positioned approximately one-third of the way up from the bottom. This provides support when the motor is being hoisted. A crane should be used in conjunction with the winch line on the rig to safely hoist the equipment to a point where the chain assembly on the motor clamp can be secured into the hook assembly in the elevators. As the blocks are raised, the crane helps support the motor's weight to prevent it from bending. Turn the elevators so that the weight is not against the latch. Figure 4-32 shows a motor being lifted with a rig winch and crane.

## Private

Figure 4-32: Lifting the motor with a rig winch and crane

<!-- image -->

## 4.5.1 Alternate Lifting Method

If a crane is not available, an alternate lifting method can be used to hoist a motor into position. The method uses a winch line and tag line. The tag line is used to control movement towards the rig floor. A tail clamp is positioned one-third of the way down from the top for the winch line. The winch line and traveling blocks are operated by one person. The motor is lifted using the winch line until near vertical and then the load is transferred onto the main blocks keeping the winch line slack. Another winch line or catline should be attached to the tag line to prevent contact with the rig floor or other obstructions. The lifting procedure is shown in Figure 4-33.

<!-- image -->

## Note

The position of the tail clamp is important. Positioning the clamp one-third of the way down from the top places the least amount of stress on the motor, preventing it from bending.

Figure 4-33: Lifting the motor with a rig winch and tag line

<!-- image -->

## 4.5.2 Motor Oiling Procedure (Single-Section)

The motor is ready for servicing once it is in a vertical position over the well.

<!-- image -->

## Note

The 456 Dominator Motor has a short Drain and Fill Valve. Alemite adaptors produced prior to 2009 may not be suitable for filling these motors, please see InTouch Content 4366376.

## Private

Proper installation of plugs is vital to ensuring the Total-Run-Life (TRL) of the ESP system is achieved. Ensure the vent plugs (standard, short and long) and drain-and-fill valves used are the latest revision per the OneCAT bill of materials.

<!-- image -->

Figure 4-34: Standard (Vent and Drain) Plug

Figure 4-35: Short and Long Vent Plugs

<!-- image -->

Figure 4-36: Drain and Fill Valve

<!-- image -->

When a plug or valve is removed and installed the following steps must be taken:

1. Remove the plug or valve. If removing the plug, use a 3/4-in wrench to backup the valve to prevent loosening the valve.
2. Remove the old lead gasket. Do not reuse lead gaskets.
3. Install a new lead gasket. Do not install two lead gaskets.
4. Install the plug (with lead gasket) or valve (with lead gasket). Torque plugs to 15 ft-lbf and valves to 35 ft-lbf.

<!-- image -->

## Vent plug and drain-and-fill valve

Potential Severity:

Light

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Machinery equipment hand tools

Caution

Ensure the vent plugs and drain-and-fill valves used are the latest revision per the OneCAT bill of materials. Make sure that a calibrated torque wrench is used to install plugs. Vent plugs should be torqued to 15 ft-lbf and the drain-and-fill valves should be torqued to 35 ft-lbf.

Confirm that all vent plug(s) and drain-and-fill valve(s) are flush to or recessed into the equipment base, body and/or head, before and after servicing.

1. At the bottom of the motor locate the drain-and-fill valve. Tighten this assembly to 35 ft-lbf.
2. Lower the motor into the well. Remove the top shipping cap, coupling and the Allen screw (shaft plug) from the center of the shaft.
3. Reinstall the shipping cap with a lock washer between the cap and motor head flange to provide a vent during the oil filling procedure.

## Private

4. Lift the motor out of the well. Remove the vent plug and lead gasket from the drain-and-fill valve at the base of the motor.

<!-- image -->

## Note

When removing the vent plug, use a 3/4-in wrench to back-up the drain-and-fill valve to prevent it from loosening.

5. Select the appropriate oil for the application and connect the oil filling pump, hose and adapter assembly to the oil can.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Purge the air from the oil filling hose with oil before filling the motor.

6. Install the adapter and slowly pump (45 rev/min) oil into the motor until it flows out of the motor head. Wait for five minutes to allow air bubbles to migrate out the top of the motor and then pump again until oil flows. Continue this process until it takes only one turn of the oil pump to cause oil to flow from the top of the motor.
7. Remove the adapter and hose from the motor and install the vent plug with a new lead gasket (p/n 15008) into the drain-and-fill valve. Torque the vent plug to 15 ft-lbf.
8. Lower the motor into the well until the clamp rests on top of the worktable. Remove the motor shipping cap and slowly pump oil down the center of the shaft to ensure all air is expelled from the motor. Rotating the shaft rapidly with a spline wrench will help displace any air.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Ensure no moisture or debris enters the motor.

9. Replace the shaft plug and tighten. Be sure the plug is not protruding past the end of the shaft when tight.
10. Replace the coupling. Ensure the shaft rotates smoothly. Servicing is now complete.
11. Check all drain-and-fill valves and vent plugs to insure that they are torqued to specification.

## Private

<!-- image -->

## Note

Confirm that all vent plug(s) and drain-and-fill valve(s) are flush to or recessed into the equipment base, body and/or head after servicing. Vent plugs are torqued to 15 ft-lbf and drain-and-fill valves are torqued to 35 ft-lbf.

## 4.5.3 Tandem Motor Connection

The motor is ready for servicing once it is in a vertical position over the well.

1. At the bottom of the motor locate the drain-and-fill valve. Tighten this assembly to 35 ft-lbf.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Confirm that all vent plug(s) and drain-and-fill valve(s) are flush to or recessed into the equipment base, body and/or head, before and after servicing.

2. Lower the motor into the well. Loosen the top shipping cap and place a lock washer between the cap and motor head flange to provide a vent during the oil filling procedure.
3. Lift the motor out of the well. Remove the vent plug and lead gasket from the drain-and-fill valve at the base of the motor.

<!-- image -->

## Note

When removing the vent plug, use a 3/4-in wrench to back-up the drain-and-fill valve to prevent it from loosening.

4. Select the appropriate oil for the application and connect the oil filling pump, hose and adapter assembly to the oil can.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Purge the air from the oil filling hose with oil before filling the motor.

5. Install the adapter and slowly pump (45 rev/min) oil into the motor until it flows out of the motor head. Wait for five minutes to allow air bubbles to migrate out the top of the motor and then pump again until oil flows. Continue this process until it takes only one turn of the oil pump to cause oil to flow from the top of the motor.
6. Remove the adapter and hose from the motor and install the vent plug with a new lead gasket (p/n 15008) into the drain-and-fill valve. Torque the vent plug to 15 ft-lbf.

## Private

7. Lower the motor into the well until the clamp is approximately 18 in from the top of the worktable.
8. Slide the motor jack assembly (p/n 100541677, 375/456/540/562-series motors or p/n 44842, 738-series motors) into position on the worktable. Ensure that both hydraulic jacks are in their retracted position.
9. Lower the motor until the clamp rests in the cradle on top of the jacks.
10. Remove the motor shipping cap and slowly pump oil down the center of the shaft to ensure all air is expelled from the motor. Rotating the shaft rapidly with a spline wrench will help displace any air.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Ensure no moisture or debris enters the motor.

11. Select the spline alignment tool from Table 4-21. A spline alignment tool is shown in Figure 4-37.

Table 4-21: Spline Alignment Tool Part Numbers

|   Motor Series | Shaft size   | Part Number          |
|----------------|--------------|----------------------|
|            375 | 0.68 in      | 44115                |
|            456 | 1.00 in      | 44271                |
|            456 | 1.12 in      | 455360               |
|            540 | 1.12 in      | 44297                |
|            540 | 1.18 in      | 44263                |
|            540 | 1.37 in      | 320937 (most common) |
|            562 | 1.37 in      | 1079920              |
|            738 | 1.50 in      | 44289                |
|            738 | 2.00 in      | 2006419              |

Figure 4-37: Spline alignment tool

<!-- image -->

12. Place the alignment tool on the motor coupling and turn the motor shaft until the sleeve slides down over the guide pin on the motor head. (There is an alignment groove machined into the motor head and base indicating the location of the guide pin.) Figure 4-38 shows the alignment tool in place.
13. Pick up the next motor and remove the lower shipping cap. Place the alignment tool on the upper motor shaft and turn until the pin of the alignment tool slips into the alignment hole on the motor base. The splines on the two shafts are now mated to ensure proper engagement of the motor coupling.
14. Remove the old O-ring from motor base.

Figure 4-38: Spline alignment tool in place for tandem motor connections

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Light

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Machinery equipment hand tools

Caution

Do not use a metal tool when removing the O-ring from the flange groove. Damaged sealing surfaces can result in short equipment runlife.

15. Lubricate a new O-ring with Dow Corning 111 (p/n 100386898). Carefully install the O-ring into its correct position. Refer to the ALFORM-D connection tables (InTouch ID: 3255850) for a complete list of O-ring part numbers, coupling and bolt torque information.

<!-- image -->

## Note

For 540 series and 562 series protector bases, a second backup O-ring is NOT required above the O-ring groove between tandem motors and on PSI units.

## Private

16. Inspect the terminal pins and insulators to ensure they are not bent or broken. Have the rig operator lower the top motor until it is approximately 4 to 6 inches above the lower motor. Then pump both jacks simultaneously to slowly raise the lower motor and engage the coupling, making sure the alignment pin slides into the respective hole and that the motor terminals are properly engaged.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Light

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Electrical

Caution

Use care not to damage the terminal insulators or O-rings.

17. Install the bolts and lock washers. Torque to the specifications listed in the connection table.
18. Lower both motors into the well. Loosen the top shipping cap and place a lock washer between the cap and the motor head flange to provide a vent.
19. Pull the motors completely out of the well and repeat the oil filling procedures; this time filling both motors. In the event that all motors cannot be pulled from the well because of limited crown room, fill from the motor head of the lowest possible motor. Replace the vent plug with a new lead gasket (p/n 15008) and ensure all other plugs are tight (15 ft-lbf).
20. Phase-to-phase resistance checks should be made after each connection. Resistances are additive and should always be balanced.
21. Check all drain-and-fill valves and vent plugs to insure that they are torqued to specification.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Confirm that all vent plug(s) and drain-and-fill valve(s) are flush to or recessed into the equipment base, body and/or head after servicing. Vent plugs are torqued to 15 ft-lbf and drain-and-fill valves are torqued to 35 ft-lbf.

22. Repeat the above procedures for each motor that is added.

## 4.5.4 Upper Tandem Motor Oiling Procedure

Ensure the vent plugs and drain-and-fill valves used are the latest revision per the OneCAT bill of materials. Make sure that a calibrated torque wrench is used to install plugs. Vent plugs should be torqued to 15 ft-lbf and the drain-and-fill valves should be torqued to 35 ft-lbf.

## Private

Before servicing the upper tandem motor, remove the allen screw (shaft plug) located in the center of the shaft. Service the motor with oil, replace the shaft plug and tighten.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Ensure the plug is not protruding past the end of the shaft when tight.

Replace the coupling and check to ensure the shaft rotates smoothly. Service is now complete.

## 4.6 Protector Assembly

<!-- image -->

Note: Maximus information

For Maximus, refer to Appendix C: Maximus.

## 4.6.1 Protector Installation

Protectors are lifted using the same methods used to lift motors. Motor lifting procedures are provided in the Motor Installation section.

1. Lift the protector to a position two to three feet above the motor.
2. Remove the lower shipping cap and gasket.
3. Remove the old O-ring from protector base.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Light

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Machinery equipment hand tools

Caution

Do not use a metal tool when removing the O-ring from the flange groove. Damaged sealing surfaces can result in short equipment runlife.

4. Lubricate a new O-ring with Dow Corning 111 (p/n 100386898). Refer to the ALFORM-D connection tables (InTouch ID: 3255850) for a complete list of O-ring part numbers, coupling and bolt torque information.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Do not use metal tool when removing the O-ring from the flange groove. This can be the reason of equipment short runlife due to damage on the sealing surfaces.

A second backup O-ring is NOT required above the groove O-ring on 540 series and 562 series protector bases, between tandem motors and on PSI units.

Always test couplings on a test shaft prior to be sent to the field. Also, once crew is on the rig site, test couplings on the equipment that is going to be used in the installation. Do not rely on part numbers only.

5. Use the spline wrench to ensure the motor and protector turn free and smooth.
6. Place the coupling on the motor shaft and have the rig operator slowly lower the protector until the shafts are engaged.
7. Turn the protector so that the flat cable slots on the protector flange and motor flange line up with each other. Lower the protector until the flanges meet, making sure not to damage the O-ring. Install the bolts and torque to specification.
8. Pick up the assembly, remove the motor clamp and lower the assembly until the weight rests on the protector clamp.

<!-- image -->

## Note

## Installation Caution, All Series Protectors to All Series Motors

If the upper snap-ring (coupling adapter retainer) is left in place on the protector's lower shaft spline, there is a possibility of a tolerance stack-up which can cause a protector problem, motor problem or both. Observe the following procedures when installing all series protectors to all series motors.

## When a Universal Coupling Adapter is on the Protector Lower Shaft Splines

1. Remove the retaining snap-ring from below adapter.
2. Remove the adapter from protector shaft.
3. Remove the upper retaining snap-ring from protector shaft.

## Private

## When a Universal Coupling Adapter is not on the Protector Shaft

1. Feel the lower protector shaft to determine if either snap-ring is in its groove. If either is present, remove and discard.
2. Proceed with installation procedure.

In either case, the protector lower shaft spline must not have any snap rings installed when connecting to a 562 motor. Leaving the snapring installed can force the protector in upthrust and the motor in downthrust, resulting in a failure.

## 4.6.2 Tandem Protector Assembly

When installing tandem protectors remove the spline adapter from the shaft of the upper protector. Remove the adapter with an ice pick.

## 4.6.3 Oil filling procedures

Protectors are filled with oil prior to shipment from the manufacturing facility. Typically, some oil is lost during field installation and refilling the protector is required. Oil refilling procedures at the wellsite are provided in 4.9: Oil Filling Procedures for Protectors.

## 4.7 Pump Shimming and Installation

Procedures and specifications for field spacing (shimming) submersible pumps are provided in this document. Select the proper thrust setting tools and shims based on the series of pump equipment and shaft sizes and then follow applicable procedures.

1. Always check the equipment first and make a note of all the nameplate data.
2. Always make sure the equipment on location is the equipment that has been designed for this particular well.
3. Always remove BOH to replace O-ring before RIH, then install BOH back using new bolts. Refer to the ALFORM-D connection tables (InTouch ID: 3255850) for a complete list of O-ring part numbers, coupling and bolt torque information.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Light

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Machinery equipment hand tools

Caution

Do not use a metal tool when removing the O-ring from the flange groove. Damaged sealing surfaces can result in short equipment runlife.

4. In large pumps (series 675 and higher) top shipping cap should be removing the first on the rig floor to purge the vacuum for easy removing bottom shipping cap in further. Then install top shipping cap on place to follow installation procedure.

On pumps built in compression construction, the shafts must be matched to the protector so that the thrust developed by the pump can be transferred to the protector thrust bearing.

High BHT applications, those above 250 degF with multiple tandem pumps, should be evaluated for possible excessive shaft growth. Please submit downhole conditions and pump configurations to InTouch for these cases.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Serious

Assets

Warning

The lower part of string should be covered while shimming.

## 4.7.4 Mixing Pumps

If compression type pumps and floater type pumps are being run in the same string the compression type pumps must be placed at the bottom of the string. Once all of the pumps are bolted together they must be turned using the correct tool to make sure the complete assembly rotates.

## Private

If a floater type AGH (advanced gas handler) is being used with compression pumps, install the motor and protector as normal then install the intake, then the AGH. No shimming is required up to this point. Install the compression pumps per the standard procedure.

For tandem pump installations with high-strength shafts, ensure the pump with the high-strength shaft is installed first, next to the intake/protector.

## 4.7.5 Factory Shimmed Equipment

When installing factory filled or shimmed equipment it is not necessary to shim the equipment in the Field. Always make sure the complete assembly rotates smoothly.

## 4.7.5.1 Mixing Factory Shimmed with non-Factory Shimmed Equipment

When mixing factory shimmed and non-factory shimmed pumps, the factory shimmed pump section should be installed as the lowest pump in the string. That is next to the intake/protector.

If factory shimmed pumps and floater type pumps are being run in the same string the factory shimmed pumps must be placed at the bottom of the string. Once all the pumps are bolted together they must be turned using the correct tool to make sure the complete assemble rotates.

Use factory shimmed coupling between factory shimmed and standard equipment, apply the standard shimming procedure and standard spacing requirements. Standard couplings can be used between standard pumps.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Factory shims sometimes get stuck in a shaft; confirm all of these shims are removed before assembling.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Check for smooth, free rotation of each individual section and overall assembly after spacing.

## Private

## 4.7.6 Shimming Procedure for Pumps (338-Series Through 562-Series Pumps Except 562-Series Pumps Containing H15500N and H21500N Stages)

<!-- image -->

## Note

The following procedure is used to shim pumps (338-series through 562-series pumps except 562-series pumps containing H15500N and HN21500N stages).

1. If a bolt-on intake or gas separator will be used, remove the shipping caps and assemble the intake/gas separator to the protector prior to beginning shaft matching. It is not necessary to shim between these units and the protector because the shaft in an intake or gas separator will sit down on the protector shaft.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Verify that the bolt-on intake/gas separator, protector shafts and coupling all touch when bolted together. Be sure that there is some lift of the intake/gas separator upper shaft end when the equipment is assembled. If there is not sufficient shaft play for the shafts to touch and there is a gap between the shafts and coupling, install sufficient shims to fill the gap up to 1/64-in lift.

2. Pick up the intake/protector assembly with the proper lifting clamp and proceed with the protector-to-motor assembly, flat cable tie-in and protector service procedure.
3. Lower the assembled and serviced motor/protector/intake section into the well until the lifting clamp is resting on the wellhead.
4. Attach the appropriate lifting clamp to the lower pump section. Remove the shipping caps and check the shaft for free rotation and endplay. Tap the shaft into the full-down position with a rubber mallet or wood block before matching.

<!-- image -->

## Note

It is advisable to record the shaft measurement at the bottom end with the shaft in the full-down position. This is to verify that the matching process is started from the full-down position after the pump is lifted vertical. This should be done on the pipe deck prior to starting the assembly.

## Private

5. Lift the pump to the vertical position approximately two to three feet above the intake head. After the pump is lifted, recheck the lower shaft setting to make sure the matching process is started from the full-down position.
6. Attach the proper thrust setting tool to the head of the intake with the coupling installed as shown in Figure 4-39. Loosen the jam nut on the center bolt and turn the bolt down until it touches the divider in the coupling. Tighten the bolt to 60 lbf in (5 lbf ft). Do not overtighten! Tighten the jam nut while holding a backup on the center bolt. Remove the thrust setting tool.
7. Install the thrust setting tool on the pump base as shown in Figure 4-40. When doing so, reverse the attaching bolts, not the tool. The center bolt head must remain next to the bottom of the pump shaft. Using shims, fill space A (see Figure 4-40) between the pump shaft and the bolt head with the appropriate amount of shims to fill, but not lift the shaft.

Figure 4-39: Thrust setting tool on the top end of the protector

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Note

Start with 1/16-in shims and graduate down in thickness until no 1/200-in shims will fit into the gap. Once this is done, there will be less than 1/200-in gap remaining.

Figure 4-40: Thrust setting tool on the pump base

<!-- image -->

8. Remove the shims from space A and add a 1/64-in shim from the shim stack. This will satisfy the spacing requirement shown in Table 4-24. Install the shim stack into the intake coupling. Remove the thrust setting tool from the bottom of the pump and install the pump on the intake. Tighten bolts in accordance with torque specifications.
9. Repeat steps 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 for each additional tandem pump.

<!-- image -->

## Note

- 1) Steps 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 may also be used for matching integral-intake lower-tandem (LT) pumps to protectors. The proper thrust setting tool will be required to match from the LT base to the protector.
- 2) Check for smooth, free rotation of each individual section and overall assembly after spacing.

## 4.7.7 Shimming Procedure for Pumps (338-Series, 387-Series and 400-Series Pumps)

<!-- image -->

## Note

Use this shimming procedure when measurements must be taken and available space restricts placing shims in the gap.

## Private

1. If a bolt-on intake or gas separator will be used, remove the shipping caps and assemble the intake/gas separator to the protector prior to beginning shaft matching. It is not necessary to shim between these units and the protector because the shaft in an intake or gas separator will sit down on the protector shaft.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Verify that the bolt-on intake/gas separator, protector shafts and coupling all touch when bolted together. Be sure that there is some lift of the intake/gas separator upper shaft end when the equipment is assembled. If there is not sufficient shaft play for the shafts to touch and there is a gap between the shafts and coupling, install sufficient shims to fill the gap up to 1/64-in lift.

2. Pick up the intake/protector assembly with the proper lifting clamp and proceed with the protector-to-motor assembly, flat cable tie-in and protector service procedure.
3. Lower the assembled and serviced motor/protector/intake section into the well until the lifting clamp is resting on the wellhead.
4. Attach the appropriate lifting clamp to the lower pump section (or AGH if being used). Remove the shipping caps and check the shaft for free rotation and endplay. Tap the shaft into the full-down position with a rubber mallet or wood block before matching.

<!-- image -->

## Note

It is advisable to record the shaft measurement at the bottom end with the shaft in the full-down position. This is to verify that the matching process is started from the full-down position after the pump is lifted vertical. This should be done on the pipe deck prior to starting the assembly.

5. Lift the pump/AGH to the vertical position approximately two to three feet above the intake head. After the pump is lifted, recheck the lower shaft setting to ensure the matching process is started from the full-down position.
6. Attach the proper thrust setting tool to the head of the intake with the coupling installed as shown in Figure 4-41. Loosen the jam nut on the center bolt and turn the bolt down until it touches the divider in the coupling. Tighten the bolt to 60 lbf-in (5 lbf-ft). Do not overtighten! Tighten the jam nut while holding a backup on the center bolt. Remove the thrust setting tool.

## Private

Figure 4-41: Shimming tool positioned on top of the intake adaptor

<!-- image -->

7. Remove the shimming tool from the flange. Measure the distance the center bolt is protruding from the horizontal part of the H (Figure 4-42). Ideally, this should be done with a vernier gauge. This is dimension A .

Figure 4-42: Measuring distance A on shimming tool

<!-- image -->

8. Slacken the jam nut.
9. Install the thrust setting tool on the pump base as shown in Figure 4-43. When doing so, reverse the attaching bolts, not the tool. The center bolt head must remain next to the bottom of the pump/AGH shaft.
10. Using your fingers, adjust the center bolt until it touches the shaft above (do not lift the shaft) and measure the distance between the center bolt and the horizontal. This is dimension B .

Figure 4-43: Thrust setting tool on the pump base

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Note

Dimension B must be less than dimension A.

Figure 4-44: Measuring Dimension B

<!-- image -->

11. Remove the thrust setting tool from the bottom of the pump.
12. Determine dimension C (C = A - B). Dimension C is the difference between dimension A and dimension B or the gap between the coupling divider and the shaft.
13. Set up value C on the caliper. Using shims, fill up the space between the caliper legs with the appropriate amount of shims to fill the gap. Refer to Figure 4-45.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Start with 1/16-in shims and graduate down in thickness until no 1/200-in shims will fit into the gap. Once this is done, there will be less than 1/200-in gap remaining.

Figure 4-45: Setting up caliper to reflect dimension C

<!-- image -->

14. Remove the shims from the caliper and add a 1/64-in to this shim stack. This will satisfy the spacing requirement shown in Table 4-24.

## Private

15. Install the shim stack on the intake coupling and subsequently install the pump onto the intake. Tighten the bolts in accordance with the torque specifications.
16. Repeat steps 4 to 15 for each additional tandem pump.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Check for smooth, free rotation of each individual section and overall assembly after spacing.

## 4.7.8 Shimming Procedure for Pumps Requiring Lift (562-Series Pumps Containing H15500N and H21500N Stages and 650-Series Through 1125-Series Pumps)

<!-- image -->

## Note

The following procedure is used to shim pumps requiring lift (562-series pumps containing H15500N and HN21500N stages and 650-series through 1125-series pumps). The shafts of theses pumps must be matched for lifting, instead of with a gap which would allow the shaft to drop as it transfers load to the protector thrust bearing. This done because larger pumps do not have a downthrust washer for the impellers to ride on.

Procedures for determining the clearance between the protector shaft and pump shaft and setting thrust are:

1. If a bolt-on intake or gas separator will be used, remove the shipping caps and assemble the intake/gas separator to the protector prior to beginning shaft matching.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Verify that the bolt-on intake/gas separator, protector shafts and coupling all touch when bolted together. Be sure that there is some lift of the intake/gas separator upper shaft end when the equipment is assembled. If there is not sufficient shaft play for the shafts to touch and there is a gap between the shafts and coupling, install sufficient shims to fill the gap up to 1/64-in lift.

2. Pick up the intake/protector assembly with the proper lifting clamp and proceed with the protector-to-motor assembly, flat cable tie-in and protector service procedure.

## Private

3. Lower the assembled and serviced motor/protector/intake section into the well until the lifting clamp is resting on the wellhead.
4. Attach the appropriate lifting clamp to the lower pump section. Remove the shipping caps and check the shaft for free rotation and endplay. Tap the shaft into the full-down position with a rubber mallet or wood block before matching.

<!-- image -->

## Note

It is advisable to record the shaft measurement at the bottom end with the shaft in the full-down position. This is to verify that the matching process is started from the full-down position after the pump is lifted vertical.

5. Lift the pump to the vertical position approximately two to three feet above the intake head. After the pump is lifted, recheck the lower shaft setting to ensure the matching process is started from the full-down position.
6. Attach the proper thrust setting tool to the head of the intake/protector with the coupling installed as shown in Figure 4-41. Loosen the jam nut on the center bolt and turn the bolt down until it touches the divider in the coupling. Tighten the bolt to 60 lbf-in (5 lbf-ft). Do not overtighten! Tighten the jam nut while holding a backup on the center bolt. Remove the thrust setting tool.
7. Install the thrust setting tool on the pump base as shown in Figure 4-46. When doing so, flip the attaching bolts, not the tool. The center bolt head must remain next to the bottom of the pump shaft. Using shims, fill space A (see Figure 4-46) between the pump shaft and the bolt head with the appropriate amount of shims to fill the space and place the shims in the coupling.

Figure 4-46: Thrust setting tool on the pump base

<!-- image -->

## Private

8. Remove the thrust setting tool. Select additional shims to achieve the correct shaft lift. The correct shaft lift is determined by the pump series. (Specifications are provided in Table 4-24.) Place these additional shims in the coupling and bolt the pump to the intake/protector. Torque to specifications.
9. Set the thrust on additional tandem pumps using procedures shown in steps 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Each additional tandem pump must be lifted the same amount as the lower pump (that is, shims must be added as in Step 8 at each tandem joint) to ensure the complete rotating assembly is lifted the amount specified in Table 4-24.

## 4.8 Flat Cable Attachment to the Motor

<!-- image -->

Note: Maximus information

For Maximus, refer to Appendix C: Maximus.

Use the following procedure to prepare the motor for cable attachment.

1. Raise the assembly until the motor head is approximately five feet above the rig floor.
2. Feed the flat cable through the cable sheave. Using a winch line, hoist the sheave to a height ten feet above the rig floor. Do not bend the cable excessively when feeding it through the sheave. The flat cable splice should be supported by a person when it is being pulled from the spool to prevent it from being stretched.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Hold the cable, do NOT pull on the pothead

3. Temporarily band the flat cable to the protector so that the pothead is just above the motor terminal cover. The numbers on the pothead should be facing out, otherwise it will not connect to the motor.
4. Remove the pothole cover and check the motor phase-to-phase resistance. (Phase-to-phase resistance values are shown in the Technical and Engineering Information section.)

## Private

<!-- image -->

## Note

Resistances are additive when tandem motors are connected.

<!-- image -->

## Note

The phase-to-ground motor resistance will be measured at the cable reel after the flat cable is connected to the motor.

5. Remove the shipping cap from the flat cable extension and the terminal cover from the motor head.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Ensure this area remains free of moisture and debris.

6. The O-ring on the pothead must be changed before the terminals can be connected. Lubricate the new O-ring with Dow Corning 111 (p/n 100386898). Refer to the ALFORM-D connection tables (InTouch ID: 3255850) for a complete list of O-ring part numbers.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Light

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Machinery equipment hand tools

## Caution

Do not use a metal tool when removing the O-ring from the flange groove. Damaged sealing surfaces can result in short equipment runlife.

## 4.8.1 Phasing the Power Cable

<!-- image -->

## Note

Phasing of the motor and cable can also be done with a Motor Rotation Indicator. Since models might differ please read the instructions accompanying the device.

<!-- image -->

## Hint

Reda equipment shafts should turn counter clockwise when viewed from the top pump down.

## Private

Achieving the correct rotation on the first start begins when the Flat Cable Extension (FCE) is attached to the motor. All motors have their terminal leads identified A, B and C at the pothole. When the power supply phasing corresponds with the motor phasing, the pump will rotate in the correct direction. Prior to making connections, the following must be determined.

- the way the incoming power is phased
- after the FCE is connected to the motor, which leads of the power cable correspond with the motor terminals A, B and C

After these are determined, the cable identified as phase A can be connected to the power supply phase A, phase B to B and C to C.

1. Determine which phase of the FCE is the easiest to connect to the motor lead marked A. Connect a jumper wire between ground and the phase identified as the one which will be connected to motor lead A. A good grounding location is any bolt on the motor. Using an ohm meter, go to the cable reel and connect one test lead to ground (the cable reel or armor). Use the other test lead to determine which of the three conductors is grounded. Mark this phase A.
2. Repeat the Step 1 procedure for B and C phases as the FCE is connected to the motor. When this is done, the three phases of cable will be identified at the top end of the spool.
3. If a field attachable connector is installed at the wellhead, care must be taken to ensure the rotation is unchanged. The procedures above can be used to track the phasing through the wellhead penetrator and upper pigtail to the junction box. The upper pigtail conductors should be marked using different color electrical tape to identify which is phase A, B and C.

Integrity of the complete string and phasing accuracy of the cable can be checked using the Motor Rotation Indicator. After the ESP has been assembled, connect the Motor Rotation Indicator terminals to the cable conductors on the cable reel. Rotate the shaft rapidly with a spline wrench in counterclockwise direction. Determine phase sequence and mark conductors with different color pieces of tapes to identify each phase A, B and C. In cases where the indicator shows no sign of rotation, indicate the that connection was missed or there is problem with the cable.

## 4.8.2 Flat Cable Tie-In

1. Using motor lead pliers and a small hammer, grip the motor lead marked A just below the terminal. Connect this lead to the corresponding pothead terminal.

## Private

<!-- image -->

## Note

Do not pull more than 2.5 inches of lead from the pothole when making this connection. Do not damage the insulation.

2. Using approximately three feet of Teflon® tape, start at the bottom and apply two half-lap layers of tape to the connection. Repeat this taping procedure for the other leads.

<!-- image -->

## Note

For motors with terminal voltages greater than 2500 V, three (four if space permits) half-wrap layers should be applied to each lead.

3. Bind the three leads together using four half-wrap layers and double knot Teflon tape to prevent it coming loose.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Do not use cotton tape. Cotton tape (p/n 521203) is obsolete. Teflon tape should be used to protect the connection in place of the cotton tape. Three or four layers, wrapped over all three conductors and knotted with two half-hitches has been used with success in high temperature applications.

4. Ensure the pothole is full of oil.
5. Carefully push the leads into the motor head. Ensure there is no foreign material between the flanges.
6. Tighten the pothead flange. To ensure a good connection, the pothead flange must be drawn down evenly, alternating from bolt-to-bolt a few threads at a time. Torque to specification. (Torque specifications are shown in the Technical and Engineering Information section.)

## 4.8.3 Non-Maximus Plug-In Pothead Installation

<!-- image -->

Note: Maximus information

For Maximus, refer to Appendix C: Maximus.

A redesign of the older X-type plug-in potheads and flat cable assemblies has been completed for 456- and 540-series motors. No parts are interchangeable between the older X-type and the new-design flat cables or pothead assemblies.

## Private

The new design uses the same installation O-rings as the tape-in pothead. Equipment tests and assembly procedures for the plug-in design are the same as tests and procedures for the tape-in design.

1. Remove the shipping cap from the flat cable extension.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Light

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Machinery equipment hand tools

Caution

Do not use a metal tool when removing the O-ring from the flange groove. Damaged sealing surfaces can result in short equipment runlife.

2. Look inside the pothead flange to determine if a flat-black colored filler washer is present. Potheads may be shipped with the filler washer loose in the protective cap or installed in the pothead cavity. If a filler washer is not installed, the light gray color of the pothead sealing block will be observed.
3. If a filler washer is present, do not permanently remove it. Apply a coating of Dow #4 grease and install it into the pothead cavity. Push it into the cavity; it will be pushed to the proper location when the pothead is plugged to the motor terminal block.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Do not install two filler washers. The installation of two filler washer may result in future disassembly problems when the pothead is to be unplugged from the motor.

4. Purge air and connect an oil-fill hose to the motor head fill valve. Pump slowly until oil comes out around the pothole block. Clean any residual contamination from the flat cable pothead.
5. Fill the pothole area with the correct oil, wet pothead terminals and insulator with oil, align terminals, then carefully push the pothead assembly into the motor pothole by hand. Install retaining nuts, tighten down evenly and torque to recommended specifications. (Torque specifications are shown in the Technical and Engineering Information section.)

## 4.9 Oil Filling Procedures for Protectors

Protectors are filled with oil prior to shipment from the manufacturing facility. Oil is lost from the protector during field assembly, therefore, some refilling is required. Oil filling procedures for the various protectors are provided in the following sections.

## Private

<!-- image -->

## Note

When using protectors with sand avoidance head, be sure that all plugs in the sand avoidance head are removed from the drain hole.

Proper installation of plugs is vital to ensuring the Total-Run-Life (TRL) of the ESP system is achieved. Ensure the vent plugs (standard, short and long) and drain-and-fill valves used are the latest revision per the OneCAT bill of materials.

<!-- image -->

Figure 4-47: Standard (Vent and Drain) Plug

Figure 4-48: Short and Long Vent Plugs

<!-- image -->

Figure 4-49: Drain and Fill Valve

<!-- image -->

When a plug or valve is removed and installed the following steps must be taken:

1. Remove the plug or valve. If removing the plug, use a 3/4-in wrench to backup the valve to prevent loosening the valve.
2. Remove the old lead gasket. Do not reuse lead gaskets.
3. Install a new lead gasket. Do not install two lead gaskets.
4. Install the plug (with lead gasket) or valve (with lead gasket). Torque plugs to 15 ft-lbf and valves to 35 ft-lbf.

## 4.9.1 66L Type (except 738, see note below)

<!-- image -->

## Note

This protector is different from 738 Type 66. Use proper procedures for the correct series protectors.

738 protector part numbers 0332841, W332841, 0662015 are to be serviced per the procedure in 4.9.1: 66L Type (except 738, see note below).

<!-- image -->

## Vent plug and drain-and-fill valve

Potential Severity:

Light

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Machinery equipment hand tools

Caution

Ensure the vent plugs and drain-and-fill valves used are the latest revision per the OneCAT bill of materials. Make sure that a calibrated torque wrench is used to install plugs. Vent plugs should be torqued to 15 ft-lbf and the drain-and-fill valves should be torqued to 35 ft-lbf.

1. Starting from the top of the protector using a 5/16-in allen wrench, remove the plug from vent 2. The number of each vent is stamped on the housing next to the corresponding hole.
2. Remove and discard the lead gasket that accompanies each plug. A new lead gasket installed over a used gasket can result in a leak. The vent plugs should be kept together where they will not be misplaced or forgotten.
3. The next vent down is stamped 'Drain.' It should not be removed but checked to ensure that it is tight. All vent plugs are torqued to 15 ft-lbf.
4. Below the drain valve is vent 1. Remove the plug from vent 1.
5. In the base of the protector is a drain-and-fill valve. Tighten this valve using a 3/4-in socket to 35 ft-lbf and tighten the vent plug that is in the center of the valve using the 5/16-in allen wrench to 15 ft-lbf.

<!-- image -->

## Note

When removing the vent plug, use a 3/4-in wrench to backup the drain-and-fill valve to prevent it from loosening.

## Private

6. All protectors are serviced from the drain-and-fill valve located in the motor head. Locate this valve and tighten it using the 3/4-in socket to 35 ft-lbf.
7. Remove the vent plug and lead gasket from the center of the drain-and-fill valve.
8. Purge the air out of the oil pump and hose/adapter assembly, then screw the adapter into the drain-and-fill valve.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Vent plugs are torqued to 15 ft-lbf.

9. Connect the oil hose to the adapter and begin pumping oil into the motor head.
10. Turn the pump handle slowly at a rate of 45 rpm (do not exceed 40 psi) to allow the air to migrate up and out of vent 1. As oil starts to flow from vent 1, it will still contain some air bubbles. Continue to pump until the oil is bubble free.
11. Reinstall the vent plug with a new lead gasket (p/n 15008). Torque vent plug to 15 ft-lbf.
12. Continue pumping until oil flows from vent 2. Again, ensure that the oil is bubble-free before installing the vent plug with a new lead gasket.
13. Continue pumping until oil flows from the weep hole located in the base of the intake.
14. Remove the adapter from the drain-and-fill valve in the motor head.
15. Install the vent plug with a new lead gasket and torque 15 ft-lbf. The protector is now serviced and is ready to install in the well.
16. Check all other drain-and-fill valves and vent plugs to insure that they are torqued to specification.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Confirm that all vent plug(s) and drain-and-fill valve(s) are flush to or recessed into the equipment base, body and/or head after servicing. Vent plugs are torqued to 15 ft-lbf and drain-and-fill valves are torqued to 35 ft-lbf.

## Private

## 4.9.2 738 Type 66 (see note below)

<!-- image -->

## Note

This protector is different from 66L Type. Use proper procedures for the correct series protectors.

<!-- image -->

## Note

738 protector part numbers 0332841, W332841, 0662015 are to be serviced per the procedure in 4.9.1: 66L Type (except 738, see note below)

<!-- image -->

## Vent plug and drain-and-fill valve

Potential Severity:

Light

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Machinery equipment hand tools

## Caution

Ensure the vent plugs and drain-and-fill valves used are the latest revision per the OneCAT bill of materials. Make sure that a calibrated torque wrench is used to install plugs. Vent plugs should be torqued to 15 ft-lbf and the drain-and-fill valves should be torqued to 35 ft-lbf.

These protectors are identified by a lower housing that is roughly 9 inches shorter than the standard 66L lower housing. Additionally, it has three vent plugs, #3, #4, and #5, that the standard 66L does not have.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Attempts to service this type of protector in the "normal" manner will result in excessive oil pump back pressure (from restricted flow) after the #4 vent plug has been replaced.

1. Mount the protector and make a conventional oil fill connection at the motor head drain-and-fill valve.

<!-- image -->

## Note

When removing the vent plug, use a 3/4-in wrench to backup the drain-and-fill valve to prevent it from loosening.

## Private

2. Remove vent plug #1 and begin pumping to evacuate all air from the coupling area and lower housing.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Vent plugs are torqued to 15 ft-lbf.

3. Pump until bubble-free oil flows from #1 vent. Stop pumping and install the #1 vent plug using new lead gasket.
4. Remove vent plug #4 and begin pumping. Continue until bubble-free oil flows from the #4 vent. Stop pumping and install the #4 vent plug using a new lead gasket.
5. Remove the oil pumping adaptor from the motor head drain-and-fill. Install the vent plug using new lead gasket.
6. Remove vent plug #2 and vent plug #3. Install the oil pump adaptor in vent #3. Lower the protector, attach the oil pump and pump until bubble-free oil flows from vent #2.
7. Remove the adaptor, Reinstall vent plug #2 and vent plug #3 using new lead gaskets. This completes the oil fill procedure for new units.
8. Check all other drain-and-fill valves and vent plugs to insure that they are torqued to specification.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Confirm that all vent plug(s) and drain-and-fill valve(s) are flush to or recessed into the equipment base, body and/or head after servicing. Vent plugs are torqued to 15 ft-lbf and drain-and-fill valves are torqued to 35 ft-lbf.

## Servicing the Protector for Rerun 540, 738 Type 66

The practice of rerunning protectors is not recommended by engineering. If the client insists, the protector should be serviced in a vertical position during the pulling operation.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Reservicing presupposes the protector to be in excellent mechanical condition, internally and externally.

1. Remove the drain-and-fill valve. Check the protector fluid for contamination (i.e., well fluid).
- If well fluid is present, the protector should NOT be rerun.

## Private

<!-- image -->

- If the oil is clear, reinstall the drain-and-fill valve with a new lead gasket (p/n 23903). Remove the vent plug, install the oil filling adapter in preparation for refilling.

## Note

Vent plugs are torqued to 15 ft-lbf.

2. Remove vent plug #5 and check for well fluid. Well fluid at this point is indicative of upper seal leakage. If there is no water present and oil is clear, reinstall the vent plug using a new lead gasket.
3. Remove vent plug #1 and vent plug #4.
4. Begin pumping and continue until bubble-free oil flows from vent #1.
5. Reinstall vent plug #1 using a new lead gasket.
6. Resume pumping until bubble-free oil flows from vent #4.
7. Reinstall vent plug #4 using a new lead gasket.
8. Remove the oil pump adaptor and reinstall the drain-and-fill vent plug using a new lead gasket.
9. Remove vent plug #3.
10. Install the oil pump adaptor and pump until clear oil is being expelled from vent tube in the protector head.
11. Remove the adaptor and reinstall vent plug #3 using a new lead gasket.
12. Clean all well fluid from the ID of protector head and fill with clean oil.
13. Install shipping caps and gaskets. This completes the reservice procedure.
14. Check all other drain-and-fill valves and vent plugs to insure that they are torqued to specification.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Confirm that all vent plug(s) and drain-and-fill valve(s) are flush to or recessed into the equipment base, body and/or head after servicing. Vent plugs are torqued to 15 ft-lbf and drain-and-fill valves are torqued to 35 ft-lbf.

## Private

## 4.9.3 PFSB (Pre-Filled Single Bag) Type

The following procedure is for the single and double bag 540- and 400-series pre-filled protectors. Filling techniques are the same as the 66L, but the design utilizes a short and long vent plug in conjunction with an inner valve.

1. Beginning from the top, torque the vent plug in PF#3 to 15 ft-lbf.
2. Remove the vent plug and lead gasket from PF#4. This vent plug is longer than the rest and should be kept isolated from the others. Figure 4-50 shows the various styles of vent plugs.
3. In the lower section of the protector there are two vents (PF#1 and PF#2) and a drain-and-fill valve (D). Remove the vent plug and lead gasket from PF#1. This is a short plug used to prevent the shipping valve (located behind the plug) from opening.

10. Continue to pump until oil flows from the weep hole located in the base of the pump.
11. Remove the adapter from the drain-and-fill valve in the motor head.
12. Install the vent plug with a new lead gasket and torque 15 ft-lbf. Servicing is now complete.
13. Check all other drain-and-fill valves and vent plugs to insure that they are torqued to specification.

<!-- image -->

Caution

Ensure the vent plugs and drain-and-fill valves used are the latest revision per the OneCAT bill of materials. Make sure that a calibrated torque wrench is used to install plugs. Vent plugs should be torqued to 15 ft-lbf and the drain-and-fill valves should be torqued to 35 ft-lbf.

## Filling Procedure

1. Remove the long vent plugs and lead gaskets from vents #3 and PF#4 in the top of the protector.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Long plugs can be identified by a slot across the head resembling a screwdriver slot.

<!-- image -->

## Note

When removing the vent plug, use a 3/4-in wrench to backup the drain-and-fill valve to prevent it from loosening.

2. Raise the protector until filling from the motor head drain-and-fill valve is possible.
3. Install an oil pump at the motor head drain-and-fill valve.
4. Remove the vent plug and lead gasket from vent #5.
5. Start pumping slowly until bubble-free oil flows from vent #5.

## Private

<!-- image -->

## Note

Vent plugs are torqued to 15 ft-lbf.

6. Reinstall vent #5 using a new lead gasket.
7. Remove the short plug and lead gasket from vent PF#1 and replace with one of the long vent plugs removed from vent #3 or PF#4 using a new lead gasket.
8. Remove vent plugs and lead gaskets from vents #2 or #6 in the middle section of the protector.
9. Pump slowly until bubble-free oil flows from either vent #2 or #6.
10. Reinstall the vent plug using a new lead gasket at the vent with oil flow.
11. Continue pumping until bubble-free oil flows from remaining open vent.
12. Reinstall the vent plug using new lead gasket.
13. Remove the short vent plug and lead gasket from vent PF#7 and replace with the remaining long vent plug and new lead gasket.
14. Continue pumping slowly until bubble-free oil flows from vent #3. Reinstall the vent plug using new lead gasket.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Short vent plugs are used in vents #3 and PF#4. Be careful not to strip threads on short plugs.

15. Continue pumping until bubble-free oil flows from vent PF#4. Reinstall the vent plug using new lead gasket.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Confirm that all vent plug(s) and drain-and-fill valve(s) are flush to or recessed into the equipment base, body and/or head after servicing. Vent plugs are torqued to 15 ft-lbf and drain-and-fill valves are torqued to 35 ft-lbf.

## Vent plug and drain-and-fill valve

Caution

Potential Severity:

Light

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Machinery equipment hand tools

Ensure the vent plugs and drain-and-fill valves used are the latest revision per the OneCAT bill of materials. Make sure that a calibrated torque wrench is used to install plugs. Vent plugs should be torqued to 15 ft-lbf and the drain-and-fill valves should be torqued to 35 ft-lbf.

1. Remove the shipping caps and install the protector between the motor and intake. Connect the cable to the motor.

## Private

<!-- image -->

## Note

When removing the vent plug, use a 3/4-in wrench to backup the drain-and-fill valve to prevent it from loosening.

2. Remove the vent plug from the drain-and-fill valve in the motor head and connect the oil fill pump and adapter.
3. Remove the lower 'S' plug from the thrust bearing center body (the first body above the base).

<!-- image -->

## Note

Vent plugs are torqued to 15 ft-lbf.

4. Slowly pump motor oil into the head of the motor until bubble-free oil flows from the open 'S' hole. Reinstall the standard plug using a new lead gasket.
5. Remove the standard plug from the 'S' hole located in the second body above the base.
6. Continue to pump motor oil into the head of the motor until bubble-free oil flows from the open 'S' hole. Reinstall the standard plug using a new lead gasket.
7. There are two ports marked 'OPEN' in the top body (4th body above the base). The two 'OPEN' ports are 180 degrees apart in the body. These 'OPEN' ports should remain open during installation into the well. The OPEN ports are NOT in the head of the protector.
8. Remove the 'S' and 'OPEN' plugs from the highest center body (fourth body above the base).
9. Continue pumping motor oil through the motor head until bubble-free oil flows from the 'S' port.
10. Reinstall the standard plug using a new lead gasket in the 'S' port.
11. Continue pumping until bubble-free oil flows from the 'OPEN' holes.
12. Confirm that the two plugs in the head of the protector are open.
13. Check all other drain-and-fill valves and vent plugs to insure that they are torqued to specification.

## Private

<!-- image -->

## Note

Confirm that all vent plug(s) and drain-and-fill valve(s) are flush to or recessed into the equipment base, body and/or head after servicing. Vent plugs are torqued to 15 ft-lbf and drain-and-fill valves are torqued to 35 ft-lbf.

<!-- image -->

## Note

The 738/562 or 738/738 BPBSL protector is not the same as a 540 or 456 modular protector. There is no valve in the base, and no PF plug used to actuate a valve, therefore installing a long plug is not necessary.

<!-- image -->

## Note

For tandem 738 BPBSL protectors ensure that the 'OPEN' holes of the lower protector are closed with standard plugs and new lead gaskets.
