## 4.10 Power Cable Banding

<!-- image -->

## Note

Signode air bander repair manual can be found on InTouch Content ID 3465535.

Inspect the condition of the rig equipment to ensure that it is in good working order. Tubing slips should be clean and sharp. The backups on the power tongs should be in good condition to prevent the tubing from rotating when making up a joint. Inspect the backup dies for buildup of paraffin that would allow the tubing to slip. Any questionable equipment should be reported to rig supervisor before proceeding with the installation.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Many power cables have been damaged because the backups were not turned over or slipped while making up the first joint.

The rig must be centered over the hole to provide adequate clearance for the cable and cable bands. This alignment should be checked periodically when running the equipment in the hole.

Instruct the person operating the automatic cable spooler to ensure the cable feeds off the reel at an even speed and tension. The practice of allowing the cable tension, as the unit is being lowered, to furnish spooling power should not be tolerated. The cable should always be spooled off the top of the reel.

54 in (1.4 m) cable sheaves are recommended because larger cable sheaves reduce stress to the cable. Once the flat cable extension (FCE) splice is banded to the tubing, the cable sheave can be raised to its running height of not more than 30 ft (9 m) above the ground. It should be secured with its load sling and a safety sling attached to a separate support.

To avoid damage to the flat cable make sure that it does not pass over any of the lock plates on the equipment. Once the FCE (Flat Cable Extension) is installed ensure it does not pass over a lock plate on the equipment as this will increase the OD of the equipment or this will reduce the available clearance and possibly cause a premature failure.

Pneumatic banding is preferred to hand banding since tension applied to the band can be controlled with far greater precision. Bands must be placed so that the buckle is located on the right hand side of the cable in the void between the cable and the tubing. This will prevent the buckle from being pushed into

## Private

the cable and damaging it when the band is being tightened. Cable bands should be tight enough to distort the armor but not crush it. If a band is loose, remove and replace it. When placing bands on the flat cable extensions, make sure the cable fits against the flat spots on the head and base of each piece of equipment. The flat cable extension splice must be a minimum of 5 ft (1.5 m) above the pump discharge head and not across a tubing collar. Bands must be installed above and below all splices to prevent any cable load from being transmitted to the splice.

Typically, two bands per tubing joint is the minimum requirement for supporting the power cable. One band should be placed 4 ft (1.2 m) above the tubing collar and one in the middle of the joint. Consideration should be given to installing several bands (10 per joint) to the first two joints. This practice provides additional cable support in the area of 'tubing cut off' that may occur during a fishing operation.

## 4.10.1 Installation of Cable Protectolisers with Non-Pre-Engaged Fasteners

The following procedure should be used to install Lasalle cable protectolisers.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Use a standard pneumatic installation kit for this procedure.

<!-- image -->

## Note

All protectolisers are supplied in the closed position.

1. Undo the saddle clamp fastener at the top of the protectoliser to enable access for the cable.
2. Undo the protectoliser cap-screw fastener using the impact wrench (supplied). This will allow the collar to be opened.
3. Move the protectoliser up to the pump component flange neck and position the cable in the slot.
4. Close the protectoliser around the pump component flange neck and engage the cap-screw fastener by at least two to three full threads into the protectoliser body using the T-bar supplied with the installation kit. (If any resistance is met, then the cap-screw fastener is cross-threaded. Any further tightening will result in the protectoliser threads being damaged and the protectoliser having to be replaced.)

## Private

5. Tighten the cap-screw fastener using the impact wrench until the unit stalls (between five to eight seconds).

<!-- image -->

## Note

The collar/body cap-screw fasteners are torqued to 30 lbf-ft. The saddle clamp/body cap-screw fasteners (if used) are torqued to 20 lbf-ft.

6. The cap-screw fastener torque applied using the impact wrench should be periodically confirmed using the torque wrench supplied with the installation kit.

## 4.10.2 Removal Of Cable Protectolisers With Non-Pre-Engaged Fasteners

The following procedure should be used to remove Lasalle cable protectolisers.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Use a standard pneumatic installation kit for this removal procedure.

1. Ensure the hexagonal bit of the impact wrench is fully inserted into the cap-screw head before activating the impact wrench.
2. Activate the impact wrench and fully remove the cap-screw from the saddle clamp and remove the cable.
3. Activate the impact wrench and fully remove the cap-screw from the protectoliser body.
4. Remove the cable protectoliser from the pump string.
5. Using the T-bar (provided in the installation kit), engage the cap-screw fasteners by at least two to three full threads into the protectoliser body and saddle clamp. If any resistance is encountered, the cap-screw fastener is cross-threaded and any further tightening will result in the protectoliser threads being damaged and the protectoliser having to be replaced.
6. Tighten the cap-screw fasteners using the impact wrench (provide in the installation kit).
7. The protectoliser can now be stored for future use.

## 4.10.3 Installation of All-Cast Cable Protectors

The following procedure is used to install Lasalle all-cast cable protectors.

## Private

<!-- image -->

## Note

Use a standard pneumatic installation kit for this procedure.

<!-- image -->

## Note

All protectors are supplied in the closed position.

1. Disengage the protector collar locking mechanism using the impact wrench. This involves ensuring the cap-screw fastener is fully retracted from the toggle mechanism. Rotate the toggle 90 degrees then remove the toggle from the locating lug of the protector body.
2. Move the protector up to the tubing ensuring the cables/control lines are correctly positioned in the appropriate slots.
3. Close the protector around the tubing ensuring the toggle is secured within the locating lug of the protector body.
4. Torque the cap-screw fasteners to 30 lbf-ft using the impact wrench from the installation kit until the unit stalls (between 5 to 8 seconds).

<!-- image -->

## Note

The cap-screw fastener torque applied using the impact wrench should be periodically confirmed using the torque wrench supplied with the installation kit. The torque applied on the first 10 protectors should be confirmed followed by 10% of the remainder. A change of installation personnel should also initiate a confirmation of torque values.

## 4.10.4 Removal of All-Cast Cable Protectors

The following procedure is used to remove Lasalle all-cast cable protectors.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Use a standard pneumatic installation kit for this removal procedure.

1. Ensure the hexagonal bit of the torque wrench or T-bar is fully inserted into the cap-screw.
2. Release the tension of the fastener a few turns prior to fully unscrewing the fastener with the impact wrench.
3. Remove the cable protector from the tubing.
4. Using the T-bar engage the cap-screw fastener into the protector body.

## Private

5. Fully tighten the cap-screw fastener using the impact wrench from the installation kit.
6. The protector can now be stored for future use.

## 4.11 Lowering Equipment into the Well

This practice will ensure that the motor is physically connected to the rest of the equipment. There is a tool ( drawing 100075454 ) available that will allow the complete string of equipment to be rotated.

Once the last pump assembled to the string the complete assembly should be rotated using the correct tool, while this is being done a rotation meter should be connected to the motor leads to determine that the motor is turning. This can also be used to determine phase rotation. If a rotation meter is not available a Fluke or Triplett may be used to detect the EMF.

When running the unit into the well, the rig operator must be aware of the cable at all times. Maintain a running speed of approximately 1000 ft/hr (305 m/hr) to allow the spooler to provide minimum cable tension. All stops and starts must be slow and smooth to prevent the tubing from bouncing. Bouncing will damage the cable and protector seals.

## 4.11.1 Suspending ESP String

It is not recommended to interrupt installation and leave equipment hanging in the well or derrick overnight. There are, however, cases were this is unavoidable. In such cases the following practices are recommended.

## Suspending Equipment Above Ground

Submersible equipment is designed to be hung and will not support its own weight. A string may be hung (not racked) in the derrick provided it is hung by equipment that is rated and certified for the specific use of lifting ESP equipment. To minimize hazards, it must also be secured in a way to eliminate horizontal movement.

## Suspending Equipment in Well Prior to Run-In-Hole (RIH)

Job timing must be taken into consideration before starting to assemble equipment. If equipment cannot be run immediately after assembly, the equipment may need to be hung in the well hole and the hole sealed for control. This most often occurs on unlit land rigs which operate only during the day

## Private

light hours. BOPs and HyDrills cannot fully seal around cable and may cause damage; therefore, the MLE should not be installed. In this case, the following procedure must be followed.

Assemble the equipment string according to the procedures in this manual, including servicing the motor. Do not connect the MLE to the motor. Completely service the protector as per procedure. Equipment can then be hung in the well and the BOP can seal around the tubing. When the equipment is retrieved, remove the long plug in the PF port before attaching the MLE (this is to reduce the amount of oil lost from the pothead.) Attach the MLE to the pothead and service the protector as per procedure, replacing the long plug when appropriate. Ensure that the oil is being pumped in through the D&amp;F Valve in the motor head. Continue running equipment in hole as per normal operating procedure.

There have been problems resulting from assembling equipment, not servicing it with oil and then lowering it into a well full of kill fluids. The equipment will always fill with well fluid in these circumstances resulting in premature failure.

## Suspending Equipment During Run-In-Hole (RIH)

If during the run it is decided the HyDrill must be closed around the cable then the closing pressure should be limited to 500 lbf/in 2 (3447 kPa) to minimize cable damage. Always electrically test and examine the cable for damage prior to continuing the run.

There is no way to fully secure the well around a cable. Closing the HyDrill around the cable as described above will minimize the leakage area but will not eliminate it. To fully secure the well the cable would have to be cut and the HyDrill closed around the tubing above the cable. Then the cable would need to be repaired (spliced) when the running operation continued.

## 4.11.2 Check Valve

A check valve may be installed at the pump discharge when installing a pump in a well where no gas problem exists. In gassy wells, the check valve should be installed one to six joints above the pump depending on the amount of gas. This practice provides a compression chamber for the purpose of avoiding a gas lock in the pump.

## 4.11.3 Bleeder Valve

The bleeder valve is installed one to two joints above the check valve. Be sure to check the bleeder plug for tightness (torque 30 lbf).

## Private

## 4.11.4 Checking Cable

Take cable readings approximately every 1000 ft (305 m). Phase-to-phase continuity tests should indicate a balanced reading that will increase as the cable is subjected to increased well temperatures. Phase-to-ground insulation tests should show a high megohm reading (greater than 1500 megohms) at the beginning and slowly drop off as the unit is lowered into the well. After the BOPs have been removed, a final cable check should be made to ensure the integrity of the power cable and motor.

## 4.11.5 Pump Setting Depth

The pump setting depth should be calculated to ensure that the motor bottom is above the perforations. If the pump will be set in the perforated area, a motor shroud must be installed to provide adequate motor cooling.

## 4.11.6 Clearance Check Before Running in the Wellbore

The field service technician should verify that the wellhead is full gauge and the blocks are centered over the wellbore. Often, the BOP stack will be installed prior to the technicians arrival at the wellsite, making visual verification difficult. If this is the case, the following procedure should be used to confirm proper alignment and adequate clearance for the cable to pass through unobstructed.

1. After installing the initial joint of tubing, it should be pulled back up and inspected to ensure there is no evidence of the cable rubbing or damage to the cable bands. Any interference, rubbing or snagging of the bands, clamps or cable must be investigated and corrected before continuing run-in-hole operations.
2. Perform clearance checks at regular intervals during run-in-hole operations to confirm the rig has not settled or shifted or other clearance problems have not developed. These checks can prevent loss of the cable and downhole equipment in the well.
3. The practice of pulling-out-of-hole one or two tubing joints should be performed several times during run-in-hole operations. This will help identify any settling or shifting of the rig, or if conditions in the wellhead or BOP change.

## Private

## 4.11.7 Landing the Tubing Hanger

The tubing hanger should be landed carefully to prevent cable damage. Because a tubing hanger is often offset, it should be landed with the cable facing in the same direction as it was pulled. This will provide a much easier task of pipe fitting the wellhead.

## 4.12 Pulling Equipment from the Well

Equipment removed from a well is valuable equipment and should be treated appropriately. Avoid any rough handling. Pulling speeds should not exceed 1000 ft/hr (305 m/hr) in gassy wells. This is to allow time for gas to migrate out of the cable at a slower rate, thus reducing the chance of damage. Cable bands should be cut off rather than pried or torn off. Tearing off a band can cause the band to cut into the cable.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Submergible equipment must not be racked in the derrick. It is designed to be hung and will not support its own weight. Equipment may be hung in the derrick provided it is hung by equipment that is rated and certified for the specific use of lifting ESP equipment.

## 4.12.1 Annulus Blowdown Requirements

Gas or vapor may be present in ESP power cables and penetrators even if the annular fluid is thought not to contain gas. This gas or vapor may or may not originate from the produced fluids and can be air, which has been entrained within the cable layers. Relieving the pressure is required to ensure that the ESP power cable is not damaged due to the effects of explosive decompression.

The field service technician shall ensure the client is aware of the proper implementation of the blowdown procedure, thereby ensuring the integrity of the power cable. If the annulus is not blown down, the risk of shortened runlife, increased expenditure or loss of revenue is enhanced.

## Definitions

| Term          | Definition                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|---------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| blowdown rate | This rate of pressure relief is set to allow a controlled expansion of any gas trapped inside the cable and to give it time to start to migrate out of the cable. The recommended blowdown rate is 50 psi/min. |

## Private

| step blowdown           | The pressure drop allowed on each blowdown stage. Fifty percent maximum step blowdown is recommended to prevent any trapped gas from expanding to a volume large enough to damage the cable before it is allowed to migrate out of the cable.                                                                   |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| rest period             | The time between each step blowdown. Once any trapped gas has expanded to its maximum volume during the 50% maximum step blowdown it is essential that time is given for this expanded gas to migrate out of the cable before proceeding to the next blowdown stage. The recommended rest period is 30 minutes. |
| final threshold         | The final pressure after the last blowdown stage. Although the potential expansion is at its greatest, once below this threshold, the mechanical integrity of the cable is sufficient to contain the pressure until it dissipates normally. The recommended final threshold is 500 psi or less.                 |
| agreed minimum pressure | This can be atmospheric in most cases but there may be variances. For example, a minimum positive pressure is maintained in an installation where the thermal dynamics may induce an undesirable vacuum in the annulus when the well is shut in.                                                                |

## Blowdown Procedure

The blowdown procedure can be used to blow down the intertubular void containing the submergible motor power cable and may be used in all situations and well conditions, independent of actual annulus or wellbore fluid, where a packer or other pressure-containment equipment separates the annulus from the process.

1. Record the starting pressure (that is, the maximum test pressure).
2. Blow down the annulus at a maximum of 50 psi/min. Continue until the annulus pressure is half of the starting pressure.
3. Shut in the annulus for 30 minutes. At the end of the 30 minute period, record the pressure.
4. Blow down the annulus at a maximum of 50 psi/min. Continue until the annulus pressure is half of the pressure recorded in the previous step (25% of the starting pressure).
5. Shut in the annulus for 30 minutes. At the end of the 30 minute period, record the pressure.
6. Repeat step 4 and step 5 until 500 psi or less has been shut in for the 30-minute period.
7. Blow down the annulus at a maximum of 50 psi/min to an agreed minimum pressure.

## Private

<!-- image -->

## Example

Example 1, maximum annulus test pressure = 4000 psi, minimum pressure = 50 psi

| Total Time   | Action Time   | Annulus Pressure   | Action                                                           |
|--------------|---------------|--------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0 min        | 0 min         | 4000 psi           | Record the starting pressure.                                    |
| 40 min       | 40 min        | 2000 psi           | Blow down at 50 psi/min to 50 % of the starting pressure.        |
| 70 min       | 30 min        | 2000 psi           | Shut in the annulus for 30 min, then record the new pressure.    |
| 90 min       | 20 min        | 1000 psi           | Blow down at 50 psi/min to 50 % of the latest recorded pressure. |
| 120 min      | 30 min        | 1000 psi           | Shut in the annulus for 30 min, then record the new pressure.    |
| 130 min      | 10 min        | 500 psi            | Blow down at 50 psi/min to 50 % of the latest recorded pressure. |
| 160 min      | 30 min        | 500 psi            | Shut in the annulus for 30 min, then record the new pressure.    |
| 170 min      | 9 min         | 50 psi             | Blow down at 50 psi/min to the minimum pressure (50 psi).        |

<!-- image -->

## Example

Example 2

If the annulus pressure starts at 0 psi, then increases to 800 psi when a tubing test is applied, the tubing must be bled back until the annulus pressure has dropped back at a maximum of 50 psi/min to 50 % of the increase (400 psi). It must be held here for 30 minutes, then bled back to the original conditions. Irrespective of the tubing pressures and volumes, the blowdown must be controlled with respect to the annulus pressure.

## 4.12.2 Information Discovery After a 'Short-Run' Event

Typically, the first person to come in contact with a 'short-run' is the Field Service Technician. For the purpose of discussion, a short run will be one less than twelve months from the last date of installation. It is the desire of all involved parties to determine the cause of the failure and correct the problem.

## Private

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Serious

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Machinery equipment hand tools

Warning

Do not teardown or inspect equipment in the field. All Schlumberger and third party equipment needs to be shipped back to a certified facility. If equipment is taken apart in the field valuable information can be lost. Failures need to be analyzed in a controlled area and done by qualified personnel. Failure to follow this rule can lead to additional cost to your customer and to Schlumberger.

Following is a listing of some conditions worth noting on the pull report whenever a short-run failure has occurred.

## Heat Indicators

- brittle, hardened, or cracked O-rings
- melted solder on motor leads (terminals or leads may pull off)
- blistered paint
- melted lead (flat cable extension)

## Housings

- evidence of corrosion, erosion, abrasives, asphaltene, scale, etc.
- burn marks or holes in the housings
- signs of erosion inside the heads and bases of pumps (this is more noticeable on pump bases, particularly near the O-ring groove)

## Shafts

- Are the splines twisted? Which piece? Head or base end?
- 'Turns Excessively Easy' Is it broken? Unless the piece in question is a 62D or S-type motor, it is relatively easy to determine if a shaft is broken.

## Motors

- phase-to-phase and phase-to-ground readings

- fluids in motor(s), type (oil, water, other)
- color (clear, discolored, black)
- bronze filings
- location (top or bottom of motor)

<!-- image -->

## Note

Do not state that a motor contained well fluid. Well fluid is a generic term and may be misleading to the client and investigators.

- Does the motor turn freely, rough, seized, or with great effort? The longer (heavier) the motor is the harder it will be to break it free.
- Are all vent plugs in place?

## Protectors

- Types of fluids in each chamber. Fluid samples should be taken while the protector is still vertical immediately after being pulled from the well.
- Does there seem to be abnormal bushing wear?
- Do you see anything unusual when looking into the top of the protector? Is there any "debris" present? If so, note it and leave it in the protector. If you don't know what the debris is don't speculate.
- Are the vent plugs where they're supposed to be? Make sure and note that the long and short plugs have been put in the "shipping" vent holes.

## Intakes

- Is the intake section plugged? If so with what? Is the screen in good condition or does it appear to be collapsed?
- Is the intake screen corroded?
- Is any foreign material visible inside the intake?
- Does there seem to be excessive bushing wear?

## Pumps

Pumps can be subjected to abuse from abrasives, misapplication, corrosion, etc. If you think there is a problem affecting the operation of the pump first look for the obvious. If there is nothing clearly wrong, you may want to draw some comparisons. How does this pump differ from a new one? Was there any foreign material in the tubing adapter or check valve? Does the intake offer any clues?

## Private

## Cable

- physical condition - burned, jacket blown out, corroded, twisted, armor pulled apart
- resistance readings abnormal
- condition of flat cable extension. If there is a good reason to suspect the motor is burned, get the client's approval to cut the flat cable extension a foot above the pothead and leave this attached to the motor. This may help to determine the cause of motor failure. If the client will not allow this, install a clean pothole cap with a new O-ring. Also look in the pothole and see if there's any sign of water entry such as water tracks or stains.

## Switchboard

- What does the recording amp chart show? Was the unit pumping off? Does the chart show erratic operation? Power spikes? Fluctuating load?
- What were the underload and overload shutdowns set at? Do these setpoints make sense?
- If the motor controller is a K095, download the data base and alarm logger history. Print this out and submit it with the pulling report.
- Are there any fuses blown?

## General

Did the client mention anything unusual such as power disruptions, someone closing a valve or having difficulty keeping the unit running? If anyone makes statements or comments that you think may be important later, write down their name for future reference. Don't speculate. Make every possible effort to provide as much data as possible but don't comment on things that are not visible such as internal conditions.

## 4.12.3 Storing Equipment for Future Use

If the possibility exists that the equipment will be reused or stored for future use, the protector should be drained and refilled with new oil. The pump should be flushed out, preferably with fresh water, then oiled and the caps installed.

The protector should not be reused unless the client will assume responsibility. If the protector will be stored or reused, it should be checked while still in the vertical position to determine whether well fluid has entered the lower section. The Protector Assembly section provides servicing instructions for protectors.

## Private

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Light

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Machinery equipment hand tools

Caution

If a protector is placed in a horizontal position without first being drained, water will flow to the other section. If stored, this can cause a seal to malfunction on the next installation, resulting in a burned motor.

If the oil in the motor contains water or is contaminated, it should be flushed out with clean oil and capped. Water can enter the motor only after passing through the protector (assuming the cable connection at the motor head and the connection between the motor and protector are secure). Since the motor is in a vertical position, any water will be in the bottom and can be checked by removing the plug in the motor base. If no water is present but the oil is dirty, the oil should be replaced.

Shipping caps should be installed where applicable to prevent the leakage of oil or the entry of moisture or dirt.

The cable should be properly spooled onto a reel, sprayed with oil and stored out the sun.

The switchboard should be kept upright unless the oil has been removed from the dashpots.

Minor items are the check and bleeder valves. A coat of oil should preserve them in good condition.

The same precautions used in handling new equipment applies to used equipment. To avoid high repair costs due to mishandling, all precautions handling the equipment must be observed.

## 4.12.4 Checking Equipment for Immediate Rerun

In addition to the items outlined above, the following guidelines will be useful in determining whether equipment is suitable for immediate rerun.

## Motors

- The motor phase-to-ground resistance should be a minimum of 1000 megohms with the megger and be balanced phase-to-phase.
- The motor should be drained, flushed and refilled with oil. Note the condition of the oil being drained from the motor. If brass fillings are present, bearing wear is likely which can lead to mechanical failure. After flushing and

## Private

refilling, check phase-to-ground resistance again. If measurements have not improved, the risk of running the motor is high. (The phase-to-ground resistance of a new motor will measure more than 2000+ megohms)

- Visually check the entire unit. Inspect the housing for corrosion. Inspect the pothead for damage. Inspect the leads for any insulation deterioration. Check the terminals for tightness and good joints. Inspect the top of the motor for cuttings of any type and inspect the flange and sealing area for any washout or damage.
- The motor should turn smoothly with no abnormal drag.
- Check tandem units individually.
- If flat cable is rerun, it should be pressure tested and inspected for any deterioration.

## Protectors

It is not recommended to rerun a protector. If the client wants to rerun a protector, then the following steps should be observed.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Always keep the protector in a vertical position.

- Check flange and sealing areas at top and bottom. Remove the O-ring on the bottom and physically check the ID and OD for any damage.
- Drain all sections of the protector, flush and reservice from the motor head drain and refill with oil. Use new lead gaskets at all vent plugs and use new O-rings. The Protector Assembly section provides servicing instructions for protectors.
- The protector should rotate freely with no abnormal drag.

<!-- image -->

## Note

If there is water in the lower section of the protector, it should not be rerun.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Do not rerun bag-type protectors. There is not a good method to check for water inside the bags.

## Pump and Intake

## Private

Deciding to rerun a pump is the most difficult decision. Many factors must be considered.

- The pump should freely rotate with no drag.
- The shaft should not have any excess side-to-side movement.
- Inspect the discharge, lower pump flange and the intake flanges for corrosion and erosion. All sealing surfaces should be carefully inspected. Carefully inspect the threads on the discharge head. This is an area where corrosion and erosion often occurs.
- Check tandem units individually.

In addition to the preceding checks, the following should be considered.

- history of scale in the well, previous runs, etc.
- number of days run and type of fluid pumped (abrasive or relatively clean)
- barrels per day being pumped at time of unit being pulled (pump or well conditions)
- Why was well pulled? Cable failure, low production, tubing leak, well stimulation, etc.?
- Check for any indication of excessive heat. Excess heat is a sign of operating in downthrust, lack of fluid flow, or both.

## 5 Cables

## 5.1 Product Description

## 5.1.1 ESP Power Cable

The ESP power cable incorporates materials with high-integrity insulation and armor systems. Various grades of armor ranging from standard galvanized steel to Monel® alloys are available. Cables are made of either a modified variant of ethylene propylene diene methylene (EPDM) or an enhanced polypropylene formulation. The polypropylene formulation supports a high temperature rating of up to 121 degC [250 degF] without compromising mechanical and insulating properties. A basic configuration of the main components covers a wide range of ESP applications and is suitable for most well conditions. Each standard cable can be customized to suit the specific requirements of a given well, including temperature and pressure ratings, corrosive properties, and gas/oil ratios.

## 5.1.2 Motorlead Extension (MLE)

The motor lead extension (MLE) designs provide the optimum combination of installation clearance and downhole performance. Polyimide is used as the primary insulation to significantly reduce cable dimensions. For extreme high temperature or specialty applications, PEEK is utilized as the insulation material. The same patented and proprietary materials used in Schlumberger power cables are used in the MLE designs as secondary insulations and jackets to maximize system reliability. The MLE designs support temperature ratings of 121 degC [250 degF] and higher.

## 5.2 Health, Safety and Environment (HSE)

## 5.2.1 Storage and Handling

## 5.2.1.1 MLE Storage

Motorlead Extensions should always be stored in a dry environment, indoors with the shipping cap on and O-rings installed. Any pothead with a lead gasket should also be stored with the provided lead gasket, O-ring and ship cap. The MLE should be left in the same coiled configuration for storage until ready for install. The cable portion coming out of the pothead flange needs to be straight at all times - any side to side or excessive bending is a risk to cause conductor movement which has potential to break the bond between the conductor to sealing mechanism. Any MLE that is received with a desiccant pack(s) in the shipping cap should be stored with the desiccant packs remaining until ready for installation. The desiccant pack(s) should be blue. For packs that have turned pink in color refer to section 5.6.1: Electrical Problems.

Once an MLE is spliced to the cable, it is recommended to still store this indoors, with O-rings and gaskets installed and the ship cap secured.

## 5.2.1.2 Cable Handling

Power cable is typically shipped on large reels. The purpose of the reel is to allow easy cable feed into and out of the well and to protect the cable during transport and handling.

Cable should always be transported on cable reels. In the event that a power cable on a reel is being transported with the spliced flat cable extension on it, independently secure the extension and the power cable. A crane and spreader bar are recommended to lift cable reels. A forklift may be used. If a forklift is used, lift the reel through the spokes from the side, never against the cable. Reels should be secured to the truck when transported. Never allow the reel of cable to roll against objects that might crush or damage the cable or reel.

## Private

Warning

Always ensure that the weight of the load is less than the load rating of the lifting equipment. Never exceed the load rating of hoists, cranes, forklifts, spreader bars, chains, slings or other lifting equipment. Refer to the Artificial Lift Mechanical Lifting Standard (InTouch ID 4557363) for more information regarding lifting.

Prior to moving the cable ensure that the path the move will take is clear. Warn all personnel in the area that the move is about to take place.

## Placement

A section of heavy-walled pipe, which has been approved for the purpose, should be inserted through the reel to serve as an axle. Lift with a spreader bar attached to the axle. A short spacer should be placed between the reel and the stand on each side.

Never handle a reel of cable by making a sling of wire line or chains that touch the cable. Protect the cable from being smashed or cut.

Always use a spreader bar when lifting cable reels. Never lift a reel of cable with a sling of wire line or chains.

## 5.4.2 Cable Construction Materials

Schlumberger uses a modular cable concept. A cable is considered a customized assembly of components (conductor, insulation, etc.). The selection of these components is based on a thorough analysis of the client's well conditions and expected performance. Through the proper selection of materials, the cable design can be precisely tailored to provide best-in-class application performance. The focus is on optimizing total value (price and performance) to the client.

Commonly used materials for various cable components are:

## Conductor

- stranded
- compacted strand
- solid

Figure 5-20: Cable conductor

<!-- image -->

## Insulation

- polypropylene copolymer
- EPDM (ethylene propylene diene methylene) rubber

## Barrier

- high-temperature tape
- lead

## Private

## Jacket

- HDPE (high-density polyethylene)
- oil-resistant nitrile rubber formation (four temperature ratings)
- EPDM rubber formation

Figure 5-21: Cable jacket

<!-- image -->

## Armor

- galvanized steel (0.020 in, 0.025 in or 0.034 in thick strips available)
- stainless steel
- monel

Depending on the type of cable and the application, the armor can be formed and wrapped in several different profiles:

- Flat profile (used for flat cables)
- Flat interlocked profile (used when a lower profile is required on round cable)
- Round profile (typically used on round cables)

The option of double armored layers is also available.

Figure 5-22: Cable armor

<!-- image -->

## Private

## Outer Jacket

For seafloor, low temperature environments, a PVC (poly-vinyl-chloride) extruded jacket can be applied on the exterior of the metallic armor layer.

## 5.5 Wellsite Procedures

## 5.5.1 Overview

<!-- image -->

## Note

In cold climates splicing tapes should be kept warm before and during splicing a cable. This can be done by keeping the tapes in a pocket. Tapes should be kept at 25 degC or 77 degF.

The following guidelines and procedures are used to ensure maximum-performance cable splices. Different procedures are used based on the cable type and configuration. Do not deviate from these procedures without engineering approval.

Rig personnel, contract consultants and clients are often critical of the time required to make a splice. There are few clients that cannot afford the extra time required to do a quality job. Do not give in to pressure placed on you by personnel who are unfamiliar with the importance of following proper cable splicing procedures. A successful cable splice starts with the following procedure.

1. Plan ahead. Make arrangements to arrive on location early if you know there is a cable splice required before running in the hole.
2. If a lower pigtail will be installed after the unit is on bottom, have the leads cut and prepped ahead of time. Have the splicing table, tools and materials ready by the time the end of the reel is reached.
3. Energize the soldering iron before the armor is applied so that it's ready when needed.

<!-- image -->

## Note

It is recommended that there is no less than 500 ft between splices. We do not have a recommendation for the maximum number of splices allowed in a cable run; however, multiple splices can severely affect run life.

## Private

## 5.5.2.3 Splicing Procedure, Round Cable to Round Cable

1. Position the ends of the two power cables on the splice bench and secure the clamps onto the armor. Do not overtighten the clamps.
2. Prepare the cable ends. Figure 5-23 shows dimensions for round cables without barriers. Figure 5-24 shows dimensions for round cables with a taped or extruded barrier between the insulation and jacket. Carefully remove the armor to the dimension shown in the figures without cutting into the jacket. Remove any burrs or sharp edges on the cut and bend the armor to fit snugly around the jacket.

Figure 5-23: Conductor preparation for cables without barriers

<!-- image -->

Figure 5-24: Conductor preparation for cables with barriers

<!-- image -->

3. Measure the jacket back to the dimension shown in the preceding figures. Slightly score the jacket with a knife at this location. Using a new piece of 50-grit emery cloth, abrade the jacket until it is smooth from the mark back to the armor.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Light

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Electrical

Caution

Never reuse emery cloth when abrading different materials such as copper, insulation or jackets. This will embed copper into the insulation and degrade the integrity of the splice.

4. Apply three tight layers of high-modulus tape on the jacket at the insulation interface. The tape prevents the jacket from splitting when the conductors are separated during the splicing procedure. It will be removed later in the procedure once the conductors are pulled back together.
5. Remove the jacket back to the dimension shown in the preceding figures using extreme care to not damage the insulation. There must be no cuts in the insulation beyond the bare conductor area.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Light

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Electrical

Caution

Cuts in the conductor insulation are not permitted past the bare conductor area. If the insulation is damaged when removing the jacket, remove the damaged area and start a new splice.

6. Remove any braid to the dimension shown. Clean the conductors using CRC (contact cleaner) or a naphtha-based solvent and a clean rag. Spread the conductors apart slightly using caution not to bend more than is necessary to apply tape. Apply three half-lapped layers of high-modulus tape to each conductor beginning against the outer jacket and extending 3 in (76 mm) toward the cut ends of the conductors. Apply the three layers tightly and continuously with no ridges at the transition areas.
7. If the cable uses barriers, remove any taped or extruded barrier back to the high-modulus tape. (See the preceding figure.)
8. Cut the conductors with a hacksaw back to lengths shown in the preceding figures.
9. Obtain the appropriate splicing sleeves. Descriptions and part numbers for the sleeves are shown in the Splicing Sleeves table in the Parts, Tools and Materials section. Remove the insulation to the dimension shown in the preceding figures.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Light

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Electrical

Caution

Be careful not to nick or ring cut the copper when removing the insulation. This can create a hot spot which can result in a failure.

10. Ensure the sleeve fits all the way on and snugly against the insulation. If too much insulation was removed, use a file to trim the copper back to the proper dimension.

## Private

11. Remove filler from the outside diameter of any stranded conductors.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Light

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Electrical

Caution

Do not remove the alloy coating covering the copper conductor.

12. Prepare the end of the cable to be spliced. Spread the conductors apart slightly and place the cable ends together such that one conductor on the second cable butts against the shortest conductor on the first cable. Mark the other two conductors and cut where indicated. (See the preceding figures.) After cutting, check to ensure all three conductors butt up to each other when placed tightly together.
13. Remove the insulation from the ends of the second cable. Taper the insulation ends that butt up against the splicing sleeve using 100-grit emery cloth. Clean the exposed conductors with a clean cloth that has been moistened with CRC (contact cleaner). Allow to completely dry.

<!-- image -->

## Note

5000-volt cable with EPDM-type insulation does not require tapered ends.

14. Use a megger to test both cables to ensure electrical integrity before proceeding.
15. Install the splicing sleeves over the conductors. Do not remove the abrasive material from the inside of the sleeves. Its purpose is to puncture the surface of the copper allowing a connection with very low resistance. Some sleeves also contain a antioxidant to prevent corrosion. Do not remove the antioxidant.
16. Use a crimping tool (nicopress tool) to place crimps in the sleeve. Refer to Figure 5-25. Place a crimp at position A . Rotate the crimping tool 90 degrees and place a crimp at position B . Rotate the crimping tool 90 degrees and place a crimp at position C .

Place a crimp at position D . Rotate the crimping tool 90 degrees and place a crimp at position E . Rotate the crimping tool 90 degrees and place a crimp at position F .

<!-- image -->

## Note

Crimp A and crimp D should be at the very end of the sleeve so there is no flare.

## Private

Figure 5-25: Splicing sleeve installation

<!-- image -->

17. Check the outside diameter of the pressed crimps with crimping gauge. The gauge must pass over the pressed crimp without binding.
18. Repeat the splicing sleeve installation procedure for the remaining conductors.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Light

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Electrical

Caution

Improper installation of splicing sleeves can result in splice failure.

19. Use a strip of 100-grit emery cloth on each sleeve to remove any burrs or sharp edges. Discard the emery cloth and clean the splice with CRC (contact cleaner) or naptha-based solvent.
20. Use a new strip of 100-grit emery cloth to roughen all exposed conductor insulation.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Do not use emery cloth on the insulation after it has been used on the splicing sleeves or a lead jacket.

21. Clean exposed insulation and splicing sleeves by wiping with a clean cloth that has been moistened with CRC or a naphtha-based solvent. Allow to dry completely.
22. Cover each splicing sleeve with five layers of high-temperature tape. Start the first layer of tape on the insulation 0.5 in (13 mm) from one end of the sleeve. Continue over the sleeve with half-lapped wraps until 0.5 in (13 mm) of the insulation is covered beyond the other end of the sleeve. Wrap the second layer in the opposite direction filling the void area in the taper flush with the nicopress sleeve. Extend each succeeding layer of tape 0.5 in (13 mm) beyond the ends of the previous layer. The tape must be wound continuously in a smooth spiral with no gaps or wrinkles.

23. Cover the exposed area of each splice with six layers of high-modulus tape. Start the first layer of tape on the insulation one inch beyond the ends of the high-temperature tape. The tape should be held taut when applying and snugly wrapped around the insulation in a smooth spiral with no gaps or wrinkles. Continue over the sleeve with half-lapped wraps until one inch of insulation is covered beyond the other end of where the high-temperature tape finished. Cut the tape and begin a second layer wrapped in the opposite direction. Extend each successive layer 0.5 in (13 mm) out from the previous, cutting the tape at the end of each layer until the final layer covers the full length of the conductor and butts up against the end of the jacket.

<!-- image -->

## Note

The sixth layer must cover the full length of the exposed insulated conductors.

24. Apply two half-lapped layers of high-temperature tape over the full length of each conductor to seal and secure the high-modulus tape.
25. Loosen the cable clamps and carefully stretch both cables to their original orientation. Remove the tape that was securing the jacket while the conductors were spread apart. Clean the exposed jacket by wiping with a clean cloth moistened with CRC (contact cleaner) or a naphtha-based solvent. Allow to dry completely.
26. Cut three lengths of Impervoil filler strip. The strip should extend the full distance of the insulated conductors between the cut ends of the jacket. Clean each length of filler strip with a cloth moistened with CRC (contact cleaner) or a naphtha-based solvent. Place filler strips between the conductors and secure with high-modulus tape.
27. Apply two half-lapped layers of high-modulus tape over the conductors and filler strips. The first layer should extend 1.5 in over the jacket at each end of the splice. The second layer, wrapped in the opposite direction, should cover the full length of the splice up to, but not on, the armor.
28. Unwrap one loop of armor at each end of the splice. Apply two half-lapped layers of glass tape over the completed taped area extending under the unwrapped armor. Bend the unwrapped armor back to fit snugly around the conductor.
29. Cut a 46-in (1.2-m) length of the appropriate armor. Pull out the tucked end; trim and flatten it. Use a round wooden rod or a piece of electrical conduit with a slightly smaller OD than the ID of the armor as a wrapping lever. Starting 2 in (51 mm) from the splice, form the armor around the splice in a spiral using the stick for leverage to draw the armor tight. Adjust the profile to expand around the spliced section while maintaining the interlock. Continue wrapping 2 in (51 mm) beyond the existing armor.

## Private

30. Cut and secure both ends by soldering the last three convolutions with acid-core solder. Wipe away excess flux with a damp cloth and remove any excess solder from the armor with a surform file.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Light

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Electrical

Caution

Avoid heat damage to the cable under the soldered area. Do not use a torch. Cool the soldered joint immediately with a water-wetted cloth. Avoid contact with hot surfaces.

31. Test the spliced cable to check electrical integrity. Test procedures are provided in .

Improper installation of splicing sleeves can result in splice failure.

17. Use a strip of 100-grit emery cloth on each sleeve to remove any burrs or sharp edges. Discard the emery cloth and clean the splice with CRC or naptha-based solvent.
18. Use a new strip of 100-grit emery cloth to roughen all exposed conductor insulation.

## Private

<!-- image -->

## Note

Do not use emery cloth on the insulation after it has been used on the splicing sleeves or a lead jacket.

19. Clean exposed insulation and splicing sleeves by wiping with a clean cloth that has been moistened with CRC or a naphtha-based solvent. Allow to dry completely.
20. Apply several layers of high-modulus tape over the insulation adjacent to the jacket. This will create a gas block. Butt one edge of the tape against the cut end of the jacket (see the conductor preparation for flat cables with barriers figure). Apply enough full-lapped layers over the insulation until the last layer of tape is even with the outside diameter of the jacket. Use four layers of high-temperature tape to cover the joint between the cut end of the jacket and the tape covering the insulation.
21. Cover each splicing sleeve with five layers of high-temperature tape. Start the first layer of tape on the insulation 0.5 in (13 mm) from one end of the sleeve. Continue over the sleeve with half-lapped wraps until 0.5 in (13 mm) of the insulation is covered beyond the other end of the sleeve. Wrap the second layer in the opposite direction filling the void area in the taper flush with the nicopress sleeve. Extend each succeeding layer of tape 0.5 in (13 mm) beyond the ends of the previous layer. The tape must be wound continuously in a smooth spiral with no gaps or wrinkles.
22. For cables that have a separate jacket on all three conductors, cover the exposed area of each splice with six layers of high-modulus tape. Start the first layer of tape on the insulation 1 in (25 mm) beyond the ends of the high-temperature tape. The tape should be held taut when applying and snugly wrapped around the insulation in a smooth spiral with no gaps or wrinkles. Continue over the sleeve with half-lapped wraps until 1 in (25 mm) of insulation is covered beyond the other end of where the high-temperature tape finished. Cut the tape and begin a second layer wrapped in the opposite direction. Extend each successive layer 0.5 in (13 mm) out from the previous, cutting the tape at the end of each layer until the final layer covers the full length of the conductor and butts up against the end of the armor.

For cables that have a jacket integral to all three phases, apply the six layers of high-modulus tape such that the final layer covers the full length of the conductor and butts up against the end of the jacket.

<!-- image -->

## Note

The sixth layer must cover the full length of the exposed insulated conductors.

## Private

23. Apply two half-lapped layers of high-temperature tape over the full length of each conductor to seal and secure the high-modulus tape.
24. Loosen the cable clamps and carefully stretch both cables to their original orientation.
25. Weave the three phases together using one-in wide Teflon tape to hold the conductors parallel.
26. For cables that have a jacket integral to all three phases, apply a small amount of Pliobond® in the ends of the jacket to help seal the jacket to the insulation.
27. Apply two half-lapped layers of high-modulus tape over the full length of the splice. Start the first layer of tape on the jacket 1.5 in (38 mm) from the armor and continue over the splice until 1.5 in (38 mm) from the other end of the armor. The second layer, wrapped in the opposite direction, should cover the full length of the splice up to, but not on, the armor.
28. Unwrap one loop of armor at each end of the splice. Apply two half-lapped layers of glass tape over the completed taped area extending under the unwrapped armor. Bend the unwrapped armor back to fit snugly around the conductor.
29. Cut a 46-in (1.2-m) length of the appropriate armor. Pull out the tucked end; trim and flatten it. Use a round wooden rod or a piece of electrical conduit with a slightly smaller OD than the ID of the armor as a wrapping lever. Starting 2 in (51 mm) from the splice, form the armor around the splice in a spiral using the stick for leverage to draw the armor tight. Adjust the profile to expand around the spliced section while maintaining the interlock. Continue wrapping 2 in (51 mm) beyond the existing armor.
30. Cut and secure both ends by soldering the last three convolutions with acid-core solder. Wipe away excess flux with a damp cloth and remove any excess solder from the armor with a surform file.

31. Test the spliced cable to check electrical integrity. Test procedures are provided in the Cable Testing - Field Insulation Resistance Values section.

## 5.5.2.7 Splicing Procedure, Cable with Injection Tube

These procedures assume that the conductors and the injection tube require splicing. Certain situations may only require splicing of the injection tube or the cable conductors; the procedures can be modified for a particular situation.

## Cable Preparation

1. Prepare the end on the first length of cable to be spliced. Remove 20.125 in (51 cm) of armor. (All of the conductors will extend 5 in (13 cm) more from the armor than on a typical cable splice.) The end of the tube should be the same length as the longest conductor. The conductor next to the tube should be the shortest of the three conductors. Trim the conductors to the lengths shown in Figure 5-31.

<!-- image -->

## Note

If the cable is a flat cable and has a layer of tape over a jacket or lead barrier, the tape should be trimmed 2 in (51 mm) from the end of the jacket or lead. If the cable is a round cable and the cable has a layer of tape, the jacket should be trimmed approximately 3 in (76 mm) from the armor and the tape should extend at least 2 in (51 mm) beyond the end of the jacket.

Figure 5-31: Cable preparation for cables with injection tubes

<!-- image -->

## Private

2. Spread the conductors and the tubing slightly apart. Bending the conductor sharply will damage the cable.
3. Prepare one end on the other cable. The conductors on the second cable should be cut so they butt against the 'mirrored' conductors. The injection tubing of the second cable should be on the same sides as the tubing of the first cable and overlap the tube on the first cable by approximately 6 in (15.3 cm). Remove the insulation, jacket and braid to the dimensions shown in Figure 5-31.
4. Splice the three conductors up to the point of applying the armor. Splicing procedures are provided in the Splicing Procedures, Round Cable to Round Cable , Splicing Procedures, Flat Cable to Flat Cable and the Splicing Procedures, Flat Cable to Round Cable sections. Do not apply the armor at this time.
5. Pull the three spliced conductors together and apply two half-lapped layers of glass tape over the three conductors.
6. Straighten the injection tubes of both cables so that they are straight and lay against the three spliced conductors. Cut the tube on the end of the second cable with a gap between the ends of the tubes for proper dimensions. Do not remove too much tubing. The ends of both tubes must be square and smooth.
7. Remove 1 in (25 mm) of the lead jacket or EPDM (if present) from the end of each injection tube. Do not cut completely through the lead or EPDM. Do not cut or mark the injection tubes. Carefully remove the lead or EPDM without nicking the tube. A raised or recessed area on the tubing may prevent the connector from sealing.

<!-- image -->

Lead is a recognized hazard to occupational health. The WCP-QHSE-S003 Personnel Lead Protection Standard is available from InTouchSupport.com (content ID 3846334).

8. Select the appropriate Swagelok® connector and slide the connector onto the end of one of the tubes. Insert the end of the second tube into the other end of the connector. The ends of both tubes should rest firmly against the shoulder inside the connector. Tighten the nuts finger-tight.
9. While holding the connector body with a wrench, tighten the nut 1¼ turns. Check to see that a 'flat side' of the nut that will be in contact with the adjacent conductor. If necessary, continue tightening the nut until the next flat is exposed. Do not tighten the nut more than one additional ¼ turn.

## Private

<!-- image -->

## Tip

Before tightening the nut, scribe a line on the nut. Watch the line as the nut is turned. This way, there will be no doubt that the fitting has been properly installed.

10. Verify that the connector has been correctly installed by placing the appropriate Swagelok Gap Inspection Gage between the nut and the body hex. If the gage will not fit, the fitting is tightened sufficiently.
11. Tighten the other end of the connector by repeating step 9. Verify the installation.
12. Use a file to remove the sharp edges on the nut. This will prevent cutting of the tape and gouging of the conductors.
13. Wrap two half-lapped layers of high-modulus tape followed by two half-lapped layers of glass tape over the Swagelok connector and exposed tube. The first layer of tape should extend at least 1 in (25 mm) beyond the end of the lead on the tubes. Each subsequent layer should extend 0.5 in (13 mm) beyond the previous layer of tape.

## Flat-to-Flat Cable

1. Pull the taped conductors and tube together. Apply two half-lapped layers of glass tape over the tube and the conductors.
2. Cut a 48-in section of galvanized or Monel round armor. (Use galvanized armor over cable splices on cables using galvanized armor. Use Monel armor over cable splices on cables using Monel armor.) Pull out the tucked end; trim and flatten it. Use a round wooden rod or a piece of electrical conduit with a slightly smaller OD than the ID of the armor as a wrapping lever. Starting 2 in (51 mm) from the splice, form the armor around the splice in a spiral using the stick for leverage to draw the armor tight. Adjust the profile to expand around the spliced section while maintaining the interlock. Continue wrapping 2 in (51 mm) beyond the existing armor.
3. Cut and secure both ends by soldering the last three convolutions with acid-core solder. Wipe away excess flux with a damp cloth and remove any excess solder from the armor with a surform file.

## Round-to-Flat Cable

1. Cut four lengths of Impervoil filler strips. The strips should reach from the cut end of the jacket on the round cable to the end of the armor on the flat cable. Clean each length of the filler strip with a cloth that has been moistened with REDA #1 thinner (or equivalent). Roughen the round jacket with emery cloth so adhesive tape can fit snugly around the jacket.
2. Apply two half-lapped layers of tape over the conductors and filler strips. The first layer should extend over the first 1 in (25 mm) of jacket on the round cable and to the armor on the flat cable. The second layer should extend to the armor at each end of the splice, using the procedure provided in the Splicing Procedure, Round Cable to Round Cable section.
3. Clean the exposed jacket by sanding off the splines and wiping with a clean cloth moistened with REDA #1 thinner (or equivalent). Allow to completely dry.
4. Cut four lengths of Impervoil filler strip. The strips should extend the full distance of the insulated conductors between the cut ends of the jacket. Place filler strips between the conductors and tube as shown in Figure 5-32.
5. Use procedures provided in the Splicing Procedure, Round Cable to Round Cable section to complete the splice.

Figure 5-32: Placement of Impervoil filler strips

<!-- image -->

## Breakout of the Injection Tube

The most desirable place to break out the injection tube is at the motorlead splice since the cable armor is already broken. Swagelok connectors can be used to splice any additional tubing to obtain the desired length of tubing.

1. Splice the power cable and motorlead cable together using standard procedures. Allow the injection tube to extend a minimum of 6 in (15.3 cm) beyond the end of the motorlead armor.
2. Pull the taped conductors and the tube together. Apply two half-lapped layers of glass tape over the tube and the conductors.
3. Apply armor over the splice and the tube until the armor extends a minimum of 4 in (10.2 cm) beyond the end of the underlying motorlead armor. Solder the end on the armor.
4. Clamp any additional length of injection tubing to the equipment.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Ground the tube during all tests.

## 5.5.3 HHS/HSM Wellhead Cable Pack-off Guidelines

Use the following guidelines for wellheads utilizing a split, rubber-type packing glands to seal off around the power cable. Illustrations of parts are available in Section 2.17 and 2.18.

- Armored round or flat cable requires armor removal through the gland area. For flat cable, remove several additional inches on either side of the gland so legs can be easily spread apart from each other. Apply high modulus tape on the conductors near the armor to prevent the armor from damaging the insulation when the conductors are spread apart.
- All round cables will be packed off against their outer jacket.
- Flat cables with tape and braid should have the tape and braid removed so the rubber gland material will pack off directly against the individual phase jacket.
- Lead jacketed cables should have the braid removed so that the gland material can smoothly seal directly against the lead jacket.
- Use caution when assembling the wellhead parts to avoid damage to lead/insulation and avoid sharp bends in the cable legs.

## Private

After the wellhead assembly has been completed, the gland may be tightened. The HHS gland is tightened with eight flange bolts. The HSM gland is tightened with six gland cap screws. 2: Parts, Tools and Materials chapter provides additional information.

- The gland should be tightened slowly and evenly. All bolts/cap screws should be hand tightened first. Then gently add tension to opposing bolts/cap screws until all are equally tight and the gap is the same all the way around the wellhead. This process should be conducted repeatedly until the appropriate tightness is achieved. Do not allow the gland to be overtightened as this can lead to premature failure.

<!-- image -->

## Note

It is possible to deform and cut cable insulation if the wellhead packing is excessively tight. This is especially critical with flat cable. A snug gland is adequate.

- Extra care in preparing cable for pack off, proper gland assembly, and correct tightening will help to assure a quality installation.
- Adequately support the cable after the cable exits the wellhead. Avoid a short bending radius. Use a cable band or other material to secure the cable to the flowline for additional support.
- When the well has been started and fluid has reached surface, a check should be made to ensure that there are no leaks around each of the conductors.
- In an emergency situation, where the cable OD is slightly smaller than the packing gland ID, high-modulus tape can be used to build up the cable OD so pack off can be accomplished.
- If flat Redalene cable is being used and the gland hole ID is smaller than the jacketed phases, removal of the Nitrile jacket is acceptable to pack off directly on the Redalene.
- RTV silicone rubber sealer may be used to supplement sealing around worn or damaged packing glands. (New rubber packing elements are recommended.)

## 5.5.4 Testing Procedures

## 5.5.4.1 Overview

This section details standard cable testing procedures, using DC Hi Potential Tester Unit. Additional testing procedures and job aids are available on the SOP Index. The Automated Cable Test System (ACTS) InTouch ID 3455075 is the preferred testing system for ART Centers.

## 5.5.4.2 Cable Preparation

Use the following procedure to prepare cables for testing.

1. Remove 10 in (25.4 cm) of armor and jacket or lead sheath from the outside ends of the spliced cable.
2. Remove insulation to expose 0.5 in to 0.75 in (1.3 cm to 1.9 cm) of bare conductor.
3. Clean exposed conductors with a clean cloth that has been moistened with CRC (contact cleaner) or a naphtha-based solvent. Allow solvent to dry.
4. Spread the conductors so that the bare ends are at least 12 in (30.5 cm) apart and are not grounded.
5. Remove 12 in of lead from the other end of the cable (ends not being connected) and spread so they are at least 12 in apart and away from any ground (the reel, ground, metal building beams, etc.).

After performing the Cable Preparation steps, use a Megger to measure the insulation resistance between each conductor and armor as ground. The insulation resistance should not be less than the values shown in .

## 5.6 Troubleshooting

## 5.6.1 Electrical Problems

- If high leakage or low megger readings are experienced on an MLE, remove moisture and clean the surface that has been touched with dirt (hands, oils, etc). Use a clean rag to wipe the insulation with CRC electrical contact cleaner or with a clean alcohol wipe. Allow cleaner to air dry before re-testing. Ensure the lead is cut back as per procedure in section for cable and MLE testing procedures and criteria.
- If the pothead has been exposed to a high humidity environment, use a hair/blow dryer to remove moisture.

<!-- image -->

## Note

DO NOT use a heat gun as the temperature could get too hot and cause damage to the conductor.

- If a pothead is received with desiccant pack(s) that have turned pink (should be blue) this indicates excessive moisture. Use a hair/blow dryer to dry the surface of the conductors and front face of the pothead.

<!-- image -->

## Note

DO NOT use a heat gun as the temperature could get too hot and cause damage to the conductor.

- Testing shows that high leakage readings for plug-in MLEs can be introduced by using a 'bike pump' to perform the pressure seal check as the 'bike pump' introduces moisture. The HiPot leakage can increase by 10 times if going from 45% to a 98% relative humidity. It is recommended to test with Nitrogen.
- If you experience high leakage or low megger readings on a cable, ensure the conductors are far enough apart, see section for cable and MLE testing procedures and criteria. For high humidity environments, put a clean bag over the 3 ends (not being tested).

## 5.7 Parts, Spares, Tools, and Supplies

Refer to the Part, Tools and Material section for a listing of splicing tools and materials.

## 5.7.1 Nicopress Tools

## 5.7.1.1 Nicopress Crimp Gauge

Each type of nicopress tool is designed to quickly and easily compress the appropriate nicopress sleeve. To make a satisfactory splice it is important to keep the amount of pressure on the sleeve constant. Each new tool has an instruction sheet, a gauge and a wrench for adjusting the tool. Check splices with the gauge provided for this purpose.

When using the gauge, hold it so that it contacts the compressed portion of the sleeve at right angles to the fins. The compressed portion of the sleeve should enter the slot without forcing. If after long use the nicopress tool wears to such an extent that the compressed sleeve does not enter the gauge, it is a simple matter to readjust the tool. Be careful not to get the compressions too small. The sleeve should enter the gauge with very little clearance.

Figure 5-33 shows a crimp gauge.

Figure 5-33: Crimp gauge used to check nicopress sleeves

<!-- image -->

## 5.7.1.2 Nicopress Tool Use, Care and Maintenance

When tools are used daily, they should receive a weekly inspection. Clean and lubricate the nicopress tool regularly.

## Private

Copyright © 2013 Schlumberger, Unpublished Work. All rights reserved.

An empty tool should work freely with a slight spring at the final closing. If the tool binds, it can be eased by slightly loosening the particular hexagon head bolt which is causing the binding. Lock the bolt after each adjustment by bending up one of the lock washer ears.

All sleeves are marked with a tool groove letter. This letter must correspond with the letter stamped near the tool groove used for compressing the sleeve.

## 5.7.1.3 Nicopress Tool Adjustment

With the tool handles in the open position, use the wrench provided with the tool to first loosen the locking screw one or two turns. Then turn in (clockwise) the adjustment screw only a fraction of a turn.

<!-- image -->

## Note

When holding the tool (shown in Figure 5-34), the bolt on the right-hand side of the tool has left-hand threads whereas the other two screws have right-hand threads.

Try the tool on a sleeve and check with gauge. Continue to turn the adjustment screw a small amount at a time until the pressed sleeve passes easily into the gauge. When the correct setting is obtained, turn up the locking screw so that the tool will hold its adjustment.

## A.1 Hotline, Hotline550 and HotlineSA3

## A.1.1 Systems Descriptions

The Hotline system is similar to a standard Schlumberger submersible lifting system but uses components that are rated for higher temperatures. The Hotline550 system is a fully integrated system specially designed for steam injection wells. The HotlineSA3 system improves reliability, increases the bottom-hole temperature rating, introduces extra functionality, and simplifies installation. Comparisons of various systems are shown in Table A-2.

## A.1.1.1 Hotline System

The Hotline system's critical motor and cable components are constructed of materials that have higher temperature ratings.

Features unique to the Hotline system are

- A combination of Aflas O-rings and high-temperature Chemraz O-rings are used throughout the system.
- special pothead design using a high-temperature Aflas seal
- Aflas protector bag
- Reda No. 7 oil for high-temperature applications
- proprietary insulation on the motor windings
- EHLB/EHLTB power cables and KELB/KEHLB MLEs
- special material selection and special design taking into consideration maximum expected different thermal expansions.

## A.1.1.2 Hotline550 System

The Hotline550 system is a fully integrated system specially designed for steam injection wells.

Features unique to the Hotline550 system are

- motor tested to 550 degF (288 degC) internal motor temperature
- special high-temperature pothead and MLE designs
- high-temperature advanced protector that uses metal bellows
- Reda No. 7 oil for high-temperature applications
- high-temperature pump intake, gas separator
- AGH / Poseidon™ multiphase pump if required
- special Hotline550 centrifugal pumps
- high-temperature power cable and MLE
- accepts optional monitoring (Hotline550 gauge retrofit) system.

## Private

## A.1.1.3 HotlineSA3 System

Unlike the Hotline550 system, which uses traditional ESP architecture, the HotlineSA3 system has a radically new architecture. The HotlineSA3 integrated motor is made up of four sections a shaft seal module (SSM), motor section, gauge section and compensator (bellows) section. The functions of the protector have been split into a shaft seal module (SSM) above the motor and a compensator section below the motor. The MLE, pothead and pumps have been developed to cope with the high temperatures inherent to thermal applications and the abrasive conditions.

Features unique to the HotlineSA3 system are

- combines the protector, motor and gauge functions into a single assembly (integrated motor).
- motor tested to 572 degF (300 degC) internal motor temperature
- special high-temperature pothead (Chimera) and MLE designs
- high-temperature integrated motor that uses metal bellows
- Ultra purified Reda No. 7 oil for high-temperature applications
- high-temperature pump intake, gas separator
- special HotlineSA3 centrifugal pumps with ceramic bearings
- high-temperature power cable and MLE
- high temperature monitoring system (motor temperature, well pressure and temperature).

## A.1.1.4 Hotline Gauge

The Hotline ESP monitoring system is an optional feature for the Hotline550 motor and is incorporated in all HotlineSA3 Integrated Motors. The gauge measures motor winding temperature, wellbore pressure, and wellbore temperature. Due to high downhole temperatures, the electronics are located at the surface and an independent downhole monitoring cable is required gauge communication and power.

There are two Hotline monitoring system configurations available. The standard configuration provides motor winding temperature and intake pressure/temperature measurements. The RTD-only configuration only provides motor winding temperature measurements.

## Private

The Hotline ESP monitoring system is supported by the Hotline Extreme interface card. The card is installed in the UniConn which is normally incorporated into the switchboard or VSD. The monitoring cable transfers the power from the card to the downhole sensors and provides sense lines from the pressure gauge and the resistance temperature detectors (RTDs) for taking the measurements to surface. The monitoring cable is terminated in a junction box at surface, after it transitions through the wellhead. A flexible cable is then run through the cable trays to the Extreme card.

Figure A-1: High Level Diagram of Hotline ESP Monitoring System

<!-- image -->

The Hotline gauge portals provide the mechanical and electrical interface between the gauges and the monitoring cable. The RTD is secured to the end ESP motor coils to measure motor temperature. The leads from each device are terminated at a common connector inside the motor. The pressure sensor and RTDs are integrated in the motor during the manufacturing process by the product center or a qualified ART center.

The gauge portal kit is installed below the motor housing at the ART center, for retrofitted Hotline550 motors.

## Private

Figure A-2: Hotline550 Gauge Portal Kit

<!-- image -->

For the HotlineSA3 motors, the gauge portal is install between the motor and compensator (bellows) section.

Figure A-3: HotlineSA3 Gauge Portal

<!-- image -->

## Surface Acquisition System Compatibility

The Hotline ESP monitoring systems are supported by the UniConn only. The UniConn controller and Extreme card firmware required to support the Hotline Monitoring system is available via InTouchSupport.com.

Configuration of the Extreme card is performed using StarView.

## A.1.3 Transport and Handling

All Hotline, Hotline550 and HotlineSA3 equipment should follow normal equipment transport and handling guidelines. The equipment should be transported in steel shipping boxes and be carefully lifted to prevent damage to the components.

The Hotline and Hotline550 motors and protectors are filled with highly viscous oil (REDA #7 oil). The HotlineSA3 Integrated Motor uses special purified REDA #7 oil. The HotlineSA3 motor cannot be drained and refilled with regular REDA #7 oil and should not be 'topped off' with REDA #7.

It will be difficult to turn the shafts and fill the equipment after transportation to a wellsite in cold weather. Consideration should be given to methods of keeping the equipment above 32 degF (0 degC) when preparing for installation.

The equipment may be stored for a period of time before installation. Standard procedures for storage should be followed for this equipment. Most of the system components have unlimited shelf life. O-rings have a shelf life of five years from date of manufacture.

## A.1.3.1 Hotline Gauge

## Gauge Specific QHSE Issues

The 7-wire armored cable is not a pressure barrier and if a leak occurs downhole, either by the armor being damaged or the connector leaking, wellbore high pressure and high temperature gases from the wellbore could be transported up the cable along the signal wires to the surface if a pressure barrier at the WHO is not present. Care must be taken when working on or around the cable end and when accessing the wires in the junction box.

## Portal and Gauge

To prevent damage during handling of the motor/gauge portal, do not remove the dummy plug protecting the portal bulkhead connection. This plug prevents physical damage of the connector during transportation. It also prevents contaminants, including moisture, from entering the connection.

## Monitoring Cable and Connector

<!-- image -->

## Note

The cable connector is installed on the 7-wire monitoring cable in the shop. Refer to Monitoring Cable Male Connector Assembly, MPI-57151(GeMS document 100787432) prior to shipping the cable to the wellsite. For recommended cable storage and handling procedure, refer to the MC Sensor Cable Storage and Handling Handbook (GeMS document 100868612).

The monitoring cable will be shipped on a reel. A portable spooler should be used to drive the reel and allow ease of cable feed into and out of the well. The reel will also protect the cable during transport and handling.
