## A.1.4.1 Motor

Hotline motors and Hotline550 motors are filled with Reda No. 7 oil, which has a viscosity of 1223 cST at 70 degF (21 degC). Reda No. 7 oil is slightly less viscous than honey at this temperature. Motors are equipped with a valve to prevent oil loss from the bottom.

The pour point of Reda No. 7 oil is -32 degF (-36 degC). As the temperature approaches this value, the motor shaft will become much more difficult to turn. Be careful not to confuse this increased drag with that encountered by a damaged or bent motor. It is best to keep the motor at temperatures above 32 degF (0 degC) if possible.

## A.1.4.2 Protector

The Advanced Protector is pre-filled with Reda No. 7 oil at the product center or service center. The wellsite installation procedures are very similar to those for standard protectors. For detailed installation information, refer to the standard protector installation procedures.

The pour point of Reda No. 7 oil is -32 degF (-36 degC). As the temperature approaches this value, the protector shaft will become much more difficult to turn. Be careful not to confuse this increased drag with that encountered by a damaged protector. It is best to keep the protector above 32 degF (0 degC) if possible when preparing for installation.

## A.1.4.3 Intake

No special procedures are required for installing intakes for Hotline and Hotline550 applications.

## A.1.4.4 Pump

Compression pumps are used in Hotline applications and Hotline550 applications. Standard installation procedures apply. Installation procedures and special shimming requirements are provided in the standard pump shimming and installation procedures.

## Private

## A.1.4.5 Pothead and Motor Lead Extension

The Hotline pothead design and the Hotline550 pothead design are different designs compared to the standard pothead design. The Hotline pothead uses an Aflas elastomer to seal the MLE to the motor. The Hotline550 pothead is a unique design developed for steam injection wells for operation at very high temperatures.

The maximum bottomhole temperature for the Hotline pothead is 350 degF (177 degC). The maximum conductor operating temperature is 450 degF (232 degC).

The maximum bottomhole temperature for the Hotline550 pothead is 425 degF (218 degC) and the maximum conductor operating temperature for the Hotline550 pothead is 500 degF (260 degC). The Hotline550 pothead installs in a 540/562 motorhead, designed with a smooth-bore pothole, sized to fit a '-029' O-ring. The Hotline550 pothead has a special configuration and will not fit a standard motor head; it can be used only on Hotline550 motors.

In addition to the pothead design, MLE material selection affects the temperature rating of the MLE and hence the application limitations. Table A-5 shows the different options for power cable and MLE materials selection.

The Hotline550 pothead design is significantly different from existing potheads and can only be used with Hotline550 motors. ## Hotline550 Pothead Installation Procedure

The Hotline550 pothead installs in a 540/562 motorhead, designed with a smooth-bore pothole, sized to fit a '-029' O-ring. The Hotline550 pothead has a special configuration and will not fit a standard motor head. The Hotline550 pothead can be used only on Hotline550 motors.

There are two designs for the Hotline550 pothead. The original design, now obsolete, is a tape-in design with a MSE seal for the pothole. The second design has two O-rings, one for high temperature and one for low temperature. The high temperature O-ring is located nearest the electrical terminals and the low temperature O-ring is located nearest the flange of the pothead.

The (obsolete) Hotline550 pothead with MSE seal is installed using the following procedure.

1. Remove MLE pothead shipping cap and inspect for damage.
2. Confirm that pre-installation tests have been done previously (pressure and electrical test)
3. Remove the black rubber shipping cap O-ring.
4. Ensure motorhead area is clean and no fluid will drip onto the splice or motorhead prior to removing cover.
5. Install the white MSE seal with the open side towards the well. The visible spring inside the seal should be facing up, that is seen from the power cable side of the pothead.
6. When placing MSE seal on, slide the whole seal on carefully, ensuring even stretching of the spring.
7. After MSE seal set inside the groove, make sure it rotate freely.
8. Tape-in as per standard procedure. Use at least three layers of Teflon tape. Use four layers of Teflon tape if space permits.
9. Fill pothole with oil until no bubbles are seen.
10. Lubricate the pothole and MSE seal with Krytox Grease GPL - 206.
11. Ensure there no foreign materials in the hole and between the flanges.
12. Align the pothead with the threaded studs or bolt holes and insert the pothead carefully and evenly so the MSE seal installs without pinching or warping.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Avoid shaking the cable as this may cause damage to the MSE seal.

13. Install lock washers and nuts. Tighten the pothead flange evenly from both sides few threads at a time.
14. Torque to specification.
15. Ensure the flanges match properly and there is no gap between them.
16. After complete servicing the protector, check pothead for any possible leak.

## Private

The Hotline550 pothead with two O-ring grooves is installed using the following procedure.

1. Remove MLE pothead shipping cap and inspect for damage.
2. Confirm that pre-installation tests have been done previously (pressure and electrical test)
3. Remove shipping O-rings.
4. Install the high temperature O-ring. This goes in the first O-ring groove, nearest the electrical terminals, nearest to the motorhead.
5. Install the low temperature O-ring. This goes in the O-ring groove nearest the flange of the pothead. It can be installed by rolling it over the high temperature O-ring.
6. Tape-in as per standard procedure. Use at least three layers of Teflon tape. Use four layers of Teflon tape if space permits.
7. Fill pothole with oil until no bubbles are seen.
8. Lubricate the O-rings with Krytox Grease GPL - 206.
9. Ensure there no foreign materials in the hole and between the flanges.
10. Align the pothead with the threaded studs or bolt holes and insert the pothead carefully and evenly to avoid damage of the two O-rings.
11. Install lock washers and nuts. Tighten the pothead flange evenly from both sides few threads at a time.
12. Torque to specification.
13. Ensure the flanges match properly and there is no gap between them.
14. After complete servicing the protector, check pothead for any possible leak.

## A.1.4.6 ESP Power Cable

The cable splice is modified. It is similar to the standard Nicopress™ field splice, except a different type of tape is used (Hi-Mod with a silicone-based adhesive). The jackets must be fused together using a small jewelers torch with 95/5 solder. The solder joint is then checked with dye penetrant. This adds a level of complexity and required skill to successfully make these cable splices. The technique is suitable for a service center but not at the wellsite.

The high-temperature cable splicing procedure is provided in the following section.

## Splicing Procedure, High-Temperature Lead Jacket Power Cables and MLE

Tools and materials required to perform high-temperature cable splices are shown in Table A-7.

Table A-7: Tools and Materials Required to Perform High-Temperature Cable Splices

| Description                           | Part Number   |
|---------------------------------------|---------------|
| standard splicing tools and materials | -             |
| dye penetrant test kit                | -             |
| jeweler's torch                       | -             |
| 95Pb-5Sn solder                       | -             |
| acid-core solder                      | 562678        |
| lead sleeves                          | 9990305       |
| silicone adhesive high-modulus tape   | R006164       |
| acrylic adhesive high-modulus tape    | 748137        |
| high-temperature tape                 | 823435        |
| Teflon™ tape                          | 521427        |
| glass tape                            | 684811        |

## Procedure

1. Position the ends of the cables on the splice bench and secure the clamps onto the armor being careful not to over-tighten the clamps. (Overtightening the clamps will distort the armor.) Remove the armor to the dimensions shown in Figure A-5 being extremely cautious to avoid cutting into the lead jacket. Remove any burrs or sharp edges on the cut.
2. Note the position of the part number on the pothead flange and orientate the part on the underside of the cable wrap as it is placed on the cable reel. The part number must be on the outboard side of pothead flange when it is installed on the motor.
3. Using acrylic adhesive high-modulus tape, tuck a single wrap underneath the armor followed by two or three wraps extending 1 in (2.54 cm) out around all three conductors. This tape will help to protect the lead when the conductors are spread apart.
4. Remove the lead jacket in accordance with the dimensions shown in Figure A-5. Use extreme care not to damage the insulation.

Figure A-5: Conductor preparation for high-temperature lead-jacket cables and MLE

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Note

Cuts in the conductor insulation are not permitted anywhere beyond the bare conductor area. If the insulation is damaged when removing the jacket, cut off the damaged area and start a new splice.

5. Use a hacksaw or wire cutters and file to cut the conductors to the lengths shown in Figure A-5.

<!-- image -->

## Note

When cutting with the hacksaw, be careful not to damage the insulation or jacket on the adjacent conductors.

6. Obtain the proper sized splicing sleeves. Remove the insulation to the dimension shown in Figure A-5.

<!-- image -->

## Note

When removing the insulation, be careful not to ring-cut the copper. Doing so can create a hot spot leading to a failure.

7. Using the appropriate splicing sleeve, check to ensure the sleeve fits all the way on and snugly against the insulation. If too much insulation was removed, use a file to trim the copper back to the proper dimension.

<!-- image -->

## Note

On motor lead extensions, remove the polyimide insulating tape from the conductor using a scraping tool and 150-grit emery cloth.

8. Remove filler from the outside diameter of any stranded conductors.
9. Prepare the end of the second cable to be spliced as instructed in Step 1, Step 2, Step 3 and Step 4.

Place the cable ends together such that the longest conductor on one cable butts against the shortest conductor on the other cable. Mark the other two conductors and cut where indicated. After cutting, check to ensure all three conductors butt up to each other when placed together tightly.

10. Strip the insulation from the ends of the second cable as instructed in Step 6. Clean the exposed conductors with a clean cloth that has been moistened with CRC and allow to dry completely.
11. Using a Megger™ tester, test both cables to ensure electrical integrity before proceeding further.
12. Place lead sleeves over the conductors and position the sleeves on the long end of the conductors to clear the splice area. The lead jacket must be exposed for at least 1 in (2.54 cm) at the splice area.

## Private

13. Install the splicing sleeves over the conductors. Do not remove the grit from the inside of the sleeves. Its purpose is to puncture the surface of the copper allowing a lower resistance connection. Some sleeves also contain an antioxidant to prevent corrosion. This should remain in the sleeve as well.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Splice failure can result from improper installation of splicing sleeves.

14. Use a crimping tool to press crimps in the sleeve. Place a crimp at position A. Rotate the crimping tool 90° and place a crimp at position B. Rotate the crimping tool 90° and place a crimp at position C. Place crimp at position D. Rotate the crimping tool 90° and place crimp at position E. Rotate the crimping tool 90° and place a crimp at position F.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Crimp A and D are to be at the very end of the sleeve so there is no flare.

15. Check the outside diameter of the pressed crimps with a crimp gauge. The gauge must pass over the pressed crimp without binding. Adjust the crimping tool, if necessary, to permit the gauge to operate properly. Nicopress tool use, care and maintenance procedures are provided in the Cables section.
16. Repeat the splicing sleeve installation procedure for the remaining two conductors.
17. Using a strip of 100-grit emery cloth, sand each sleeve to remove any burrs or sharp edges on the splicing sleeve. Discard the emery cloth and clean thoroughly.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Do not use the emery cloth on the insulation after it has been used on the splicing sleeves or lead jacket.

18. Using a new strip of 100-grit emery cloth, roughen up all exposed insulation.
19. Using a new strip of 150-grit emery cloth, remove any oxidation on the lead jacket.
20. Clean exposed conductors well by wiping with a clean cloth which has been moistened with CRC or a naphtha-based solvent and allow to completely dry.

## Private

21. To create a gas block, apply several layers of silicone adhesive high-modulus tape over the insulation adjacent to the lead jacket. One edge of the tape must be butted against the cut end of the lead sheath. Apply enough full-lapped layers over the insulation until the last layer of tape is even with the outside diameter of the jacket. Use four layers of high-temperature tape to cover the joint between the cut end of the jacket and the high-modulus tape.

<!-- image -->

## Note

When applying the four layers of high-temperature tape, only tape onto the lead jacket 0.5 in (1.27 cm). This will allow a bare location for solder when replacing the lead sheath.

22. Cover each splicing sleeve with five layers of silicone adhesive high-modulus tape. Start the first layer of tape on the insulation 0.5 in (1.27 cm) from one end of the sleeve. Continue over the sleeve with half-lapped wraps until 0.5 in (1.27 cm) of the insulation is covered beyond the other end of the sleeve. Wrap the second layer in the opposite direction filling the void area in the taper flush with the Nicopress sleeves. Extend each succeeding layer of tape 0.5 in (1.27 cm) beyond the end of the previous layer. The tape must be wound continuously in a smooth spiral with no gaps or wrinkles. Tension should be applied to stretch the tape such that the tape is uniformly wrapped without creases or wrinkles. The tape can be stretched to decrease the width to about 85 % of its original width. Excessive stretching is not desirable.
23. Cover the exposed area of each splice with five layers of silicone adhesive high-modulus tape with the exception of a one in. to 2 in (2.54 cm to 5.08 cm) area at the end of the lead jacket. Start the first layer of tape on the insulation 1 in (2.54 cm) beyond the ends of the previous layers. Continue over the sleeve with half-lapped wraps until 1 in (2.54 cm) of insulation is covered beyond the other end of where the previous layer finished. Cut the tape and begin a second layer wrapped in the opposite direction. Extend each successive layer 0.5 in (1.27 cm), cutting the tape at the end of each layer until the fifth layer covers 1 in (2.54 cm) of the lead jacket. Leave 1 in (2.54 cm) exposed for a soldering area.
24. Apply a small amount of silicone lubricant to the taped splice. Position the lead sleeve so the ends of the sleeve are positioned over the lead barrier. Fit the sleeve into place, cut excess sleeve and file seams smooth. Remove oxidation from the lead sleeve.
25. Clean off any oxidation on the lead jacket. Apply solder flux. Tin the 1 in (2.54 cm) area of lead at each end of tape with 95Pb-5Sn solder. Round to a smooth contour with emery cloth or file as necessary.

## Private

26. Apply solder flux to the lead sleeves and apply 95Pb-5Sn solder around both ends of the sleeve. Apply solder flux to the longitudinal seams. Solder the longitudinal seams with 95Pb-5Sn solder. Stop 0.125 in (0.32 cm) from completely sealing the splice. Wait five minutes to allow the hot gases to escape and then seal the remaining 0.125 in (0.32 cm) seam. File any sharp points and buff with 150-grit emery cloth.
27. Inspect the soldered joints for pinholes. Perform a dye penetrant inspection test to check for pinholes.

<!-- image -->

## Note

It is critical that no voids or pinholes exist in the solder.

28. Apply one layer of half-lapped acrylic adhesive high-modulus tape over the braid to the armor on each end of the conductors.
29. Use high-temperature tape to fill in and smooth out the bottleneck at each end of the lead sleeve for an approximate length of 2 in (5.08 cm).
30. Apply two half-lapped layers of acrylic adhesive high-modulus tape across the lead sleeves and beyond the high-temperature tape.
31. Loosen the cable clamps and carefully stretch the spliced conductors to a parallel orientation.
32. Using 1-in (2.54-cm) wide Teflon™ tape, weave the three phases together to hold the conductors parallel.
33. Apply two half-lapped layers of acrylic adhesive high-modulus tape over the full length of the entire splice. Start the first layer of tape on the jacket 1.5 in (3.8 cm) from the armor and continue over the splice until 1.5 in (3.8 cm) remain at the other end of the armor. The second layer, wrapped in the opposite direction, should cover the full length of the splice up to, but not on the armor.
34. Unwrap one loop of armor at each end of the splice. Apply two half-lapped layers of glass tape over the completed taped area extending under the unwrapped armor.
35. Bend the unwrapped armor back to fit snugly around the conductor.

## Private

36. Cut a 64-in (1.6-m) length of the armor. Pull out the tucked end, trim and flatten it. Use a round wooden stick or a piece of electrical conduit with a slightly smaller outside diameter than the inside diameter of the armor as a wrapping lever. Starting 2 in (5.08 cm) from the splice, form the armor around the splice in a spiral using the stick or conduit for leverage to draw the armor tight. Adjust the profile to expand around the spliced section while maintaining the interlock. Continue wrapping until 2 in (5.08 cm) overlap the existing armor.
37. Cut and secure both ends by soldering the last three convolutions with acid-core solder. Wipe away excess flux with a damp cloth and remove any excess solder from the armor.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Use care to avoid heat damage to the cable under the soldered area. Cool the soldered joint immediately with a water-wetted cloth. Be careful to avoid contact with hot surfaces.

## Pre-Installation Checks

Perform the following checks before running the ESP string into the well to verify that the gauge is operational.

## Connector and Cable Check

1. Remove the protective cap from the cable connector and visually inspect the connector and pins for damage.
2. Measure the resistance on each monitoring cable conductor and verify continuity is good. Compare the measured resistance readings and verify with the reference cable length according to the cable electric properties (17 ohms per 1000 ft of cable at 20 degC).
3. Megger test the cable conductor to conductor and conductor to ground (cable armor) to verify that the insulation is intact. All measurements need to greater than 10 MOhms.

## Private

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Light

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Electrical

Caution

Only a 500-V megger should be used for testing the cable insulation.

## Gauge Function Test

1. Remove the protective plug from the portal bulkhead and visually inspect the portal for damage. Connect the test cable connector to the portal, securing the connector with the securing nut. The gauge and monitoring cable are now ready to be function tested.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Care should be taken not to scratch the conical sealing surface inside the portal when inserting the cable connector.

2. Connect surface equipment (UniConn with Extreme card) to the other end of the cable according to the following figures.

Figure A-6: Gauge Configuration

<!-- image -->

Figure A-7: Winding Temperature Configuration (RTD only)

<!-- image -->

## Private

3. Verify that the correct coefficients have been downloaded on the Extreme card for the pressure sensor and RTD. Refer to the Hotline Extreme Card User Manual (InTouch ID 5447042) for details on how to download and verify coefficients.
4. Begin logging the data from either or both the Uniconn and ExtremeView using StarView.
5. Use a hydraulic pump or simple hand pump to apply pressure to the gauge through the gauge's pressure communication port. The port requires a Swagelok interface.
6. Confirm that the applied pressure corresponds with the values displayed on the UniConn and ExtremeView. (Non-Applicable for RTD only).

<!-- image -->

## Note

The Hotline550 pressure sensors are only calibrated from 35 degC to 225 degC. Outside this temperature range, accurate pressure readings cannot be guaranteed. If a sensor will be installed in a cold environment, the gauge must first be checked at the shop and again at the wellsite.

Due to internal bellow in the Hotline550 pressure sensor (Sapphire), pressure readings at atmosphere might not be accurate (15 psi ±10 psi). Apply pressure of about 200 psi and check for accuracy.

7. Power off all the equipment and record all function tests.
8. Carefully disconnect the test cable from the portal bulkhead and replace the protective plug to protect the portal connection.

## Running in Hole

## Equipment Assembly

1. The monitoring cable sheave positioning and suspension should be performed as outlined in the standard transport and handling procedures.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Ensure that the cable connector is adequately protected during these operations. Should anything untoward occur during the makeup or hanging of the cable sheave a Megger test of the monitoring cable is recommended.

2. Power cable lifting should be performed as outlined in the standard transport and handling procedures.

## Private

3. Motor installation performed using the alternate lifting method outlined in the standard motor installation procedures.
4. Connect the cable connector and portal bulkhead connection.
- a. Remove the plug from the portal bulkhead and visually inspect the bulkhead and female connector inside.
- b. Remove the shipping cap from Kemlon connector. Place one O-ring and two back-up rings into the groove on the connector body. Lubricate the O-ring with the Krytox Grease.

<!-- image -->

## Note

For O-ring and back up rings installation, ensure that taper surface is always facing the O-ring. If a dot is found on the back up ring, it will be the flat surface. Rotate the scarf cut of back up rings 180° apart from each.

Figure A-8: Back-up rings and O-ring Orientation

<!-- image -->

- c. Insert the Kemlon connector in the gauge portal, aligning the connector keyway with the keyway inside the bulkhead. Be very careful while handling the cable and connector end to avoid placing any bending stresses on either.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Once the key is aligned with the keyway, the Kemlon connector should slide in by hand, don't force the connection.

- d. Apply the Anti-gall threading compound to the secure nut. Thread the nut into the bulkhead with a 1-3/4 in wrench. The torque setting is 45 lbf-ft.
- e. Connect the surface equipment to the end of the monitoring cable.
- f. Power up the surface equipment and confirm gauge functions properly, recording all function test results.

## Testing While RIH

1. After the ESP string is assembled, the gauge should be checked immediately to make sure nothing was damaged or disturbed during the assembly process.
2. Connect the surface equipment to the end of the monitoring cable.
3. Power up the surface equipment and confirm gauge functions properly, recording all function test results.
4. Repeat function test every 20 joints or every hour (whichever comes first) to ensure that the gauge is functioning properly while running into the well.

Figure A-9: Surface Test Gauge

<!-- image -->

## Power Cable Banding

Power cable banding should be performed as outlined in the standard power cable banding procedures. The rig must be centered over the hole to provide adequate clearance for the power cable, monitoring cable, and cable bands/clamps. The monitoring cable should be run alongside of the power cable. This alignment should be checked periodically when running the equipment in the hole.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Always align the monitoring cable besides of the power cable, and secure them by using bands or clamps.

## Landing Tubing Hanger

1. Make up the tubing hanger assembly to the tubing. Make sure the hanger seal is in place first.
2. Determine the length of monitoring cable that will be required between the wellhead and the junction box.
3. Spool off enough cable to cover the span plus an additional 5-ft safety margin.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Do not spool off much more than is required. This will make handling the cable difficult.

4. Cut the cable using tubing cutters.

<!-- image -->

## Note

Cut straight through the cable so that the end is flat. This will make it easier to feed the cable through the tubing hanger.

5. Feed the cut end of the monitoring cable through the hanger until all of the cable is through and the cable is straight and taut.
6. Verify that the Swagelok fitting is in good condition and intact before you start to push it over the monitoring cable.
7. Carefully pull the Swagelok fitting over the monitoring cable. This may be easier to do with the compression nuts opened.
8. Make up the compression fitting to the top of the tubing hanger.
9. Test the gauge again once the hanger landed.

## Remove BOPs and Assemble the Wellhead

1. When the rig crew removes the BOP assembly, make sure the crane lifts the BOPs directly vertical to a height of approximately 2 m.
2. Carefully pull the excess monitoring cable through the BOPs. Try to keep the bending stress on the tubing hangar fitting to a minimum.

## Private

3. Verify that the fitting (Swagelok or Conax) is in good condition and intact.
4. Install the fitting in the corresponding port on the top of the wellhead bonnet. Leave the nut of the fitting opened, this will be easier to feed the cable through.
5. Feed the cable through corresponding port in the bonnet using the same procedure as the tubing hanger.
6. Lower the bonnet onto wellhead flange carefully.
7. After the bonnet has been secured, make up the compression fittings on the top of wellhead bonnet.
8. Perform a gauge function test after the wellhead is connected.
9. Seal of the end of the monitoring cable with tape to avoid moisture entry.
10. Roll up and secure the monitoring cable in a safe place.

## A.1.5 Equipment Retrieval Procedures

Work with the client to ensure that safe working procedures are in place and understood before initiating the retrieval process. Ensure a systematic and controlled method is used to cool the wellhead, production tubing and pumping system.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Major

Potential Loss:

Personnel

Hazard Category:

Fire flammable

Danger

Be aware of the temperature and pressure of the wellhead and piping before loosening any connection. Liquids can easily flash to vapors when the pressure is relieved and cause severe burns.

The difference between the downhole operating temperature and the temperature at the surface is substantial. Procedures must be in place to ensure that the equipment is not 'shocked' by a rapid temperature decrease.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Major

Potential Loss:

Personnel

Hazard Category:

Fire flammable

Before loosening any connection on the pumping unit, make certain the temperature is cool to the touch. If there are pockets of contained liquids under pressure, these could flash to vapors and cause a severe injury.

## A.1.5.1 Motor, Protector, Intake and Pump

The motor, protector, intake and pump are unbolted and handled using the same procedures as a conventional units. Procedural information is provided in the standard pulling equipment from the well procedures.

## A.1.5.2 Pothead

The pothead is unbolted from the motor using the same procedures as a conventional unit. A shipping cap should be placed on the pothead before returning it to the service center. These additional checks should be made:

- Position of conductor tips relative to the pothead bolting face.
- Ensure the gland and the hole is clean and free of scratches.

## A.1.5.3 Cable

The cable should be handled using the same procedures as a conventional cable. Procedural information is provided in the Cables section.

## A.1.6 Servicing and Testing

All Hotline equipment and Hotline550 equipment can be repaired at a Schlumberger Service Center. Special instructions are provided in the following sections to determine whether the equipment can be reused.

## A.1.6.1 Motor

The motor should be tested electrically in the same manner as a conventional motor. The motor can be tested using the Motor Idle Slant Test (MIST) procedure with the following changes.

<!-- image -->

Potential Severity:

Serious

Potential Loss:

Assets

Hazard Category:

Machinery equipment hand tools

Warning

Do not perform a MIST test on a motor filled with Reda No. 7 oil as serious personal injury or equipment damage may occur.

## Private

- The motor shall be drained, then filled and tested using Reda No. 5 oil. Reda No. 5 oil is synthetic oil and will blend best with Reda No. 7 oil. There will be a viscosity reduction.
- The motor must pass the standard MIST test with the Reda No. 5 oil.
- Drain the Reda No. 5 oil immediately after the completion of the test while the motor is still warm. It is preferable to elevate the head and/or hang the motor vertically while draining the oil. It is also preferable to allow the motor to drain for at least 12 hours before refilling.
- Fill the motor with Reda No. 7 oil before shipping.

## A.1.6.2 Protector

There will be more drag during a protector spin test due to the increased viscosity of the fluid. The protector must pass a helium leak test before reuse.

## A.1.6.3 Intake, Pump and Pothead

The intake, pump and pothead are serviced and tested using standard service center procedures.

## A.1.6.4 Cable

The cable is serviced and tested using standard service center procedures. Note that the braid may be carbonized to the point of disintegration for cables that have been installed in high-temperature environments. This should have no impact on the performance of the cable as the braid is used only to aid in the armoring process during fabrication.

## A.2 D8-42 Series Poseidon Multiphase Flow Pump

## A.2.1 Product Description

The presence of free gas in a submersible (centrifugal) pump causes degradation of head and flow performance, up to a level where gas locking occurs. Before now, conventional submersible pumps have not been considered for applications when more than 15% to 25% free gas is present at the pump intake. The D8-42

Poseidon™ multiphase pump is a mechanical pre-conditioner/charge pump, bolted to the base of a submersible pump, which allows the submersible pump to pump fluids with free-gas percentages up to and above 75%.

In high-percentage free-gas applications, significant degradation of head and flow performance occurs in the lower stages of a submersible pump when used with the Poseidon multiphase pump, but gas locking should not occur. The energy transferred to the fluid in these lower stages of the centrifugal pump compresses the gas (head development). Once in the upper stages of the pump, the fluid (with gas compressed) behaves much like a single-phase fluid and pump performance also behaves as though handling single-phase fluids. To attain this level of gas handling requires a submersible pump design that includes bottom stages used to compress the gas that do not add appreciably to net lift.

## A.2.2 Installation

The D8-42 Series Poseidon multiphase pump should always be installed using the standard pump installation procedures. It should always be installed between the intake/gas separator and submersible pump.

The D8-42 Series Poseidon multiphase pump CT version was designed to bolt directly to a D20-60 VGSA, which has a recessed shaft. This required that the end of the D8-42 shaft extend below its base flange. The recessed shaft allows the shaft coupling to be placed below the restricted inside diameter found in the D20-60 VGSA head.

The LT version was designed to be used in applications where gas cannot be vented out the casing.

## Shimming

The D8-42 Series Poseidon utilizes the CR-style (compression ring) thrust design and requires shimming. It should be shimmed so that the bottom impeller thrust washer does not wear into the diffuser down-thrust pad, but instead just contacts the diffuser down-thrust pad. No seal is required between the down-thrust washer and down-thrust pad, as is typical with compression-type submersible pumps.

The average shaft end play of the D8-42 Series Poseidon multiphase pump is only 1/32 inch. It is essential that free shaft rotation is confirmed once the Poseidon multiphase pump is bolted to the intake/gas separator.

## Installation Tools

Poseidon multiphase pumps use standard pump installation tools.

## Private

## A.2.3 Connections

Connection details and part numbers are available in the ALFORM-D connection tables (InTouch ID: 3255850). The D8-42 Series Poseidon Multiphase Flow Pump can be used on 400-series (with DN-3000 stages) and larger pumps. For the 400-series and larger pumps the screw used to bolt it to those pumps must be a hex socket cap screw. For smaller pumps, the hex head cap screw can be used.

## A.2.4 Poseidon Configurations (CT and LT versions)

The Poseidon is available in two configurations: center tandem (CT) and lower tandem (LT). Both versions have the top end of their shafts recessed into the head, like the D20-60 CT AGH. The Poseidon multiphase pump CT version has the bottom end of its shaft extended from its base flange like the 400-series (DN-4300 stages) CT pump. The LT version has an integral intake, and the bottom end of its shaft is flush with the base flange. The recessed shaft in the head of both versions requires long couplings for installation with pumps smaller than the 400-series (DN-4300 stages). See for coupling part numbers.

## A.3 S50-90 Series Poseidon Multiphase Pump

## A.3.1 Product Description

The presence of free gas in a centrifugal pump causes degradation of the head and flow performance. Conventional submergible pumps have not been considered for applications when more than 15% free gas is present at the intake. The S50-90 Series Poseidon multiphase pump is a mechanical pre-conditioner that increases the fluid mixture pressure in order to compress the gas to a point where the fluid can be pumped with a submergible pump. The free-gas bubbles are compressed until their volume decreases to a point where the vapor-to-liquid ratio becomes much smaller. Additional compression above bubblepoint causes the gas to go into solution, further decreasing the vapor volume while increasing the liquid volume. The fluid then begins to behave more like a single-phase fluid.

This technical information release provides information required to install the S50-90 Series Poseidon multiphase pump. The S50-90 Series Poseidon multiphase pump is specifically designed to be used with the higher volume 540and 538-series submergible pumps.

## Private

## A.3.2 Installation

The S50-90 Series Poseidon multiphase pump should be installed using the pump installation procedures provided in the standard pump shimming and installation procedures. It should always be placed between the intake/gas separator and pumps.

The S50-90 Series Poseidon multiphase pump utilizes the CR-style thrust design and requires shimming. Shimming procedures are provided in the standard pump shimming and installation procedures.

## Installation Tools

Poseidon multiphase pumps use standard pump installation tools.

## A.3.3 Connections

Connection details and part numbers are available in the ALFORM-D connection tables (InTouch ID: 3255850).

## A.4 M90-470 Series Poseidon Multiphase Pump

## A.4.1 Product Description

The presence of free gas in a submersible (centrifugal) pump causes degradation of head and flow performance, up to a level where gas locking occurs. Before now, conventional submersible pumps have not been considered for applications when more than 15% to 25% free gas is present at the pump intake. The M90-470 Poseidon™ multiphase pump is a mechanical pre-conditioner/charge pump, bolted to the base of a submersible pump, which allows the submersible pump to pump fluids with free-gas percentages up to and above 75%.

In high-percentage free-gas applications, significant degradation of head and flow performance occurs in the lower stages of a submersible pump when used with the Poseidon multiphase pump, but gas locking should not occur. The energy transferred to the fluid in these lower stages of the centrifugal pump compresses the gas (head development). Once in the upper stages of the pump, the fluid (with gas compressed) behaves much like a single-phase fluid and pump performance also behaves as though handling single-phase fluids. To attain this level of gas handling requires a submersible pump design that includes bottom stages used to compress the gas that do not add appreciably to net lift.

## Private

## A.4.2 Installation

The M90-470 Series Poseidon multiphase pump should always be installed using the pump installation procedures provided in the pump shimming and installation . The M90-470 Poseidon is designed to bolt directly to a 738 series protector. The Poseidon is only available in lower tandem (LT) configuration with integral intake.

## A.4.2.1 Shimming

The M90-470 Series Poseidon utilizes the C-style (compression) design non-factory shimming and requires shimming. It should be shimmed so that the bottom impeller thrust washer does not wear into the diffuser down-thrust pad, but instead just contacts the diffuser down-thrust pad. No seal is required between the down-thrust washer and down-thrust pad, as is typical with compression-type submersible pumps.

The average shaft end play of the M90-470 Series Poseidon multiphase pump is only 1/32 in. It is essential that free shaft rotation is confirmed once the Poseidon multiphase pump is bolted to the protector.

## Installation Tools

Poseidon multiphase pumps use standard pump installation tools.

## A.5 Extended Runlife Protector

## A.5.1 Product Description

The Extended Runlife Protector (also known as Advanced Protector) is a component of the Extended Runlife project. It is a new protector system that will substantially increase runlife in hostile applications.

## Private

The function of the protector is to handle the down-thrust load from the pump section and to act as the compensation section for the pressure-balanced, oil-filled motor. Protector failure or even a small leakage past the seals allows well fluid into the high-voltage motor section which usually results in catastrophic system failure.

The current protectors, when only a single tandem is used, can handle benign environment wells but are in many cases the weak link in the submersible pump system. The use of tandem protectors has eliminated the majority of the system failures that are protector related, however, wells with high bottomhole temperature, wells with a high percentage of H 2 S and wells with high abrasive content are still problematic even for tandem protectors. As such, Extended Runlife Protectors are targeted at the following type wells

- Wells with high bottomhole temperatures The operating temperature limit of existing protectors is 400 degF (204 degC) and is limited by the elastomers used in the protectors. To exceed this limit, the High-Temperature Extended Runlife Protector uses metal bellows to replace elastomer bags and Chemraz™ seals to replace Aflas and HSN seals.
- Wells with high H 2 S For applications with a high percentage (up to 30%) of H 2 S at low-to-moderate temperatures (100 to 300 degF [38 to 150 degC]) the elastomer bag currently being used is ineffective as an H2 S barrier. H2 S can easily migrate through the bag to attack the copper wires and other copper base components inside the protector and motor. The Corrosion-Resistant Extended Runlife Protector uses a metal bellows (Inconel 625 material) to block the migration of the H 2 S.
- Wells with high abrasive content Abrasives in well fluids tend to settle on the top end of the protector where it is connected to the pump intake. Accumulations of abrasives in this area will either directly damage the mechanical shaft seal located there or will damage the adjacent journal bearings that are used to support the shaft seal. The Abrasion-Resistant Extended Runlife Protector uses a new seal body design in conjunction with a shroud to reduce the accumulation of abrasives around the mechanical shaft seal. The Extended Runlife Protector also uses dual-head shaft bearings (shaft sleeves and bushings) made of abrasion-resistant tungsten carbide to reduce bearing wear and improve shaft stability.

Five configurations of the Extended Runlife Protector have been developed and are available to address runlife issues in the hostile well conditions noted above. The various configurations are shown in Table A-10. Table nomenclature is defined in the last table row. Technical features are shown in Table A-11. ## A.5.2 Health, Safety and Environment

This section reviews the manufacturing and field handling procedures and the potential hazards shop and field service personnel may experience while assembling, testing, installing, pulling and dismantling an Extended Runlife Protector.

## A.5.2.1 HSE summary

The Extended Runlife Protector has undergone independent HSE reviews by SRC and BPC engineering, manufacturing and QHSE personnel. The findings of the review are

- No hazardous materials such as radioactive or explosive materials are used in any of the Extended Runlife Protectors.
- No electrical components are used in any of the Extended Runlife Protectors.
- No high-pressure components are used in any of the Extended Runlife Protectors.
- Only normal wellbore temperatures are experienced in the Extended Runlife Protectors.
- All of the Extended Runlife Protectors contain hydraulic oil and require normal hygiene precautions.

- The Extended Runlife Protectors can be heavy. Manual lifting is not recommended. Standard lifting methods are provided in the Wellsite Procedures section.

## A.5.2.3 Assembly

## Quality

All material handling shall be performed in accordance with QAD 3054. General assembly shall follow QAI and TI 3019 Assembly Quality Plans.

## Private

- Oil All current motor fluid used in protectors is considered nonhazardous.
- Thread lube Current lubrication used on housings and head, base and body threads is food grade and is considered nonhazardous.
- Loctite® Thread locking chemicals are considered nonhazardous.
- Teflon® tape Nonhazardous.
- Bellows The bellows are constructed of Inconel 625. This material is already common within the system and not considered hazardous.

## Safety

- Handling and lifting During the course of assembly, several awkward and/or heavy components will require lifting. The most notable of these is the housing and the assembled unit. In each case, lifting should be done with a lifting sling and a hoist in accordance with MPI 57101.
- Other heavy items such as the head, base and shaft should be lifted and transported using proper stepping, handling and lifting procedures.
- When possible all shop transport of long heavy objects should be done using a housing dolly.
- Making up joints Protector joints are routinely tightened to only 200 ft-lbf. Appropriate documentation and tooling is available and in place.

## A.5.2.4 Final test

## Quality

Standard protector test parameters and procedures will apply except for the following:

- Valve pressure setting An increase from 10 psi to 20 psi requires a change in the testing procedure for both the individual valve and the top-level assembly after the valve is installed. (See QAI 2013.)
- Metal bellows A pressure and vacuum test needs to be performed on the bellows.

## Safety

- Lifting for test Lifting should be done with a lifting sling and a hoist in accordance with MPI 57101.

## Private

- Pinch points When making flange to flange connections, keep fingers clear while mating the units.

## A.5.2.5 Shipping

## Quality

All material handling should be performed in accordance with QAD 3054. Boxing and/or loading of equipment should be done in accordance with MAT-B019.

## Safety

The protector should not be lifted by hand. Lifting of the unit either for loading in a shipping box or loading onto a truck shall be done with a hoist and sling in accordance with MPI 57101 or with a forklift in accordance with QAD 3054.

## A.5.2.6 Equipment installation

## Quality

The unit installation and wellsite procedures will be in accordance with current practices. Unit flange bolts will be tightened in accordance with the torque requirements in ED-119.

## Safety

- Lifting This unit should not be lifted by hand. All lifting clamps shall be used in accordance with FSB 119/rd and lifting should be performed in accordance with procedures provided in the Wellsite Procedures section.

## A.5.6 Installation Procedures

## A.5.6.1 Transport and handling

Transport and handling procedures for the Extended Runlife Protector are provided in the Wellsite Procedures section.

## A.5.6.2 Equipment preparation

Equipment preparation procedures for the Extended Runlife Protector are provided in the Wellsite Procedures section.

## A.5.6.3 Lifting clamp installation

Lifting clamp installation procedures for the Extended Runlife Protector are provided in the Wellsite Procedures section.

## A.5.6.4 Protector installation

Protector assembly procedures for the Extended Runlife Protector are provided in the Wellsite Procedures section.

## A.5.6.5 Shimming procedures

Extended Runlife Protectors are equipped with a factory-shimmed shaft; all Extended Runlife Protector shafts are shimmed at the manufacturing facility. Shaft-to-flange dimensions of the protector and the connecting equipment shall be rechecked at the wellsite. Apply shims when necessary. Shimming procedures (including dimension measurement) for the Extended Runlife Protector are provided in the Wellsite Procedures section.

## A.5.6.6 Oil filling procedures

Protectors are filled with oil prior to shipment from the manufacturing facility. Typically, some oil is lost during field installation and refilling the protector is required. Oil refilling procedures at the wellsite are provided in the Wellsite Procedures section.

## A.5.6.7 Running equipment in the wellbore

Run procedures for the Extended Runlife Protector are provided in the Wellsite Procedures section.

## A.5.6.8 Pulling equipment from the wellbore

Pull procedures for the Extended Runlife Protector are provided in the Wellsite Procedures section.

Perform a visual inspection of the protector for physical damage and missing parts before installation.

## A.5.10 Rerun Procedures

Extended Runlife Protectors should not be rerun in a well after being pulled. All pulled Extended Runlife Protectors should be sent to an Artificial Lift Service Center for disassembly, inspection and reassembly before being returned to service.

## A.6 VGSA Product Update for Abrasive Applications

## A.6.1 VGSA Product Update for Abrasive Applications

## A.6.1.1 Summary

The VGSA design has changed to improve performance in abrasive applications.

## A.6.1.2 Details

The stainless steel liners and compression tubes are being upgraded to a white iron material for all VGSA products. GeMs records are updated to reflect the changes. Manufacturing has qualified one vendor for the white iron components and is in the process of qualifying a second vendor.

The list of affected liners and compression tubes is shown in Table A-22.

Table A-22: VGSA Affected Liners and Compression Tubes

|   Current Stainless Steel Part Number |   Replacement White Iron Part Number | Description                        |   Quantity |
|---------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|------------------------------------|------------|
|                               2003123 |                            100109890 | Liner, D20-60                      |          2 |
|                               2003128 |                            100109887 | Comp Tube, 400, D20-60             |          1 |
|                               1307784 |                            100109896 | Liner S20-90                       |          1 |
|                               1297472 |                            100109899 | Liner S70-150                      |          2 |
|                               1307792 |                            100109892 | Comp Tube, 538, S20-90 and S70-150 |          1 |

## A.6.1.3 Reason

Testing was performed on a D20-60 VGSA in response to a SQI submitted by WCP-AL operations. In the SQI, seven VGSA units showed excessive erosion of the stainless steel liner that extended through to the structural housing. In two of the seven units, the structural housings were severed which resulted in the lower parts of the units falling into the wellbore. Sand production rates varied from 300 to 750 ppm in these applications.

Engineering testing confirmed the white iron liner is superior to the existing stainless steel liner in abrasive conditions.

## A.6.1.4 Action

Based on test results, the engineering recommendation is to replace existing stainless steel liners with white iron liners in all VGSA units for new product sales. The bearing support material also changes from Ni-Resist to abrasion/corrosion resistant 5530 to increase the erosion resistance and improve the reliability of the VGSA in long-run abrasive applications. These changes are effective immediately for products ordered from the Bartlesville or Singapore product centers.

It is the responsibility of the field to determine if existing VGSA units in the field need to be upgraded to the latest design. Section 1.5 shows part numbers and descriptions for components required to upgrade existing VGSA units for abrasive service. The current VGSA units with stainless steel liners will work in applications where the sand production rate is less than 250 ppm.

For VGSA units that are installed in highly abrasive applications (greater than 250 ppm sand content), the use of silicon carbide bearings (ES-SS) is recommended to reduce the radial wear and further improved system reliability. Table A-23 can be used as a guideline for selecting a VGSA for abrasive applications.

## B Logging Bypass Section

## B.1 Introduction

## B.1.1 Description and Operation

The Logging By-pass System is a solution to enable intervention or logging with wireline or coiled tubing below an electrical submersible pump (ESP) without the need for workover

The junction in the bypass system is created by a standard or an Auto Y-Tool, which aligns the axis of the bypass tubing with the axis of the production tubing above, thus creating an intervention conduit to below the ESP.

By-pass tubing is clamped to the ESP. The ESP discharge fluid enters the tubing string through the eccentric leg of the Y-Tool and is prevented from re-circulating down the bypass tubing by either a diverter in an 'Auto Y-Tool', or by a blanking plug in a 'Standard Y-Tool'.

Wireline and Coiled Tubing plugs are available to enable intervention work to be carried out below the ESP under either static or dynamic conditions.

Figure B-1: Logging Bypass System

<!-- image -->

## B.2 Available Sizes

Bypass systems are available for an extensive range of casing sizes and weights. The size (OD) of the bypass tubing which can be accommodated for a given application is a function of the casing drift ID, and the ESP OD (Series). In standard logging bypass systems, the bypass tubing typically has a flush joint connection, so as to maximize the tubing OD, within the available casing space.

Table B-1 lists the possible flush joint bypass tubing sizes for some typical casing sizes.

## Private

## Applications

- Wireline logging below the pump
- Coiled tubing logging below the pump
- Retrieval of plugs below the pump
- Memory gauge deployment below the pump
- Back-up pump deployment on bypass tubing
- Bridge plug setting for water shutoff
- Tubing-conveyed perforating gun deployment and detonation below the pump
- Well stimulation through coiled tubing or by-pass tubing
- Wireline perforating below the pump
- Bottomhole samples deployment

## B.3.1 Elastomers

Where applicable the bypass system equipment is available with a choice of Viton or Aflas elastomers with Durometer 90 hardness.

## B.4 Standard Y-Tool Bypass Systems

The Y-Tool is supplied as a part of an assembled, pressure tested sub assembly ready for use in the field; see Y-Tool Sub Assemblies.

The junction in the Bypass System is created by the Y-tool, which aligns the axis of the bypass tubing with the axis of the production tubing above, and thus creates an intervention conduit to below the ESP.

The standard Y-Tool requires a Blanking Plug to be set in the telescopic swivel nipple to prevent recirculation of the production fluids down the bypass tubing.

Where intervention work is required in a bypass system with a standard Y-Tool, the Blanking Plug must first be retrieved.

Y-Tools are available to suit a range of casing sizes (7 in, 7-5/8 in, 9-5/8 in, 10-3/4 in).

## B.5 Auto Y-Tool Bypass Systems

The Auto Y-Tool is supplied as a part of an assembled, pressure tested sub assembly ready for use in the field; see Y-Tool Sub Assemblies.

## Private

The junction in the Bypass System is created by the Auto Y-tool, which aligns the axis of the bypass tubing with the axis of the production tubing above, and thus creates an intervention conduit to below the ESP.

The Auto Y-Tool has an internal diverter, which seals over the bypass tubing when the ESP is operating to prevent recirculation, and automatically closes over the ESP discharge leg when the ESP is shut down, to allow intervention access through the bypass tubing. The function of the diverter replaces the Blanking Plug which is required in a Standard Y-Tool.

Where intervention work is required in a bypass system with a standard Y-Tool, the Blanking Plug must first be retrieved. In a bypass system with an Auto Y-Tool this is not necessary.

Y-Tools are available to suit a range of casing sizes (7 in, 7-5/8 in, 9-5/8 in, 10-3/4 in).

## B.6 Logging Bypass System and Optional Accessories

## B.6.1 Y-Tool Sub Assembly

The Y-Tool is supplied as a part of an assembled, torqued and pressure tested sub assembly ready for use in the field. The Y-Tool Sub Assemblies (standard or Auto) are supplied with the following:

| Term                          | Definition                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Handling Sub                  | This is available with a choice of connection for field make up. Additional crossovers can also be supplied to suit alternative production tubing threads. |
| Top Nipple Profile (Optional) | This accepts a Standing Valve for pressure testing tubing or is required in order to use an Isolation Tool                                                 |
| Y-Tool                        | Standard or Auto Y-Tool body. A cable clip is included to secure the MLE.                                                                                  |
| Pump Sub                      | For connection to ESP discharge head. Available with a choice of connection.                                                                               |
| Telescopic Swivel Nipple      | Available with a choice of seal bore sizes to accept bypass plugs, and a choice of bypass tubing connections.                                              |

## Private

Blanking plugs are available with Lantern collets, or with a locking facility for use in free flowing wells.

## B.6.1.1 Additional Features

- PMJ thread is used for inter connecting on 9-5/8 in systems.

## Private

- Y-Tool body has AISI 410 22RC Metallurgy as standard
- Available with Low alloy steel or 13Cr for the remaining Y-tool sub assembly components.
- Available for 9-5/8 in, 7-5/8 in and 7 in casing.
- Selection of elastomers.
- 2-3/8 in or 2-7/8 in PTJ bypass tubing connections as standard for 9-5/8 in Systems.
- Y-Tool comes with an MLE Cable Clip fitted to one side as standard.
- An additional cable clip is required for the opposite side of the Y-Tool for applications with additional service lines, i.e. chemical injection lines. This is available separately (p/n 100238282).

## B.6.1.2 Handling

The Y-Tool sub assembly is supplied as an assembled, torqued and pressure tested assembly ready to be used at the well site.

It is recommend to drift the Y-Tool sub assembly as part of pre-job checks. The drift size will depend on either the bypass tubing size, or the teleswivel seal bore diameter (whichever is smaller).

The Y-Tool sub assembly can be picked up on the rig using 3-1/2 in side door (square shoulder) elevators fitted to the 3-1/2 in handling sub. B-1 See Figure B-4.

## B.6.2 Bypass Tubing

The Phoenix Taper Joint (PTJ) thread is the standard connection manufactured on the bypass tubing. The thread can be used on standard bypass systems or on more specialized bypass completions that require a structural and pressure tight bypass tubing thread B-2 .

For Standard Logging Bypass Systems the bypass tubing is supplied in 15 ft lengths, and can be made up to its optimum torque without the need to use power tongs. Some special applications may require joints of specific lengths, and the use of power tongs to perform make ups.

Swivel lifting nubbins should be used to pick up and handle the bypass tubing joints. These are available to suit the bypass tubing size and thread.

B-2. Although PTJ can be used for some specialist applications, alternative threads may still require to be used in some cases. This will be dependant on individual application requirements.

Figure B-5: PTJ Bypass Tubing

<!-- image -->

## B.6.2.1 Features and Benefits

- Robust structural and pressure tight connection that can be made up to shoulder without the need to use power tongs
- 2.875 in 6.4 lb/ft and 2.375 in 4.6 lb/ft tubing sizes (Standard 9-5/8 in sizes)
- L80 Type 1 or L80 Type 13Cr Metallurgy
- Flush joint connection for maximum clearance
- Hooked thread design to provide maximum joint strength
- Primary Metal to metal nose seal

## Private

- Secondary metal to metal external seal
- External torque shoulder to prevent back off and over torque of the connection.

## B.6.3 Universal Bypass Clamp

The Schlumberger bypass clamps are fitted to each Electrical Submersible Pump (ESP) neck in logging bypass completions. B-3

The clamp also serves to secure and protect cables and lines passing the ESP.

B-3. Bypass clamps should not be fitted directly below an intake. Where a bolt on intake will be used, the clamp can be fitted above. Where an integral intake is used, the clamp should be omitted.

For the most common 9-5/8 in casing applications, a universal bypass clamp is used. The universal clamp has adjustment to enable it to be fitted to a range of ESP necks. Two types of universal clamps are available to suit either 2-3/8 in or 2-7/8 in bypass tubing. Additional inserts are available for the 2-7/8 in clamp to convert it to smaller bypass tubing sizes.

The Universal Bypass clamp includes slots to secure 2 x ¼ in control lines, 2 x 3/8 in control lines, and 2 x universal cable clips (one each side). Each universal clips can secure an MLE or flatpack with dimensions ranging from 0.400 in x 1.750 in to 0.610 in x 1.750 in (width x depth).

Individual ESP neck bypass clamps are available for those applications for which the universal clamp cannot be used.

## B.6.4 Wireline Re-Entry Guide

The Wireline Re-Entry Guide (WEG) is made up to the end of the bypass tubing. The purpose of the WEG is to ensure the logging string passes freely back into the bypass tubing upon retrieval.

WEGs are available to suit the bypass tubing thread and size. Two types of WEG are available, 'Plain', and 'Finned'.

## Private

The finned WEG should be used when the bypass tubing tailpipe is to enter a lower liner or when stabbing past a sharp profile. Finned WEGs can be supplied in various ODs to suit the liner in these applications.

Both Plain and Finned WEGs are available in AISI 4140 Rc 18-22 (low alloy carbon steel), or AISI 420 Rc 18-22 (13Cr Stainless Steel) Metallurgy.

## B.6.5 Motor Base Plug

The Motor Base Plug can be made up to the base of the ESP assembly (or Gauge) to provide an additional location for an MLE or bypass clamp. The motor base plug should be used in situations where there is no lower neck profile on the base of the lower motor. Single section or lower tandem motors typically do not have a lower neck. The motor base plug should also be used where a 'long' ESP gauge is fitted to base of the motor.

## Private

The Motor Base Plug has a 2-3/8 in EUE pin connection for make up to a REDA motor base or gauge assembly. The plugs are available with different ODs to match the ESP motor series.

Universal bypass damp will fit to any REDA 456-562 Motor Base plug and any Centrilift 456-544 Motor Base plug.

## B.6.6 Blanking Plug - Lantern

The Blanking Plug is seated in the telescopic swivel nipple seal bore profile immediately below the Y-Tool. The plug prevents re-circulation of the produced fluids down the bypass tubing when the ESP is operating.

The plug can either be run pre-installed in the nipple, or set by slickline after installation to prevent fluids passing through the pump. The blanking plug with lantern collets is deployed and retrieved by standard slickline tools.

Upon retrieval of the plug, ports are opened which allows and hydrostatic pressure above to be equalized.

The blanking plug with lantern collets is not suitable when deployment on coiled tubing is necessary, or where the well can naturally free flow.

- Supplied as part of standard Y-Tool Sub-Assembly
- Prevents recirculation of production fluids down the bypass tubing during ESP operation.
- 3000 psi Maximum pressure from above
- Available in various sizes to suit the telescopic swivel nipple seal bore size.
- Top No-Go
- AISI 420 18-22 Rc/AISI 63017-4 PH Metallurgy
- Viton or Aflas Elastomers
- Redress kits available separately.

## B.6.7 Blanking Plug - Locking

The Blanking Plug is seated in the telescopic swivel nipple seal bore profile immediately below the Y-Tool. The plug prevents recirculation of the produced fluids down the bypass tubing when the ESP is operating.

The plug can either be run pre-installed in the nipple, or set by slickline after installation to prevent fluids passing through the pump. The blanking plug with lock is deployed and retrieved by standard slickline tools, or can be deployed using coiled tubing.

Upon retrieval of the plug, ports are opened which allows and hydrostatic pressure above to be equalized.

The blanking plug with lock should be used when deployment on coiled tubing is necessary or where the well can naturally free flow.

## B.6.8 PL Blanking Plug

- Base plug design that can be dressed for 2.312-in nipple sizes upwards by changing out Vee-rings, no-go, seal spacers (Dress Kit), and lock nut only (makes holding stock easier for field and manufacturing)
- Simple low cost locking plug design (6 main parts which don't change between seal sizes), which can be used for free flowing wells removing the option of choosing either lantern collet and locking plug designs (current options)
- Fast equalising
- Shear down to set, shear up to release using 2-in JDC running/pulling tool (CAMCO P/N 15156)
- No restriction when pulling out of hole in the unset position (collets fully close in both directions whether unset or set)
- Fits existing nipples
- Uses same dressing kit as PL Wireline Plug and PL Standing Valve
- Debris seal for cleaning / protecting nipple seal area
- Aflas seals as standard

## B.6.9 Standing Valve

The Standing Valve is used in conjunction with the Top Nipple situated above the Y-Tool. The Standing Valve can be landed in the nipple against a full column of fluid and is used to pressure test the production tubing string to surface, or for setting of a hydraulic packer.

The standing valve can be run in hole installed in the Top Nipple, if required, saving a wireline run. The Standing valve has an internal ball valve which will allow any pressure below the valve to equalize.

Figure B-12: Standing Valve

- Viton or Aflas Elastomers

## B.6.11 Isolation Tool

The Isolation Tool can be deployed in all standard bypass systems which are equipped with a Top Nipple.

The plug has two sets of seals and straddles the seal bores of the Top Nipple and Teleswivel Nipple. The plug has a through bore to allow bullheading or injection fluids to be injected through the bypass tubing, while fully isolating the ESP.

The plug can also be used in dual ESP bypass systems, where the flow rate may be too low for the Auto Y-Tool. The plug creates a flow path past the back up ESP, preventing recirculation. Locking plugs are available for this application.

Figure B-13: Isolation Tool

<!-- image -->

## Private

## B.6.11.1 Features and Benefits

- Fully isolates the ESP during bull-heading/injection of fluids through production tubing
- Prevents unnecessary pump wear (wind-milling)
- Available in various sizes to suit the Top Nipple and Telescopic Swivel Nipple seal bores.
- Available with Locking Option where flow may be seen from below to above.
- Can be deployed and retrieved with slickline using standard Otis GS tools. Locking type can also be run on Coiled Tubing.
- AISI 420 ST/ST Rc 18-22 Metallurgy.
- Viton or Aflas Elastomers
- Redress kits available separately

## B.6.12 Wireline Logging Plug

The Wireline Logging Plug can be deployed in all standard bypass systems. The plug allows wireline strings to be suspended beneath the ESP through the bypass tubing.

The plug seals between the telescopic swivel nipple bore and the wireline outside diameter enabling wireline work to be carried out under both dynamic and static conditions.

Wireline grapples are required for seating wireline logging plugs. The grapple is made up to the wire at the same distance above the tool string, as the distance between the zone to be logged and the Y-Tool. When the logging tool sting is on depth, the grapple lands on top of the W/L plug. The grapple ensures the W/L plug remains seated as the pump is switched on. When the pump is running the logging string can be moved up and down to log as required.

Inserts for the cable grapple and flow tubes for the logging plugs are ordered separately to suit the wireline/slickline diameter.

Grapples are not required for the Self-seating logging plugs as wireline tractors deploy these.

- Enables dynamic logging using wireline with an ESP

- Available in various sizes to suit the Telescopic Swivel Nipple seal bore
- Available with Tool String Catcher Facility
- Interchangeable flow tubes to suit various wire sizes
- Available in self seating option for deviated wells with the use of a wireline tractor.
- AISI 630 17-4 PH Stainless Steel Metallurgy
- Viton or Aflas Elastomers
- Redress kits available separately.

## B.6.14 Coiled Tubing Logging Plug

The Coiled Tubing Logging Plug can be deployed in all standard by-pass systems. The plug allows Coiled Tubing stings to be suspended beneath the ESP through the bypass tubing.

The plug seals between the telescopic swivel nipple bore and the Coiled Tubing outside diameter, enabling Coiled Tubing work to be carried out under both dynamic and static conditions.

The plug can be used for various combinations of coiled tubing strings and telescopic swivel nipple size.

It has been utilized successfully in the past for clean out operations, production-logging runs and also as a means of running downhole samplers below the ESP's on horizontal reservoir sections.

Figure B-15: Coiled Tubing Logging Plug

<!-- image -->

## Private

## B.6.14.1 Features and Benefits

- Enables dynamic logging using Coiled Tubing with an ESP
- No need to pull the completion to perform Coiled Tubing work
- Available in various sizes to suit the Telescopic Swivel Nipple seal bore.
- Available to suit different Coiled Tubing ODs and wall thickness
- AISI 630 17-4 PH ST/ST Rc 28-33 Metallurgy
- Viton or Aflas Elastomers
- Redress kits available separately

## B.6.14.2 Coiled Tubing Sizes

The maximum coiled tubing size which can be used (for logging) is dependant on seal bore size of the coiled tubing plug and teleswivel, and the bypass tubing size. Table B-28 andTable B-29 show the maximum CT sizes for 2-3/8 in and 2-7/8 in bypass tubing.

## B.6.14.3 Coiled Tubing Plug Connectors

Coiled tubing plug connectors are required to attach the coiled tubing plug to the coil, and a crossover is required to make up to the tool string. The required parts are:

## Private

## 1. Roll-On Connector.

This is connected directly to the coil. The roll-on connector will be specified to match the CT size and wall thickness. The roll-on connector is formed onto the coiled tubing and will require to be replaced between operations.

## 2. Sleeve B-6

The sleeve makes up to the roll-on connector and has a profile to accept the coiled tubing plug retaining sleeve. This is specified by CT size

## 3. Crossover

The crossover makes up to the sleeve. Crossovers are specified by CT size and by the different connections to make up to the coiled tubing tool string

## B.6.15 Handling Equipment

Specialist handling equipment is available to assist safe installation of the logging bypass system. The handling equipment for a bypass system consists of:

1. Swivel Lift Nubbin
2. Safety Clamp
3. Stove Pipe (ESP/ Bypass worktable)

## B.6.15.1 Swivel Lift Nubbin

The swivel lift nubbin is used to handle and pick up the joints of bypass tubing. The swivel lift nubbin has a pin thread for making up to the tubing, and a swivel shackle for attaching to the tugger line/air winch. It is recommended that two swivel lift nubbins be available at the well site. This will allow one to be in use on the rig floor, and one made up to the next bypass joint required saving time.

Swivel lift nubbins are available in different threads and sizes to match the bypass tubing.

## Private

For specialist applications where the weight of the bypass tubing string exceeds load rating of the standard swivel lift nubbin, an alternative design is used which fits into 3-1/2 in side door elevators to support the string weight.

The standard Swivel lift nubbin is rated to 8960 lb (2-3/8 in and 2-7/8 in versions).

## B.6.15.2 Safety Clamp

The safety clamp is designed to secure the bypass tubing, while alongside the ESP assembly. This enables subsequent bypass tubing joint make ups. The clamp rests on the stovepipe and supports the weight of the bypass tubing string. Clamps are available to suit the various bypass tubing ODs.

For specialist applications where the weight of the bypass tubing string exceeds load rating of the standard safety clamp, alternative designs are used which can support higher tensile loads.

## Private

The standard Safety Clamp B-7 , uses 'die' type inserts to achieve a load rating of 44,800 lb (2-3/8 in and 2-7/8 in versions).

## B.6.15.3 Stove Pipe (ESP/ Bypass worktable)

The stovepipe is a worktable designed for the installation of ESP bypass systems. The stovepipe is positioned over the rotary table and is used as a work platform to land the ESP lifting clamps and bypass tubing safety clamp between make ups.

The standard stovepipe has a 7 in profile to allow up to 675 series ESP equipment and is rated to 22,400 lb.

For specialist applications where the weight of the string exceeds load rating of the standard stovepipe, alternative designs are used which can support higher tensile loads.

## B.7 ESP Bypass System Installation Procedure

## B.7.1 Overview

The following procedures apply to the installation of a Generic SPPC By-Pass System.

As these procedures are generic only, consideration should be made for the exact configuration of the individual ESP and bypass assembly. The procedures should be reviewed and modification may be necessary.

## B.7.1.1 Responsibilities

It is the responsibility of the testing engineer to ensure that all relevant permits are in place and that concerned parties are notified of any work being undertaken.

It is the responsibility of the testing engineer to ensure that any problems encountered are documented and submitted in Quest. The product center should be notified of any problems related to bypass equipment quality.

## B.7.1.2 Safety

Toolboxes, A-Frames with control lines etc. should be laid out on the rig floor so as not to pose a hazard to personnel.

Tools should be kept clean and in the Toolbox when not in use. Damaged or worn tools should not be used.

Hand tools should be tied off to avoid the potential of objects being lost downhole.

An on-site risk assessment should be carried out prior to commencing any work on the installation of any equipment. Any generic risk assessments used should be reviewed to reflect job specific hazards and risks.

A toolbox talk should be held prior to commencement of the installation to brief all involved parties on the operation of installing the bypass equipment.

## B.7.2 Special Handling Equipment

Table B-40: Special Handling Equipment
